title: Esophagus
html:
Anatomy

Pharyngeal-esophageal junction (with upper esophageal sphincter) to cardia (with lower esophageal sphincter)

UES = cricopharyngeal muscle and lower pharyngeal sphincter fibres (has minimal resistance area → Killian triangle → Zenker diverticulum)

Length: 18-26 cm; C5-T11

Cervical contact: trachea, spine, carotid arteries, thyroid gland

Thoracic contact: trachea, aortic arch, tracheal junction

Abdominal segment: left hepatic lobe and caudal lobe, gastric fornix, diaphragm and aorta Enters abdomen through esophageal hiatus → connects to diaphragm through phrenoesophageal ligament (Leimer Bertelli)

Arterial supply

Cervical → inferior thyroid a.

Thoracic → intercostals, aorta, bronchial a.

Abdominal → left gastric, lower left phrenic and splenic a.

Venous drainage

Upper segment → SVC

Middle segment → Azygos v.

Lower segment → Gastric v.

Lymphatic drainage

No segmental nature → rapid lymphatic metastasis

Metastasis often found in the lesser curvature

Nerves

Parasympathetic - vagus nerve or through branches of (lower) recurrent laryngeal nerve Plexus with sympathetic fibres emerges from the cervical sympathetic ganglia Lower third esophagus - vagal trunks rotate clockwise and become frontal vagus (left) and distal vagus (right) plexus

Histology

Stratified non-keratinous epithelium

Continued by cylindrical epithelium at esogastrical junction

Junction btw. them = Z line

Inner circular muscle layer

Outer longitudinal muscle layer

Congenital malformations: atresia, esotracheal fistula, stenosis and duplications

Paraclinical

1. Barium enema (not routinely used anymore)

2. Esophagoscopy (allows biopsy!)

3. Manometry

4. Esophageal pH-metry

Common clinical element – esophageal snd

Dysphagia

  • Discomfort or impossibility to swallow
  • Incomplete = only for solids
  • Complete = for solids and fluids + regurgitation
  • Paradoxal = for liquids and absent in solids = achalasia
  • Progressive, continuous and rapid evolution = esophageal cancer
  • Minimal dysphagia, discomfort with temporary pain = initial stages of esophageal disorders
  • Can eventually affect the nutrition state

Regurgitation/ Reflux

  • Involuntary retrograde flow into oral cavity
  • Occurs with dilation of an esophageal segment → volume of regurgitation increases with increased dilation
  • Reduced in esophageal cancer and important in advanced achalasia
  • Can cause respiratory complications of gastric content speeds into respiratory tree Pain

Cervical, dorsal, retrosternal and epigastric pain

Due to reflux or esophagitis (stasis in dilated segment → infection → inflammations and ulcerations of mucosa)

Esophageal cancer is pain free for extended periods

Sialorrhoea

  • Reflux of abundant oral salivary secretion
  • Result of esophageal stenosis → disables deglutition of saliva
  • Accentuated by high volume secreted through vagal reflex stimulation

1. Corrosive esophagitis (post-caustic) (not in presentation)

  • By ingestion of caustic substances (acids, bases, salts)
  • ➔ Strong acids = coagulation necrosis → transmural necrosis rarely
  • ➔ Bases = liquefying necrosis → can erode entire wall, less pain during ingestion → higher intake
  • Stages: necrosis → inflammation → granulation tissue → scarring → stenosis

Clinically

  • Shock → intense pain
  • Dysphagia
  • Sialorrhea
  • Odynophagia
  • Hoarseness
  • Dyspnea
  • Stridor
  • Later: fever, mediastinitis (→ perforation)

Diagnosis

  • Sample of vomited liquid
  • X-ray thorax/ abdomen → mediastinitis
  • Endoscopy (stopped in necrotic area → risk of perforation) → used to place a stent in stenosis
  • Barium is reserved for stenosis, iodine contrast in perforation

Complications

  • Perforation → mediastinitis, peritonitis → prognosis
  • Laryngeal edema (→ tracheostomy)
  • Stenosis → high risk of cancer

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids → not generally recommended; if hoarseness, stridor, dyspnea; prevents stenosis; can mask mediastinitis/ peritonitis
  • Penicillamine (synthetic collagen inhibitor) → not yet recommended
  • Esophagectomy with esophagoplasty in severe stenosis and to prevent cancer

2. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

  • Normal physiological phenomenon experienced intermittently by most people, particularly after a meal
  • GERD = amount of gastric juice that refluxes exceeds normal limit → symptoms with or without associated esophageal mucosal injury (ie. esophagitis)
  • GERD = all symptoms produced by gastroesophageal reflux
  • LES - normal length and pressure, normal transient relaxation (relaxation in absence of swallowing)
  • GEJ - located in abdomen (positive pressure), length of abdominal esophagus must be 1-2.5 cm, Hiss angle
  • Diaphragmatic crura/ esophageal hiatus = extrinsic/ external sphincter
  • Esophageal clearance must be able to neutralize acid refluxed trough LES
  • a) Mechanical clearance = esophageal peristalsis
  • b) Chemical clearance = saliva
  • Stomach empties properly

Pathophysiology

  • Functional (frequent transient LES relaxation) or mechanical problem of LES is most common cause
  • Certain foods (coffee, alcohol), medications (calcium channel blockers, nitrates, beta-blockers), hormones (progesterone) can decrease pressure of LES
  • Obesity, pregnancy, ascites, coughing (rise of intraabdominal pressure)
  • Smoking
  • Surgical interventions on the stomach: gastrectomy, vagotomy, Heller operation
  • Hiatal hernia → 50% of patients with age HH have reflux

Type 1

= gliding hiatal hernia (axial); when GEJ rises above the diaphragm

Type 2

= rolling hiatal hernia (para-esophageal); with the GEJ under the diaphragm and the important tuberosity reached though the lateral-esophageal hiatus Type 3

  • Cardio-esophageal malpositions

Typical symptoms

  • Pyrosis/ Heartburn: most common; postprandial, after effort and when lying down
  • Regurgitation: effortless return; sour or bitter taste
  • Dysphagia: mechanical stricture or functional problem

Atypical symptoms

  • Coughing, wheezing: aspiration of gastric content, vagal reflex produces bronchio-construction
  • Damage to lungs (pneumonia, asthma, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis)
  • Vocal cords, hoarseness (laryngitis, cancer): especially in the morning
  • Ear (otitis media)
  • Teeth (enamel decay)
  • Chest pain: reflux, might resemble MI → ECG and cardiac enzymes

Alarm symptoms

  • Weight loss, dysphagia, anemia, upper digestive hemorrhage

Esophagitis

  • s. oben classification
  • Barrett esophagus = chronic reflux of gastric juice into esophagus → squamous epithelium of esophagus is replaced by intestinal columnar epithelium → 8-15% develop adenocarcinoma Savary-Miller classification of reflux esophagitis (only remember grade 4)

Grade 1 Non-confluent erosions

Grade 2 Multiple, confluent, non-circumferential erosions

Grade 3 Confluent erosions involving the whole circumference of the esophagus Grade 4 Complications: ulcer, stenosis, Barrett´s esophagus (BE)

Complications

  • Esophageal stenosis
  • BE
  • Esophageal ulcer + ulcer perforation
  • Upper GI hemorrhage

Prognosis

  • Good, but patients daily life affected

Diagnosis

→ Based on typical symptoms + confirmation with paraclinical examinations 1. pH-metry (pH < 4 for 5 min at least 3x in 24h); correlation between symptoms and episodes of reflux; patients with endoscopy confirmed esophagitis do not need pH monitoring

Indications

  • Persistence of symptoms while taking adequate antisecretory therapy, such as proton pump inhibitor therapy
  • Recurrence of symptoms after discontinuation of acid-reducing medications
  • Investigation of atypical symptoms, such as chest pain or asthma, in patients without esophagitis
  • Confirmation of the diagnosis in preparation for anti-reflux surgery

2. Manometry: LES < 10 mmHg and peristalsis

3. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy: presence and severity of esophagitis/ Barrett’s esophagus, exclusion of other diseases (e.g., peptic ulcer)

4. Chest X-ray: retrocardiac air bubble in hernia

5. Barium swallow: presence and location of strictures, type and shape of hernia

6. Scintigarphy

DD by endoscopy with biopsy or therapeutic test with nitrites and omeprazole

  • Esophagitis
  • Achalasia
  • Cancer
  • Diffuse esophageal spasm
  • Esophageal diverticulum
  • Functional heartburn = classic heartburn but normal upper digestive endoscopy (including biopsies); without changes in investigations; affects women more; associated with other functional gastrointestinal disorders and psychological comorbidities; treatment - neuromodulators and psychological counseling
  • Hypersensitive esophagus = functional; gastroesophageal reflux within normal limits (normal pH-metry), but positive correlation between physiological episodes of reflux and heartburn; more often women; often with other functional disorders (dyspepsia, non-cardiac chest pain, IBS); treated with esophageal neuromodulators (TCA, SSRI), surgical anti-reflux treatment important

Treatment

1. Disappearance/ alleviation of symptoms

2. Reduction/ disappearance of esophagitis

3. Prevention/ complications: stenosis, dysphagia, BE and adenocarcinoma, hoarseness, chronic coughing

4. Maintenance of remission

1) Lifestyle changes

  • Weight loss
  • Giving up smoking
  • Raised position of bed support for the head by 15-25 cm
  • Avoiding lying down 3 hours after eating
  • Reduction in fat consumption
  • Avoiding certain foods (chocolate, alcohol, mint, garlic, onions, citric or tomato drinks, coffee)
  • Avoid large meals
  • Avoiding medications which aggravate: teofilin, beta 2 agonists, alpha-adrenergics, anticholinergic drugs, dopamine, nitrites diazepam, calcium channel blockers
  • Avoiding stress and practice relaxation techniques

2) Drug therapy

Uncomplicated GERD

  • H2 receptor blocker (Famotidine, Nizatidine, Roxatidine)
  • Or prokinetic (Cisaprid, Metoclopramide, Domperidone (increases resting sphincter tone and relaxes pyloric sphincter))
  • Or PPI’s (Omeprazole, Lansoprazole, Pantoprazole) (all once per day)

Complicated/ refractory GERD

  • Treatment enhanced by H2 blockers in double dose
  • Or H2 blocker in standard dose associated with

Prokinetic or PPI, 2 doses/day

  • Increase in omeprazole also possible

H2 receptors = antacids

PPIs = most powerful, few long term side effects

Prokinetics = only in mild symptoms, long term use has serious complications

3) Surgery

  • Indications for surgical treatment
  • Lack of response to conservative treatment
  • Persistence of esophagitis
  • Psychological factors (difficulties in accepting a long-term treatment)
  • Economic factors
  • Appearance of complications (extraesophageal complications, BE)
  • Favorable moment – during remission period
  • Objectives of antireflux procedures are well standardized and include

1. Re-establishment of pressure in LES through fundoplication

2. Reconstruction of Hiss angle

3. Putting in contact the cardia with the right pillar of the diaphragm

4. Obtaining a 4-5 cm long abdominal segment of the esophagus

5. Reduction of hernia

6. Prevent recurrence

7. Preserved deglutition, vomiting, eructation

Nissen 360° fundoplication;

Toupet posterior hemivalve;

Dor anterior hemivalve.

  • Choosing the right procedure
  • Normal sized esophagus with good contractibility – 360° fundoplicature of Nissen
  • Low contractibility and faint peristaltic wave - anterior Dor or posterior Toupet hemi valve
  • All performed laparoscopically or laparo- and thoracoscopically
  • Contraindications to laparoscopic approach: cirrhosis and previous history on the supramesocolic level
  • Laparoscopic fundoplication
  • Performed under general endotracheal anesthesia
  • 5 incisions are used
  • Fundus of stomach is wrapped around esophagus to create a new valve at level of GEJ
  • Valve length is maximum 3 cm and must be free of tension (floppy-Nissen)
  • Essential elements

I. Mobilization of fundus (with or without division of short gastric vessels)

II. Reduction of hiatal hernia

III. Calibration of esophageal hiatus

IV. Obtaining at least 3 cm abdominal esophagus segment

V. Creation of an over 40 French intraesophageal tube (Nissen fundoplication)

  • Partial fundoplications have a lower continence, which translates into a slight increase in reflux episodes but also by reducing dysphagia
  • Hiatal hernia repair
  • Suturing of dilated hiatus done posteriorly
  • Use of prosthetic materials should be avoided due to risk of erosion with esophageal fistula
  • Autologous fascia lata plastic surgery is cheaper than heterologous biological grafts
  • Post-OP evolution
  • Good, with minimal dysphagia
  • Limiting food intake to fluids for 2-3 days
  • Prolonged dysphagia requires barium transit
  • In case of post-fundoplication stenosis, endoscopic dilation may be necessary
  • Postoperative follow-up based on clinical data, except for patients with Barrett's esophagus → periodic endoscopy
  • In recurrence of reflux or dysphagia → begin with barium swallow and continue with endoscopy and pH-metry
  • Slightly slipped fundoplication in chest (less than 2 cm) and without symptoms has no surgical indication
  • Complication
  • Nissen stenosis
  • Vagus nerves can be damaged by dissection too close to esophageal wall, but gastric paresis and secondary pyloric spasm occur only if both vaguses are injured

Other procedures not in the book but slides

Collis gastroplasty

= simplified variant, which does not require a thoracoscopic approach but only laparoscopic, prolongs the esophagus by a wedge resection (wedge-fundectomy) of a fundic segment

  • Patients with morbid obesity and GERD should benefit from gastric bypass on the Y en Roux loop, as this bariatric intervention has proven anti-reflux valences
  • Performed mainly in recurrences, the Belsey Mark IV operation consists of a partial fundoplication by thoracic approach, the advantage being maximum in recurrences because it avoids passing through the subphrenic adhesion area with reduced risk of splenic and esophageal damage
  • Endoscopic application techniques are part of the range of endoscopic surgery through natural orifices (NOTES- Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery) and are tempting for the patient, but the medium and long term results are clearly inferior to the surgical background. More well known is the TIF technique which uses a device called Esophyx which is mounted on an endoscope and performs a "full-thickness" partial valve fixed with a type of plastic T-shaped buttons. It is an expensive, laborious technique with inferior results to laparoscopic fundoplications
  • Endoluminal gastroplication
  • Endoscopic procedures → Stretta procedure
  • Radiofrequency energy delivery catheter and guidewire
  • Ethylene-vinyl alcohol injection

3. Esophageal diverticuli

= dilations at different levels of the esophagus, which communicate directly with esophageal lumen Cervical Diverticuli = Zenker diverticulum

Parabronchial diverticuli

Epiphrenic diverticuli

  • Men over 60
  • Often together with hiatal hernias
  • Due to dyssynergy of cricopharyngeal muscle which contracts prematurely, creating a pressure zone at pharyngo-esophag. junction level → distal wall becomes thinner → protrusion through mucosa and submucosa
  • Clinically: dysphagia, typical gurgling noise at liquid ingestion, undigested foods, stasis and decomposition → foetor ex ore (halitosis) and appearance of diverticulitis
  • Diagnosis: latero-cervical formation of variable volume, contrast X-ray/ Ba swallow (additional image left paravertebral region), esophagoscopy (biopsy)
  • Complications of diverticulitis: hemorrhage, perforation, malignization, nocturnal aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess, bi-tonal voice
  • Treatment
  • Surgical always indicated - dissection of diverticular neck, resection, wall reconstructed by two-layer suture
  • Cricopharyngeal myotomy mandatory to prevent recurrence
  • Retro scarring retraction of a mediastinal lymph node adhering to the esophageal wall
  • In general after infection with Koch bacillus
  • All the normal layers
  • Mostly asymptomatic, can cause coughing by adherence to trachea, dysphagia
  • Complications: hemorrhage, perforation, pericarditis, pleuresia, esobronchial fistula
  • Treatment: surgical resection in symptomatic p., suture of fistula, interposition of healthy tissue to prevent recurrency
  • Located immediately above diaphragm (larger)
  • Due to esophageal dyskinesia
  • Frequently associated with hiatal hernia and achalasia
  • Clinically: dysphagia, intermittent regurgitation, postprandial pressure, high epigastric pressure
  • Diagnosis: dysphagia with postprandial onset which is alleviated after regurgitation, contrast X-ray (typical aspect), esophagoscopy (not routinely necessary)
  • Complications: diverticulitis, haemorrhage, perforations or even malignization
  • Treatment: indicated in symptomes; thoracotomy → resection and double suture, associated esophageal conditions (achalasia, hiatal hernia)

4. Achalasia (megaesophagus)

= failure in LES relaxation and lack of peristaltic waves

Pathogenesis

  • Degeneration of the Auerbach plexus

Clinically

  • Dysphagia - most constant and precocious symptom; at beginning intermittent; accentuated in cold food; paradoxical; paroxistic, appearing in episodes separated by lull; over time, becomes permanent
  • High or retrosternal epigastric pains - rare
  • Regurgitation – usual; more frequently at night, in clinostatism
  • Sialorrhoea

Complications are related to stasis esophagitis

  • Ulcerations
  • Hemorrhage
  • Esophageal cancer (7x more frequent)
  • Aspiration pneumonia and lung abscesses

Paraclinical investigations

  • Barium swallowing – dilation, uncoordinated or missing peristalsis; Glucagon relaxation test to differentiate from organic stenosis; “birds beak” at the end; overtime lengthening and curved esophagus
  • Endoscopy with biopsy - DD from cancer
  • Manometry (persistent pressure >25 mmHg) - uncoordinated contractile wave, relaxation is incomplete

Diagnosis

  • Symptoms + prolonged evolution without affecting nutritional state are typical of achalasia
  • Radiological aspect and manometry data confirm

DD

  • Esophageal cancer - progressive dysphagia, rapid evolution and affects general state
  • Epiphrenic diverticuli complicated by esophagitis - distinguished based on barium swallow, manometry in diverticulum is normal, diagnosis is more difficult in cases of associating epiphrenic diverticulum with achalasia/ hiatal hernia
  • Hiatal hernia - difficult to distinguish clinically, requires barium swallow in Trendelenburg position and fibroscopy; manometry reveals low values of LES tonus, by contrast to achalasia for which values are higher

Treatment

  • Life style - avoiding stress, too hot/ too cold food, small meals
  • Mechanical - forced, mechanic, pneumatic or hydrostatic dilation has good results
  • Pharmacological - calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, verapamil)
  • Botulinium toxin
  • Surgical - Heller myotomy (extramucous esocardiomyotomy → longitudinal incision of 6-8 cm on esogastric junction, with sectioning of muscles reaching up to mucosa)

+ Nissen fundoplication in case of hypermotility

+ Anterior Dor hemi valve in case of hypomotility

5. Benign tumors of the esophagus

Inflammatory polyps or granulomatous lesions in esophagitis - require biopsy for diagnosis Leiomyoma = most common benign lesion, within the wall, stenosis of lumen, mucosa intact Congenital cysts or esophageal dedoubling - lower esophagus Lesions can be seen on contrast X ray - benign stenosis, dilations are rare, peristalsis not affected except for congenital diseases

6. Esophageal cancer

Epidemiology

  • Especially Asia
  • 45-65 years men
  • High alcohol consumption, hot food and liquids, vitamin or nutritional deficiencies, poor oral hygiene, nitrosamines in environment or food, smoking, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, static/ caustic/ peptic esophagitis → squamous carcinoma
  • Pre-existing esophageal lesions = BE → adenocarcinoma

Pathomorphology

  • Vegetative form – can be ulcerative
  • Infiltrative, circumferential forms - causing obstructive symptoms
  • Cervical and thoracic (upper 2/3) = squamous cell carcinoma
  • Lower thoracic and abdominal (lower 1/3) = adenocarcinoma
  • Extends on mucosa, invades esophageal wall and neighboring tissues, disseminate through lymph and blood
  • Cervical - cervical lymph nodes (anterior jugular and supraclavicular groups)
  • Thoracic - mediastinal, supraclavicular and sometimes subdiaphragmatic lymph nodes
  • Abdominal - celiac and small gastric curvature nodes
  • Upper 2/3 - rapidly invade airways, large vessels, pleura, thoracic outlet and recurrent nerves
  • Blood metastases: liver, lungs, bones
  • Presence of mediastinal syndrome, eso-tracheal or eso-bronchial fistula, bitonal voice, Virchow-Troisier’s sign = radical intervention impossible

Clinical picture – 3 stages

1. Onset

  • Dysphagia (progressive, feeling that solid food stops, burning sensation at warm liquids)

2. Status

  • Dysphagia becomes permanent (first only for solids, then also for liquids)
  • Regurgitation, sialorrhea, bad breath, hiccup, dysphonia/ hoarseness
  • Pain (epigastric, retrosternal) due to spasm

3. Complications

  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Eso-tracheal and eso-bronchial fistulas
  • Mediastinitis and hemorrhage
  • Pain due to invasion of mediastinum/ pleura
  • Weight loss !!!, asthenia, dehydration, anorexia

Dysphagia = always indication for barium swallow and endoscopy

Physical exam

  • Often normal
  • Lymphadenopathy in latero-cervical or supraclavicular (Virchow) areas → sign for metastasis → FNA → contraindication for surgery
  • Liver metastasis might cause jaundice → contraindication for surgery
  • Anemia (pallor)

Diagnosis/ Paraclinical investigations

  • Lab: anemia (iron or chronic disease); abnormal transaminases, PT and aPTT → hepatic dysfunction

Barium esophagography/ swallow (double contrast) ! o Images suggestive for esophageal cancer

  • irregular contour stenosis (apple core aspect)
  • eccentric stenosis with slight suprajacent dilation
  • marginal emptiness
  • niche
  • rigidity
  • irregularity
  • presence on all images even after administration of pharmacodynamic agents

Esophagoscopy (EGD) o Direct tumor visualization ! , location, type (infiltrative, vegetative, ulcerated) and biopsy ! (histology) o Location/ distance: point A = dental archade (incisors); point B = location of tumor

Endoesophageal ultrasound (EUS) o = Golden standard - depth and penetration of tumor (T staging) and N staging

Abdominal, chest, pelvic CT contrast o M staging for lungs and liver

Bronchoscopy for cancers in middle and upper 1/3 of thoracic esophagus and exclusion of trachea/ bronchi involvement Bone scan → bone metastasis Laparoscopy and thoracoscopy → staging of regional lymph nodes PET-scan

Positive diagnosis

  • Clinical, radiological and endoscopic methods
  • Often found at advanced stage
  • Any patient over 40 with dysphagia should be fully investigated
  • Typical patient: male, consumer of spirits, with progressive permanent dysphagia, long time without pain

DD

Achalasia – paradoxical, paroxystic intermittent dysphagia, prolonged evolution; nutritional state normal; barium meal or manometry, fibroscope goes easily beyond cardia Asymptomatic diverticuli – barium meal Benign stenoses - history of post caustic, reflux, infectious, drug induced esophagitis, or radiation therapy of chest; barium meal or endoscopy + biopsy Extrinsic compressions - mediastinal adenopathy or tumors, retrosternal gout, vertebral osteophytosis, aortic aneurysm, pulmonary hydatid cyst

Prognosis

  • Severe - 5 year survival = 5%
  • Postoperative mortality high (mediastinitis has worst prognosis)

Treatment

→ depending on stage (radical/palliative)

TNM staging

Pre-operative care o Improvement of general status (nutrition) o Preparation of colon for possible esophagoplasty o Improve/ check respiratory function (CT of lungs and spirometry) (thorax involvement during surgery, can develop post-OP problems) o

+/- Neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy to downstage tumor → depending on costs, perioperative morbidity, delay in surgical intervention

Operation o Radical esophagectomy in neoplasms of upper or middle third → replacement of esophagus by another segment of GI tract o Partial esophagectomy in neoplasms of lower third with upper polar gastric resection (6-10 cm from tumor) → within oncological safety, under observation due to multifocal development of esophageal cancer o Resection also involves removal of surrounding lymph nodes + lymph drainage Techniques → transthoracic, transhiatal, en bloc Orringer technique

  • Cervical and abdominal incision → transhiatal, both hands go into thorax
  • No opening of thorax
  • Advantages: pat. with poor pulmonary status, prior major thoracic surgery, avoidance of intrathoracic anastomosis
  • Disadvantages: risk of limited access in case of bleeding, limited resection of large tumors, greater potency of local tumor spillage, greater stretch of stomach to reach neck → ↑ risk for anastomotic failure due to tension, ischemia → Ideal for local limited diseases of distal esophagus (Barrett’s)

Ivor-Lewis technique = historical, right transthoracic and abdominal incision

  • Gastro-esophageal anastomosis is located in right chest
  • Visually direct resection of tumor, BUT ↑ morbidity

McKeown technique = tri-incisional esophagectomy (cervical, right thorax, abdomen)

!

  • Similar to Ivor-Lewis → including cervical incision and cervical gastroesophageal anastomosis (↓ risk for anastomosis leakage)
  • For lesions in proximal/ mid-esophagus
  • Advantages: wider surgical margins, ↓ risk for anastomosis leakage

En bloc resection

= left thoracic incision

  • Used for distal esophageal tumors extending into stomach
  • Advantage: cleaner oncological resection

Laparoscopic

Advantages

  • Less post-op pain
  • Faster post-op recovery → shorter hospital stay, more rapid return to normal life
  • Thoracoscopic dissection of esophagus is nowadays more common instead of open thoracotomy

Orringer

o o o

After esophagectomy → esophagoplasty

Uses stomach, colon, jejunum

Depends on availability (previous gastrectomy, vascular disease), location of resected esophagus segment and surgeon’s preference

1. Stomach

2. Left colon

3. Jejunum

= Dan Gavriliu’s method

  • Most frequently used
  • Gastric tube made from greater stomach curvature (removal of other stomach parts)
  • After hilum splenectomy and ligation of left gastric and gastroepiploic artery
  • Vagus n. is divided during esophagectomy → pyloromyotomy to facilitate gastric emptying
  • Brought to chest → end-to-end anastomosis
  • Vascularization via right gastric and gastroepiploic arteries

Advantages: rich vascular supply, ease of surgical mobilization as a vascular pedicle, need to create fewer GI anastomosis Disadvantages: risk of fundus ischemia, risk of post-op GERD Can be done in 2 ways a. Through resected esophageal space in post. mediastinum b. Through retrosternum (only if a. is not possible)

Advantages: longer available length → longer and more relaxed reach to cervical esophagus, favorable vascular anatomy, close size match, colon is more resistant to reflux Disadvantages: need to perform 2 additional anastomosis, greater technique experience needed in assessing & mobilizing colonic vasculature, pre-op colonoscopy + visceral angiography

  • Rarely used
  • Used as free graft, especially when a short segment of the cervical esophagus is resected → jejunal reconstruction via Roux-en-Y connection can be used when a total gastrectomy is combined with distal esophagectomy

Post-op care o Enteral nutrition 4-6 weeks o Once normal diet started → decreased stomach size → need to eat more frequent and smaller meals → weight loss is possible

Complications

Cancer related

  • Esophageal stenosis
  • Tracheoesophageal fistula → poor vascularization and lack of serosa

Surgery related

  • Anastomosis leaks → poor vascularization and lack of serosa → mediastinitis and purulent pleurisy almost always fatal
  • Recurrent laryngeal n. injury

Others

  • Dysphagia
  • Reflux
  • Dumping syndrome
  • Mediastinitis
  • Purulent pleurisy

Palliative treatment o = are indicated in case of local and regional spread as well as remote metastases o Survival time of up to 18 months may be obtained o To provide a “comfortable” quality of life in the limited time available o To relief severe symptoms/ complications (dysphagia, obstruction) o These methods are surgery, radiation and chemotherapy

  • a) Dilation → balloon expansion (risk of perforation)
  • b) Stents, transtumoral endoprosthesis → for mid/ distal esophageal tumors; pat. with tracheoesophageal fistula and when chemoradiation therapy is contraindicated
  • c) Photodynamic therapy, endoscopic laser ablation
  • d) Radiation- and chemotherapy → reduce tumor size and improve dysphagia (complications: actinic lung, pericarditis and tumoral necrosis with fistula formation)
  • e) Surgery → palliative esophagectomy with incomplete tumor removal, alimentation gastrostomy

Barium swallow: presence and location of strictures, type and shape of hernia
Re-establishment of pressure in LES through fundoplication
Putting in contact the cardia with the right pillar of the diaphragm
Obtaining a 4-5 cm long abdominal segment of the esophagus

title: Gastric cancer
html:
Epidemiology

  • 4th common cause of cancer related death
  • More common in males
  • Black race
  • Individuals with low socio-economic status
  • In developing countries
  • In Asia (Japan, Korea)

Risk factors

1. H. pylori infection !!!

2. Smoking

3. Excessive salt ingestion; salt/smoke preserved food

4. Diet low on fresh fruits and vegetables

5. Hereditary GC or HNPCC (hereditary non polyposic colon cancer

syndrome) (Lynch II; gastric and colic cancer)

6. Predisposing gastric disease

→ Giant hypertrophic gastropathy (Menetrier’s) (inner lining of stomach forms huge folds, due to excessive overgrowth of mucous) → Adenomatous polyps (≥ 2cm) (present atypia)

→ Chronic atrophic gastritis → Partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer (not done any longer; 20-30 y. ago) → Intestinal metaplasia (often in smoking, H. pylori)

Carciogenesis

1. Intestinal metaplasia - chronic inflamed gastric mucosa morphing into intestinal mucosa

2. Dysplasia - structural degeneration in 3 degrees (light, medium, severe)

  • Light dysplasia may not require surgical treatment
  • Severe dysplasia = carcinoma in situ; requires endoscopic mucosal excision or surgical gastric resection

3. Invasive carcinoma = final step

Pathology

External aspect

Endogastric aspect (gastroscopy)

  • Advanced tumors are visible and palpable on surface of stomach → firm, infiltrated, white/ grey colored
  • Can differentiate between 2 types of GC
  • a) Early gastric CA
  • b) Advanced gastric CA

EARLY GASTRIC CA (EGC)

  • Local adenoCA limited to gastric mucosa or submucosa
  • With or without lymph node metastasis (N0, N1)
  • Best prognosis with 5-year survival rate >90%
  • Diagnosis in early stage of disease is established by endoscopy only (active mass screening !)

Paris endoscopic classification of EGC

Type 0-I

  • Protrusive, exophytic
  • Rough, protrusive, malignant small polyp

Type 0-IIa - Slightly elevated (up to 5mm above the surrounding mucosa)

Type 0-II

Type 0-IIb - Flat, discolored mucosa

Type 0-IIc - Slightly depressed

Type 0-III - Superficial ulceration

ADVANCED GASTRIC CA (AGC)

  • Extension of malignant infiltration beyond submucosa

Borrmann classification system

Type I

  • Protrusive, proliferative

Type II

  • Ulcerative, with elevated uneven margins

Type III - Ulcerative-infiltrative uncertainly contoured tumor with deep central crater Type IV - Extensive infiltrating with important thickening of the gastric wall

Histology

  • Majority → adenocarcinomas (> 90%)
  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumors = GISTs
  • Non-Hodgkin gastric lymphomas
  • Neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid, gastrinoma)

Shah’s classification (2010) + Lauren’s classification (1963) for adenocarcinoma subtypes → important for gastric location, prognosis and carcinogenetic mechanism Intestinal type - Body or antrum (non-diffuse, non-proximal)

  • Most common variant
  • Chronic inflammation → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → invasive CA

GEJ and cardia (proximal !)

Diffuse type

Risk factors

  • Helicobacter pylori infection
  • Cigarette smoking
  • High salt intake
  • Alcohol consumption
  • Infection with H. pylori seems to have protective effect (resulted severe atrophic gastritis and aclorhydria, diminishes risk of gastroesophageal reflux)
  • Prognosis is worse and resectability rates are lower
  • Triggered by gene (E-cadherin) mutation
  • Malignant cells progressively + diffusely infiltrate gastric wall → extended thickening of entire stomach → rigid tube
  • Diffuse, total infiltration of entire stomach = linitis plastica/ gastric schirus
  • Tends to appear in younger patients
  • Has the worst prognosis
  • No precursor lesion has been identified

Diagnosis of gastric cancer

  • Often no specific clinical symptoms

Unspecific signs and symptoms (early)

  • Epigastric discomfort
  • Flatulence
  • Discrete swollen belly after meals (postprandial meteorism)
  • Early satiation
  • Malaise

Alarm symptoms (advanced)

  • Dysphagia
  • Upper GI hemorrhage
  • Fatigue
  • Anemia
  • Weight loss
  • Selective anorexia (for meat, bread)
  • Epigastric palpable tumor

Juxtaorifcially situated tumors (eso-gastric junction or pyloric) can manifest earlier

  • Early dysphagia/ GERD (heartburn, regurgitation) → eso-gastric tumors
  • Delayed gastric emptying by malignant gastric outlet obstruction/ stenosis, fullness, bloating, vomiting, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, emaciation → distal antro pyloric tumor
  • Anemic syndrome (common finding in malignant GI tumors)
  • Upper GI bleeding is occult → clinically undetectable, but persistent → Chronic iron deficiency anemia → headache, physical and psychic asthenia, decreased productivity, pallor of skin and mucosa, weakness, fatigue → doing an hemoccult test, if positive → endoscopic evaluation (chance of early diagnosis !)

Upper GI bleeding

  • Dramatic, fulminant, immediately life-threatening bleedings can occur (rare)
  • Moderate bleedings – hematemesis and/or melena

Abnormal nutritional status

  • weight loss despite initial normal appetite
  • anorexia (first selective, later general)
  • cachexia (end stage)
  • best reflected by albumin

In very advanced stages (always indicating irresectability !)

  • Jaundice → liver metastasis or CBD compression
  • Irregular liver margins → large liver metastasis
  • Intense and persisting epigastric pain → invasion of celiac plexus or pancreas
  • Increase in abdominal volume → ascites → peritoneal carcinomatosis
  • Virchow nodule (left supraclavicular or laterocervical)
  • Krunkenberg tumor → ovarian metastasis (CA 125)
  • Sister Mary Joseph nodule → umbilical metastasis
  • Blumer shelf → mobile tumor detected in Douglas pouch during DRE

Paraclinical diagnosis

1. Barium exam

(not used anymore)

2. Gastroduodenofibroscopy

(Gastroscopy)

3. Endoscopic US

4. Percutaneous US

5. CT

6. MRI

7. PET

8. Staging laparoscopy

9. Tumor markers

  • Double contrast, segmental rigidity of infiltrated area, lacunar image

= main examination → direct visualization and possibility of biopsy (only way of pre-OP diagnosis !) → negative biopsy doesn’t rule out existence of cancer !

  • Red, irregular tumor or ulceration, grey/necrotic areas, quick to bleed when touched
  • Malignant ulcerations may be mistaken for benign ulcers
  • If biopsy is negative → endoscopic re-exam in 6-8 weeks or whenever suspicion for malignancy arises
  • Brushing cytology exam (gentle brushing of lesion) may detect malignant cells where biopsies failed to confirm malignancy Modern endoscopic techniques to detect very small, superficial lesions
  • Magnifying endoscopy
  • Narrow band imaging
  • Chromoendoscopy

= most accurate examination in terms of local tumor extension (T)

  • First intent to see lymph nodes (N stage), ascites or liver (M stage; especially with CEUS)
  • They offer valuable information about local tumor extension and distant metastasis of GC (liver, lung) → Perfect for T, N, M staging!
  • Only in selected cases; not routinely
  • May detect small (mm) lesions, which cannot be detected by any other exam (peritoneal carcinomatosis = M1, disseminated disease – stage IV ! → operation is not indicated because it does not offer survival benefits) → CEA, CA 19.9, CA 72.4, CA 50
  • Lacking specificity → prognostic factors
  • Increased mostly in advanced stages

10. Circulating RNA

  • Play role in appreciating accuracy of surgical resection (should drop post-OP)
  • May rise during post-OP follow-up → metastasis, local recurrence

= circRNA → may detect early GC (EGC) with sensitivity of 77.5 %

Evolution and prognosis

  • Untreated - 1 year survival
  • Proper treatment (gastric Ro resection) - 20% survive 5 years
  • EGC, when treated → survival rate at 5 years > 90% (importance of early diagnosis !)
  • GC at body or fundus are frequently found too late (lacking symptoms)
  • Distal (antro pyloric) tumors have highest respectability rates and best prognosis

Complications (similar to ulcers)

  • Hemorrhage
  • Stenosis
  • Perforation
  • Invasion of neighboring viscera, metastasis
  • Blumer's shelf (metastasis in Douglas pouch) or Krukenberg tumors

Treatment

  • Based on T and N staging
  • Radical, complete (R0) resection

EARLY GC

  • Tis, T1a, T1b → endoscopic resection
  • Preserving morphologic and functional integrity of abdominal wall and stomach !
  • Only in intestinal types (not diffuse !)
  • Confined to mucosa/ submucosa (Tis, T1a/b)
  • Without lymph node involvement (N0)
  • Eradication of H. pylori is mandatory ! to prevent metachronous gastric carcinoma
  • a) Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR)
  • Confined to mucosa
  • Well differentiated, elevated, < 20mm
  • Well diff., depressed, < 10mm, no ulcer
  • Larger lesions cannot always be totally resected (risk of recurrence – R1 resection!)

ADVANCED GC

≥ T2 tumor or N1

1. Neoadjuvant therapy → N1

2. Surgery → R0 resection

3. Adjuvant therapy

BUT NOT SURGERY FIRST!

  • The only treatment for actual healing is R0 radical surgical resection (margins 5-6 cm from tumor) → Removal of stomach along with regional lymph nodes → no tumor cells left behind !
  • a) Wedge resection → Only in well selected early submucosal gastric CA → Appropriate for GISTs
  • b) Subtotal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
  • b) Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) → In distal (antropyloric) gastric tumors
  • Mucosal: well differentiated, > 20 mm, no ulcer
  • Resection includes duodenum (3 cm distal from
  • Mucosal: well differentiated, ≤ 30 mm, with ulcer pylorus), pylorus and distal 3/4 or 4/5 of stomach
  • Submucosal: well differentiated, ≤ 30 mm

+ gastro-duodenal / gastro-jejuno-anastomosis

  • Allows larger/ deeper resection
  • c) Total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
  • c) Endoscopic full thickness resection (EFTR) → Tumors located proximal (body, fundus)
  • Allows biopsy of small tumor with all layers
  • Entire stomach + 3-5cm of distal esophagus around tumor (“full thickness”)

+ ROUX en Y eso-jejunostomy → Resulted gastric wall defect is closed with clips Both gastrectomies require omentectomy (large and small) and regional (D2) lymphadenectomy * Omentectomy removes perigastric lymph nodes (groups 1, 3, 4, 5, 6)

Extension of lymphadenectomy (stations 7-12) = D2 lymphadenectomy

Reconstruction

After subtotal gastrectomy

1. Duodenal stump

(termino-terminal gastro-duodenostomy –Bilroth I )

2. First jejunal loop

(termino-lateral gastro-jejunostomy – Bilroth II )

3. Roux-en-Y jejunal loop

(termino-lateral Roux en Y gastro-jejunostomy)

After total gastrectomy

  • Duodenal stump is closed

1. Roux-en Y jejunal loop

(termino-lateral eso-jejunostomy)

2. Bilroth II with Braun anastomosis

(in cases in which, due to anatomy/vascular “1.” can’t be prepared)

  • Nowadays the laparoscopic approach for all procedures in preferred

Complication and palliative therapy

1. Hemorrhage → endoscopy → if not working, emergency gastrectomy, vascular pedicles ligation 2. Perforation → spilling gastric content (with tumor cells !) into peritoneal cavity → diffuse “carcinomatous seeding” → resection is only option (this time for palliation only)

3. Stenosis/ gastric outlet obstruction → endoprosthesis/ endoscopic stenting → if it fails, open gastro-enterostomy → local extended tumor (unresectable) → latero-lateral gastro-jejunostomy → for proximal stenoses (GEJ) producing impressive cachexia → endoprosthesis or gastrectomy/ jejunostomy
sections: Excessive salt ingestion; salt/smoke preserved food
Diet low on fresh fruits and vegetables
Hereditary GC or HNPCC (hereditary non polyposic colon cancer
Dysplasia - structural degeneration in 3 degrees (light, medium, severe)

title: Benign gastric disorders
html:
1) Peptic ulcer

= localized histopathological lesion → “lack of substance” involving mucosa, muscularis mucosae, submucosa; sometimes affects also muscularis layer, progressing through serosa

  • Both locations (stomach and duodenum)
  • Can be perforated or not
  • Duodenum – young males
  • Stomach – older age, low social status

Gastric ulcers

  • Imbalance between defending mechanism of mucosa and hydrochloric acid aggression Mucosal defense factors Mucosal aggression factors
  • Intense cellular turn-over
  • H. pylori infection (inflammation)
  • Secretion of mucus
  • NSAIDs (lowers PG´s)
  • Secretion of HCO3 in duodenum
  • Acid hypersecretion (gastrinoma, Zollinger-Ellison)
  • Adequate blood supply
  • Duodeno-gastric reflux (bile)
  • Gastric stasis
  • Alcohol and smoking = irritants → decreased production of PG’s and gastric mucosal ischemia Duodenal ulcers
  • Acid hypersecretion
  • H. Pylori, NSAIDs, motility disorders of the stomach (rapid evacuation → high amounts of acid), smoking Clinical features and diagnosis
  • Epigastric or hypochondriac pain (towards left = gastric; towards right = duodenal) (gastric ulcer → aggravated by food, worse during day; duodenal ulcer → relieved by food, worse during night)
  • “Painful hunger”, relieve by milk
  • Nausea, vomiting, fullness, weight loss/ gain
  • Physical exam – nonspecific; epigastric dullness at palpation
  • Lab test – nonspecific; BUT H. pylori breath and fecal test!!!
  • Gold standard → Endoscopy with biopsy (from lesion and surrounding tissue to rule out CA and to check for H. pylori)
  • Radiology with hydrosoluble contrast - “Haudek niche” is characteristic for ulcers Johnson classification of ulcers (related to ulcer location)

Type I

= single ulcer, localized at gastric angle

Type II

= gastric and duodenal ulcer

Type III = consists in single lesion located pre-pyloric

Type IV = located high on lesser curvature, right under cardia

Type V

= caused by use of NSAIDs; located anywhere on stomach

Type I + IV = typical gastric ulcers, are not caused by hyperacidity

Type II + III = manifest more as a duodenal ulcer, hyperacidity

Acute ulcers: < 1 cm, fine wedges

Chronic ulcers: > 2 cm, fibrous, infiltrated wedges

Treatment (uncomplicated ulcer)

  • Gastric antisecretory drugs (PPIs, histamine antagonists)
  • Antacid
  • Gastro-duodenal mucosal protection (magnesium, aluminum salts, prostaglandins)
  • H. pylori eradication (Maastricht therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin)
  • Surgery only in cases of life-threatening complications or no responds to drug therapy

Complications

  • Perforation
  • Hemorrhage (more often)
  • Gastric outlet obstruction (due to chronic evolution)

2. Perforated peptic ulcer

  • Due to progression of lesion (ulcer) through entire gastric/ duodenal wall
  • Followed by discharge of gastric content into peritoneum → chemical peritonitis → bacterial peritonitis (typically localized)
  • Mainly anterior wall ulcers
  • Especially males, thirties or forties

Free perforation

Covered perforation

Penetration

= classical form, frequent

  • With generalized secondary peritonitis
  • Clinical manifestation varying
  • Frust form - perforation diameter is small and it is covered from beginning by peritoneal reaction
  • Or localized peritonitis (peritoneal abscesses)
  • Represents erosion towards and through neighboring organs
  • When penetration happens into cavitary organ → fistula (gastro-colic, duodeno-colic)

Symptoms

  • 20% present with perforation without prior manifestations
  • Aggravation factors found in 50%: smoking, NSADs, aspirin, stress

Pain

  • First epigastric, can radiate towards shoulders (diaphragmatic irritation), then to right flank and at the end generalized
  • Either progressive or sudden-severe

Vomiting

  • Not mandatory
  • Can be due to pain
  • Can present with hematemesis
  • Abundant in paralytic ileus

Shock state

  • Peritoneal irritation → vago-vagal reflexes → bradycardia, hypotension, pallor, sweating
  • Hypovolemic or toxic due to bacterial peritonitis

Peritonitis

  • “wodden abdomen” = involuntary guarding
  • Rectal/ vaginal exam is very painful → irritation of Douglas pouch
  • Later abd. distension disappears
  • Superficial respiration
  • Paralytic ileus

Disappearance - Result of gas accumulation and phrenic irritation, but they are not constant of hepatic dullness Respiratory impairment Acute phase Intermittent stage Late phase

0-2 h

Chemical peritonitis → pain, abdominal contracture

2-12 h

Bacterial peritonitis onset → clinical eased

> 12 h

Bacterial peritonitis – Toxico-septic shock → Clinical signs dominated by massive abdominal distension

Lab

  • Leukocytosis
  • ↑ serum and urine amylase

Imaging

  • Plain abdominal X-ray → pneumoperitoneum (free gas under diaphragm; mainly right)
  • Barium swallowing is forbidden
  • CT
  • Upper endoscopy is totally forbidden → gas insufflation will increase pneumoperitoneum and will accelerate spill of gastric content; in cases with covered perforation, gas insufflation could separate adventia that block ulcer

Positive diagnosis

  • Pat. history and pneumoperitoneum → 3 cardinal signs of perforated peptic ulcer = acute pain, abdominal rigidity, history of ulcer

DD

  • Ulcer penetration
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Acute cholecystitis
  • Renal colic
  • Intestinal infarction
  • Inferior MI
  • Basal pneumonitis
  • Zona zoster

Treatment

1. Resting in bed

2. Installation of naso-gastric tube and active aspiration of content

3. Establishment of intravenous ways – at least two, administration of crystalloid solution

4. Inject PPI´s iv (alternative anti-H2)

5. Broad spectrum antibiotics iv

6. Administration of iv short acting time antalgic (petidine)

7. Urgent transport in surgical emergency unit

A. Non-surgical treatment = always 2nd choice → Taylor therapy

  • Nihil per os (no oral intake!)
  • Nasogastric aspiration
  • Hydroelectrolytic rebalance
  • iv PPI´s
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • H. pylori eradication therapy (involves initial antibiotic regimen for 2 weeks and inhibition of gastric acid for 4)

Indications for conservative treatment

1. absolutely certainty that perforation is blocked and no signs of generalized peritonitis 2. perforation occurred days ago and status of patient is stable 3. presence of two rules above + patient could be evaluated clinico-radiological every time needed 4. no surgical facility available (ships, oil rigs, isolated sites)

5. elderly patients with no signs of peritonitis, but with high anesthetic and surgical risk

Contraindications for conservative treatment

1. Positive signs of peritonitis

2. Contrast spill at radiology

3. Hemodynamic instability, state of shock

4. Elderly, but with low operatory risk

5. Impossibility to follow course of patient

6. Failure of conservative treatment after 12-24h

B. Surgical treatment

= optimal method with best results → 1st choice!

1. Suture of ulcer with patch of great omentum and abundant peritoneal wash out

2. Gastric resection (definitive treatment)

→ Usually not preferred, only in …

  • a) Perforation is accompanied by GI hemorrhage
  • b) Perforation is accompanied by stenosis
  • c) There is a suspicion of a malignant gastric lesion
  • d) Suture perforation leading to stenosis
  • e) Perforation occurs after a correctly and appropriate treatment

Follow-up

  • i.v. PPI (continuous perfusion or bolus administration)
  • Drainage tube ex usually in first 3 days (when they don’t leak any liquids)
  • PPI treatment for at least 4 w
  • Control gastroscopy will assess healing of ulcer
  • If H. pylori infection present → eradication is mandatory

3. Peptic ulcer hemorrhage

  • 70% of upper GI hemorrhage
  • Can become life threatening
  • Bleeding from mucosal/ submucosal vessel mainly acute ulcers → usually spontaneous hemostasis
  • Bleeding of major vessel (pyloric/ gastroduodenal/ left gastric/ splenic artery) mainly chronic ulcers → requires endoscopic or surgical hemostasis

Clinically

  • Pallor, restlessness, faintness
  • Thirst and cold
  • Tachycardia, hypotension → Externalization of bleeding is by hematemesis and melena → Upper GI endoscopy = first indicated maneuver (diagnostic and therapeutic)

Forrest classification → offers treatment options

Class I

Ia

Pressure (jet arterial) bleeding → emergency surgery

Ib

Slow continuous bleeding – endoscopic hemostasis

Class II

IIa

Stopped bleeding with clot adherent to crater → intensive drug ulcer therapy IIb Stopped bleeding, visible vessel in crater → emergency surgery high risk of re-bleeding IIc Bleeding stopped, black crater of lesion → standard drug treatment Class II No signs of bleeding ulcer, it appears only in history → standard drug treatment

DD

  • Epistaxis, hemoptysis
  • Hemangiomas
  • Vascular abnormalities, atherosclerosis
  • Thrombocytopenia, Hemophilia, Anticoagulant therapy
  • Ruptured esophageal varices
  • Mucosal erosions
  • Pharyngeal, esophageal or gastric tumors
  • Mallory Weiss syndrome

Treatment

1. Resuscitation

2. Hemostasis

3. Surgical

treatment

  • i.v. line for administration of crystalloids/ colloids and possible transfusions
  • Nasogastric suction tube
  • Uretrovesical catheter to monitor urine output and water balance
  • Check of blood group and Rh, Hb, Hct (cross-matching)
  • First choice is endoscopic

1. Submucosal injection of vasoconstrictor and sclerosing substances

2. Thermoregulation

3. Application of clips to bleeding vessels

  • Type Ia, IIa
  • Less common due to good endoscopic treatment

Clinical features that indicate surgery

1. Age > 60 years

2. Long history of ulcer

3. Frequent relapse on full treatment

4. Continued melena or hematemesis

5. > 4 units of blood transfusion required during resuscitation

Endoscopic features that indicate surgery

1. Active bleeding (Forrest Ia)

2. Visible vessel (Forrest IIb)

3. Continued bleeding despite correct endoscopic ther.

4. Relapse after endoscopic treatment

5. Torrential bleeding that make impossible entification

of the lesion

4. Gastroduodenal outflow obstruction

= pyloric stenosis or other parts of stomach (e.g., mediogastric stenosis)

  • Result of long evolution of duodenal and pre-pyloric ulcers → development of fibrosis and wall deformation → Gastric stasis > 200ml after fasting and pediatric endoscope cannot pass through narrowed area
  • Stomach is compensating by dilatation and hypertrophy of muscularis → failure of mechanism = dilation and vomiting Clinical
  • Stenic phase = first
  • stomach fighting stenosis
  • few symptoms
  • Atonic phase → stomach evacuation failure syndrome
  • main symptoms occur
  • vomiting with gastric juice, food ingested 1 or 2 days before and always free from bile
  • fullness in left hypochondrium
  • loss of weight
  • dehydration
  • constipation
  • weakness
  • pain +/- late stage: dilatation of stomach, severe dehydration, complete digestive intolerance to food/ water, shock
  • Vomiting = outstanding symptom → first vomiting is accompanied by nausea, then becomes effortless, explosive without any premonitory signs
  • Humoral-metabolic syndrome = Darrow syndrome (hypoNa, hypoK, hypoCl with metabolic alkalosis and paradoxical aciduria)
  • Visible peristalsis (in skinny, dehydrated pat. = Kuessmaul sign)
  • “sloshing/ splashing sounds” (= Clapotage sign)

Diagnosis

  • Endoscopy: dilated stomach, chronic ulcer and stenosis, usually in pyloric region, insurmountable by pediatric endoscope
  • Barium meal → stenic phase: hyperkinesis of antrum, weak duodenal passage, barium seen as snowflakes due to high amount of gastric juice → atone phase: dilated stomach appears dropped in pelvic area looking as “in sink” DD: gastric CA, benign tumors, foreign bodies, compression from outside, corrosive stricture, achalasia

Treatment

1) Rebalance of hydration and acid base status

  • a) Insert nasogastric tube for aspiration
  • b) At least two venous access point, Saline solution with supplement of ions if necessary, will be administrated, under control of ASTRUP parameters (Na, K)
  • c) Protein solution (amino acids, albumin) in hypoproteinemia
  • d) If anemia, blood transfusion → surgery can be done only when the patient is well balanced → high risk of cardiac arrest (electrolyte imbalance) + anastomotic fistula (hypoproteinemia)

2) Relieve of obstruction

  • a) Endoscopic dilation (high surgery risk)
  • b) Gastric resection with gastro-duodenal (Pean or Billroth I) or gastro-jejunal (Hoffmeister-Finsterer or Billroth II)

a. distal gastro-duodenal resection (Pean-Bilroth I); b. termino-terminal gastro-duodenostomy; c. termino-lateral Reichel-Polya gastro-jejunostomy; d. termino-lateral Hoffmeister-Finsterer gastro-jejunostomy

Post-gastrectomy complications

1. Dumping syndrome

Early Dumping syndrome

Late Dumping syndrome

→ 15 min after ingestion of osmotic meals (sugars)

  • Anxiety, weakness, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and, frequently, palpitations (i.e., vasomotor symptoms)
  • Extreme weakness, crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea
  • Pathophysiology: sudden discharge of hyperosmotic meal into the intestine – movement of liquid from intravascular into intralumenal
  • The release of several hormonal substances, including serotonin, neurotensin, histamine, glucagon, VIP, kinins

Treatment

  • Fractionated, multiple meals per day
  • Avoidance of hyperosmotic food
  • Liquids 30 minutes before or after the meal
  • Somatostatin usage
  • Surgical conversion to Roux-en-Y gastro-jejunal anastomosis → 3h after meals
  • Anxiety, diaphoresis, tachycardia, palpitations, weakness, fatigue, and a desire to lie down
  • No diarrhea or borborygmi
  • Serum glucose levels are increasing rapidly – insulin secretion overcome needs – hypoglycemia

Treatment

  • Small snacks after the meal
  • Acarbose (α-glycosidase hydrolase inhibitor)

2. Post-vagotomy diarrhea

  • Enhanced intestinal motility (vagal denervation), rapid gastric emptying, bile malabsorption and bacterial overgrowth
  • Diarrhea that is explosive in onset, is not related to meals, and occurs without warning
  • Fuid intake is restricted
  • Antidiarrheal/antimotility agents such as codeine, diphenoxylate hydrochloride, or loperamide

3. Blind loop syndrome

  • Bacterial overgrowth in the limb of intestine that is excluded from the ﬂow of chyme
  • Diarrhea, weight loss, and weakness, and they are often anemic (megaloblastic – lack of vitaminB12)

4. Afferent loop obstruction

= a kink in the afferent limb adjacent to the anastomosis

  • Severe cramping abdominal pain that occurs immediately after the ingestion of a meal followed by nausea and vomiting of a dark brown, bitter-tasting material

5. Alkaline reflux gastritis

  • Gastro-duodenal or gastro-jejunal anastomosis (Billroth 1 and 2)
  • Weakness, weight loss, persistent nausea, and epigastric abdominal pain that often radiates to Back
  • Edematous, bile-stained gastric epithelium that is atrophic and erythematous
  • Conversion Roux-en-Y

6. Marginal and recurrent ulcer disease

  • Ulcer on the jejunal of the anastomosis
  • Abdominal pain during eating as well as nausea and vomiting
  • Stop tobacco use and initiation of a PPI → Insufficient gastric resection/ vagotomy → Hyperparathyroidism → Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

7. Metabolic disturbances

  • Vitamin B12 or folate deﬁciency – megaloblastic anemia (20%)
  • Iron deficiency (low absorption or chronic loss) – microcytic anemia (50%)
  • Altered bowel function is common (25%)
