title: Small intestine
html:
Anatomy

  • Part of GI tract between stomach and colon → pyloric valve → Bauhin ileocecal valve
  • Length = 5-6 m → Duodenum (D1-D4; between pylorus and angle of Treitz) → Jejunum – proximal 2/5 → Ileum – distal 3/5
  • Duodenum = retroperitoneal organ; anterior covered by serosa, posterior only adventitia
  • Jejunum and Ileum can´t be differentiated from the outside → only internal structure is different
  • Ileum: lumen narrows, vascular arches become more irregular, circular folds of mucosa shorten and become rarer, Peyer’s plaques The mesentery
  • Reflection of posterior parietal peritoneum → form visceral peritoneum on bowl loops
  • Fixes small bowel to posterior wall of abdomen
  • Contains fatty tissue, mesenteric vessels, lymphatic nodes and nerves → posteriorly – 10-20 cm, oblique from left side of L2 to right sacroiliac joint → anteriorly – free part 5-6 m, represents the insertion of the jejunum and ileum

Arteries, veins, lymph, innervation

Arterial supply

  • Jejunal and ileal arteries derive from upper mesenteric artery
  • Antemesenteric margin is less vascularized → ischemic small bowel occur here fist

Venous drainage

  • Upper mesenteric vein = consecutive branch of portal vein

Lymph vessels

  • Start with central chyliferous vessel → go through mucosa, submucosa and subserosa, then lymph nodes in mesentery
  • From here lymph reaches intestinal trunk and Pequet’s cistern

Nervous innervation - Parasympathetic innervation → right vagus

  • Sympathetic innervation → great and small splanchnic nerves
  • Intestinal pain being mediated only by afferent sympathetic nerves

Intestinal layers and cells

Serosa

  • Visceral peritoneum

Muscularis - Auerbach plexus

  • Internal circular and external longitudinal

Submucosa = most mechanical resistant sheath

  • Containing nerves (Meissner plexus) + vessels

Mucosa

  • Muscularis mucosae, Kerckring valves, Villi, Crypts, Brunner/ Lieberkühn glands
  • Peyer’s patches

Intestinal epithelium contains 4 cell types

Cylindrical cells

  • Achieve absorption

Calceiform cells

  • Secrete mucus (mature cell form)

Paneth cells

Entero-endocrine cells

= Argetaffins, enterochromaffins

Physiology

  • Digestion and absorption
  • All ingested food, fluid and secretions from stomach, liver, pancreas reach small bowel
  • Total volume 9 l/ 24 h → 7 l will be absorbed; 1-2 l follow on tract to colon for further processing 2 types of small bowel contractions Segmentation contraction - Mixes chyme with digestive juices and puts it into contact with absorption surface
  • Moving it slowly downwards

Peristaltic contraction

  • Is a wave moving on 10-15 cm, and then disappears
  • Strong peristaltic waves going full length are not physiological in humans Digestion and absorption Starch
  • Starts with salivary amylase, completed by pancreatic amylase at duodenal/ upper jejunal level
  • Whole bowl can absorb monosaccharides → finished at level of upper jejunum Cellulose = Not digestible
  • Form fibers important in increasing fecal mass and avoiding constipation Proteins
  • Digested mainly due to trypsin

Lipids

  • Digested due to pancreatic lipase, bile acids (→ forming micelles)

Vit. B12 and

  • Forming complex with intrinsic factor from stomach → decomposed at ileum cells other → penetrating cells through pinocynosis/ combined with transporter vitamins
  • Folic acid, thiamine, ascorbic acid → absorbed by active mechanism
  • Hydrosoluble vit. diffuse passively through mucosa
  • Fat-soluble vit. are dissolved by formation of micelles (→ bile!) → absence of bile prevents their absorption, with exception of vit. A

1. Malformations of the small bowel

  • Classified according to Duhamel and Hagel

1. Development abnormalities

2. Position, rotation, joining abnormalities

  • All manifest in form of occlusion → Agenesia = usually fatal → Atresia = neonatal surgery, risk of malnutrition by loss of an important intestinal segment → Stenosis = may stay asymptomatic for long time → Duplications = mostly in ileum, tubular or cystic → Abnormal persistence of embryonic elements = complete or partial persistence of omphalo-mesenteric canal (complete → elimination of gas/ meconium/ ileal content through pinpoint orifice at umbilical level) → Meckel’s diverticulum = derived from limited fibrosis between the umbilicus and omphalomesenteric canal (vitellin duct)
  • a) Total absence of rotation
  • b) Partial absence of rotation
  • c) Malrotation or inverse rotations (situs inversus)

3. Abnormalities by extrinsic compression

(ring pancreas)

4. Histological structure abnormalities

(related to nerves and epithelia)

2. Small bowel diverticuli

  • Uncommon
  • Increases with age >70
  • Males more affected
  • Usually asymptomatic, incidentalomas
  • Classification - congenital (rare)/ acquired

Primary acquired

  • False diverticula = no muscular wall, only from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through muscular layer
  • Frequently associated with colon diverticulosis
  • Abnormalities of myenteric plexus with motor dysfunctions

Congenital

  • True diverticula = full thickness of wall
  • Often limited to duodenum and ileum
  • Duodenal diverticula: usual incidental finding, often located within 2 cm of papilla of Vater (area of weakening)
  • Merkel´s diverticulum

Signs and symptoms

  • 80% are asymptomatic
  • Non-specific symptoms → Colicative pain/ cramps, localized periumbilical, after meal → Gain loss → Malabsorption syndrome (anemia, Vit. B12 def., hypoproteinemia)

Diagnosis

  • Esogastroduodenoscopy (limited to duodenum)
  • Colonoscopy with last cm of ileum
  • CT
  • Small bowel fluoroscopy with barium contrast (irigography)
  • Capsule endoscopy
  • Enteroscopy (can visualize jejunum and ileum)

Treatment

Conservative

Surgical

  • NSAIDs, antibiotics
  • In case of complications
  • Small bowel segmentary resection with entero-enterostomy

Complications

  • Acute inflammation → diverticulitis
  • Hemorrhage
  • Occlusion
  • Malabsorption

Meckel’s diverticulum

  • Most frequently congenital malformation of GI tract
  • True diverticulum
  • Persistence of omphalomesenteric canal from intrauterine life
  • Appears like a cul de sac 1-12 cm long, open on antimesenteric side of small bowel
  • In 90% located in last 60 cm of ileum; in 10% connection between tip of diverticulum and post. surface of umbilicus
  • Contains its own blood pedicle
  • May have ectopic tissue → 80% gastric mucosa → Pancreatic tissue → Duodenal/ colonic/ jejunal mucosa

Signs and symptoms

  • Mostly asymptomatic → becomes symptomatic through complications → Acute diverticulitis
  • Intermittent abdominal pain
  • Anorexia, vomiting
  • Fever
  • Leukocytosis, neutrophilia
  • May mimic acute appendicitis (DD !!!!) → check last 80-100 cm of ileum when performing an appendectomy

Complications

  • GI bleeding (hematochezia/ melena and anemia) – most common in children (other causes have to be ruled out)
  • Diverticular peptic ulcer (heterotopic gastric mucosa)
  • Diverticulitis → perforation → peritonitis
  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception/ enterolites)
  • Incarceration → Littre inguinal hernia
  • Carcinogenesis → adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis

  • Enteroclysis
  • Intestinal fluoroscopy
  • Endoscopic capsule
  • CT (blind end, inflamed structure in mid abdominal cavity)
  • Atechnetium-99mTc (identifies gastric mucosa; inverstigation of choice in children)

Treatment (surgical)

  • In case of complications → emergency (peritonitis, occlusion, bleeding) → If bleeding is occult, causing anemia but no other symptoms → barium enema prior to surgery !
  • Antisecretory or H2 receptors blocker in ulcers
  • Symptomatic diverticulum needs to be removed
  • Laparoscopic resection
  • Small bowel wedge resection = diverticulectomy or segmentary enterectomy with entero-enterostomy

Acquired diverticuli

  • Macroscopically = sack-like cavities (false diverticula)
  • Usually diverticuli are multiple and decrease in frequency from Treitz’s ligament to ileocecal-valve
  • Becoming symptomatic mostly > 60 years
  • Most common complication → bleeding, perforation; rarely malabsorption
  • Therapy of choice = segmental resection of small intestine

3. Crohn’s disease

= chronic, transmural inflammatory process of bowel characterized by abdominal pain, diarrhea and extraintestinal s.

  • High risk of complications (fistulas, abscesses (intra-abdominal or anoperineal), intestinal occlusion)
  • Affects any part of GI tract from mouth to anus, highest incidence in terminal ileum
  • Granulomas (similar to tuberculous)
  • Evolves in active bouts

Epidemiology and etiology

  • Ethnic factor: Jewish people followed by Caucasians
  • Age-sex: Two incidence peaks – 3rd decade (15-35 years) and 6th decade of life, females
  • Genetic factor: HLA-B27
  • Geographical factor: developed countries, disease incidence increased constantly in last 40 years
  • Idiopathic (cause unknown)
  • Infections, psychosomatic, environmental (smokers), nutrition (ingestion of food antigens), immunological
  • Smoking – increases risk 3 folds
  • Relationship between gut mucosa – gut bacteria deranged → T cells in intestinal lamina propria overreact to contact with certain antigens → uncontrolled intestinal inflammation

Pathology

Macroscopic

Microscopic

  • 50% ileo-colic, 30% colon, 30% small bowel, 2% gastric or duodenal
  • Thickened intestinal wall and mesentery
  • Enlarged lymph nodes
  • Multiple, deep, longitudinal, curvy and transversal ulcers
  • Cobblestone mucosa with edema and hyperemia → intestinal loops will stick together forming bundles → fistulas, abscesses
  • Parts of normal mucosa (discontinous)
  • Affects all the layers (transmural) → fibrosis forms stenosis → occlusion
  • Transmural ulcers; aphthous
  • Loss of layering, submucosal edema of villi
  • Rich lymph plasma infiltrate → causing thickening
  • Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells

Signs and symptoms

  • Acute abdominal pain !
  • RUQ → involvement of terminal ileum
  • Food ingestion often triggers pain → weight loss → growth retardation in children, delayed puberty/ menstruation; rarely due to malabsorption
  • Stenosis → obstruction → colics
  • Diarrhea ! with pathological fluids (mucus, blood, pus (→ skin patches)
  • a) Incomplete recovery of bile salts (osmotic diarrhea) → cholestyramine treatment (binds bile salts)
  • b) Bacterial infection → tetracycline, metronidazole
  • c) Fistulas → esp. duodeno-/ jejuno-colic; shunting whole intestinal absorption surface → diarrhea due to undigested bolus reaching colon; only solution = surgery
  • d) Extensive colon involvement in inflammatory process → mucosal destruction → sulphosalazine, corticoids
  • Ano-perineal or perineal suppuration
  • Abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting
  • Intermittent, low-grade fever
  • Tender mass in right iliac fossa
  • Secondary anemia due to occult bleeding, rarely hematochezia → pallor, fatigue

Extraintestinal manifestations

  • Joint disorders: ¼ of cases, coincide with active phases, large joint (frequently knee), ankylosing spondilitis
  • Skin lesions: erythema nodosum, gangrenous pyodermitis during active phases
  • Eye disorders: uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, episcleritis; associated with spondylitis
  • Intraabdominal fistulas and abscesses: entero-colic/ entero-vesical/ entero-enteric/ entero-cutaneous/ recto-vaginal/ ano-perineal, intestinal perforations of ulcerations are not free but rather inside bundles or blocks built by adhesions → intestinal abscesses; high recurrence
  • Bile lithiasis: alteration of bile composition, interruption of entero hepatic cycle, secondary to advanced terminal ileitis or surgical removal (only side to reabsorb bile salts), decrease of bile salts concentration → “lithogenic bile”
  • Renal lithiasis (oxalic): secondary to injuries to terminal ileum or surgical removal, deficient reabsorption of free fatty acids that will “bind” endoluminal calcium,
  • Risk of malignancy: after long evolution (18-20 years), adenocarcinoma, 70% involve terminal ileum; prognosis more severe (diagnosis is delayed → symptomatology masked by primary disease and endoscopic access often impossible duet o stenosis); usually multiple (synchronous), located on ceco-ascending portion

Complications (exam !!!)

Intestinal

  • Strictures → bowel obstruction
  • Fistula
  • Perforation → peritonitis
  • Intraabdominal and perianal abscess
  • Mesenteric lymphadenopathy
  • Neoplasm

Systemic

  • Arthritis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Sclerosing episcleritis
  • Uveitis
  • Sclerosing cholangitis
  • Oxalate stones (renal)
  • Bile lithiasis (↓ bile salts)
  • Erythema nodosum
  • Pyoderma gangrenosum

Post-OP

  • Early complications
  • Recurrences at other intestinal segments
  • Anastomotic fibrostenosis
  • Adhesional obstruction
  • Fistulas
  • Dehiscence of intestinal sutures

Positive diagnosis

  • No specific symptoms → late

Patient history

  • Body weight loss
  • Recurrent digestive compliants (pain, diarrhea)
  • History of anemia
  • Fever of unknown cause
  • Undeveloped stature in children
  • Positive family history

Physical exam

  • Pallor
  • Weight loss
  • Inflammatory tumor in right iliac fossa
  • Peri-anorectal fistulas or abscesses
  • Extraintestinal manifestations (fever, anemia, joint pain)

Lab analysis

  • Anemia by iron deficiency
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Increased ESR

Paraclinical tests

  • Barium enema/ irigography (segmental, stenosis of terminal ileum, fistulas, damaged intestinal segments alternating with healthy ones (cobblestone aspect)
  • Endoscopy/ enteroscopy
  • Colonoscopy (normal lower colon and rectum or evidence of complications, early aphtoid ulcerations with normal surrounding mucosa, later extensive ulcers, edematous mucosa, cobblestone, stenoses)
  • CT (intestinal stenosis, wall thickening, interileal abscesses, DD with intestinal tuberculosis, lymphoma, ilio cecal tumours)

Histology

  • Confirms diagnosis

DD

  • Mainly UC !!!
  • Intestinal TBC (pulmonary signs, bacillus history)

Treatment

  • Maintaining remission of disease
  • Control of symptoms
  • No curative treatment available

Conservative

Etiological

  • Lifestyle changes
  • Amino salicylates (Sulfasalazine, Mesalazine) !
  • Corticosteroids (Prednisone, Methylprednisolone) !
  • Immunosuppressive drugs (Azathioprine, Methotrexate, Mercaptopurine) only if both above fail
  • Biologic agents anti-TNF (Infliximab, Adalimumab)
  • Antibiotics
  • Loperamide for diarrhea

Symptomatology - Anemia → iron, vit. B12, folic acid

  • Malnutrition → calories supplements; parenteral nutrition
  • Eye, skin, joint disturbances → corticosteroids, NSAID’s

Surgical

  • Surgeries are emergencies or elective
  • In case of complications: stenosis/ obstruction, fistulas/ perforations, abscesses, neoplasia
  • In case of failure of medical therapy

1) Intestinal stenosis/ obstruction → depending on size, duration → Right hemicolectomy + ileo-colic anastomosis or ileostomy → Ileo-colic or ceco-ileal excision + anastomosis of ileal stump to cecum/ ascending colon or ileo transverostomy/ ileostomy → Jejuno-ileal segmental resection + entero-enteric anastomosis → Internal bypass of super and substenotic segments → Stricturoplasty

2) Fistula → perforation

  • Internal f. a. Ileo-cecal or ileo-ileal: rarely require surgery, only with abscesses → limited ileo-cecal or ileo-colic resection + end-end or end-side anastomosis b. Ileo-sigmoid: most frequent, ileo-cecal or -colic and sigmoid resection + anastomoses c. Ileo-colic: total colectomy + ileostomy d. Ileo-vesical: frequent; hematuria, pneumaturia, fecaluria, pyuria, pollakiuria; ileal segment resection + anastomosis e. Recto-vesicle, colo-vesicle f. Ileo-vaginal, recto-vaginal, colo-vaginal g. Colo-jejunal, colo-gastric and colo-duodenal
  • External f.: spontaneous, very rare, at anastomotic sutures, often require reoperation, drainage of peri-fistular abscess, late fistulas occur with new active bout
  • Free perforation into peritoneal cavity → colostomy, Hartmann resection

3) Intraabdominal/ hepatic abscess → drainage or by US/CT guided puncture 4) Hemorrhage → rarely massive 5) Toxic megacolon (more common in UC)

  • X ray → empty abdomen with gas column of >5 cm + leukocytosis, tachycardia, >38°C
  • Subtotal colectomy with ileostomy
  • Antibiotics

6) Fulminant colitis has the same therapeutic management which, applied in time, improves and eventually cures toxemia

  • Diarrhea after removal of ileum (over 1 m) subsides with cholestiramine

4. Entero-mesenteric infarction (= EMI)

= abrupt and persistent suppression of blood flow in main trunk/ branches of upper/ lower mesenteric arteries/ veins or even capillary microcirculation → hemorrhagic necrosis of involved intestinal segment

Epidemiology

  • Age > 50y

Classification and etiology

I. EMI of arterial trunk origin

II. EMI of venous trunk origin

III. Obstruction in partial microcirculation

→ 60%

A. Embolic

B. Thrombotic (37%)

C. Other causes → 40%

  • Only thrombotic → 20%

A. Mesenteric artery embolism

  • From left ventricle or atrium, rarely paradoxical embolism (shunt from right to left)
  • Favoring diseases → MV disease, HF, acute MI, subacute bact. endocarditis, AF (most common, 80%)
  • Thrombo-embolic (61%), athero-embolic

B. Mesenteric artery thrombosis

  • > 50 y → atheromas → art. HTN, blood stasis (MI, HF)
  • < 40 y → inflammatory Buerger’s thromboangiitis, periarteritis nodosa

C. Other causes

  • Aortic dissection
  • Closed abdominal trauma

Pathogenesis

  • Suppression of blood flow in tributary to obstructed vessel
  • Embolus causes strong reflex arterial spasm both above and below
  • Causes secondary extensive postembolic thrombosis above and below site of injury
  • Arterial EMI - mostly by upper mesenteric artery (90%) and only 10% due to lower mesenteric artery → SMA has sharp angle when branching from aorta, lower one has wider, arch like, angle
  • Venous EMI - 96% in upper mesenteric vein, history of pelvic or lower caval phlebitis, hypercoagulation (polycythemia, hemoconcentration, post splenectomy thrombocytosis), venous stasis (portal hypertension, extrinsic tumoral compression on portal vein), suppurative processes (peritonitis, colic diverticulitis), abdominal trauma, irradiation, surgery
  • EMI → ischemia → necrosis → perforation and septic endotoxic shock (bacterial load of intestine, massive increase of microbial flora in ischemic and distended small bowel → endo and exotoxins that penetrated
  • Hypovolemic due to rapid massive accumulation of plasma and blood cells in intestinal wall thickness and lumen

Pathomorphology → Infarction develops in 3 stages

1. Apoplexy

  • Characterized by plegic dilation, secondary to prolonged spasm, of capillary circulation, with intraparietal plasma exudates (cyanotic, edematous red loop)
  • Potentially reversible

2. Infarction proper

  • In which capillary effractions occur, allowing blood flooding of lumen and intestinal wall (true intraluminal and intraparietal hemorrhage), intraparietal hematoma is constituted, loop being purplish-black

3. Gangrenous stage - Loop appears greenish-gray, limp, presenting multiple perforations

  • Stercoral peritonitis
  • Lesions might be segmental or extended, clearly deliniated

Clinically

  • Onset brutal, with signs of acute abdomen, continue to aggravate
  • Altered general state
  • Pallor, sweaty, restlessness with cold extremities, marbled skin → state of intense shock (low Bp, high HR)
  • Abdominal pain is very severe, violent and persistent, maximal intensity in peri-umbilical area
  • Distended abdomen, intestinal transit for feces and gas is absent (obstipation)
  • Diarrhea with enterorrhagia appears later
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Can be preceded by “abdominal angina” (intermittent, reversible attacks of mesenteric ischemia during meals)

Physical exam

  • Abdominal distention, painful to palpation, maximal at affected loop, which is sometimes felt as a soft sausage
  • Signs of peritoneal irrigation appear rapidly, generalized muscle contraction (peritonitis)
  • Percussion → tympanism (distension and dullness due to peritoneal fluid)
  • Auscultation → “deadly silence” (absence of peristalsis)
  • DRE → rounding and sensitivity of Douglas’s pouch, bloody stool

Paraclinical exam

  • Lab → leukocytosis (> 15.000), low Hb and Hct, low K, metabolic acidosis, hyperazotemia, hyperamylasemia
  • X-ray of empty GI tract → marked aerocolia (selective angiography of upper mesenteric a.)
  • Abdominal US → dilation of loops above, ischemic loops with thickened walls, without peristalsis, peritoneal fluid
  • Doppler US → may detect level of obstacle and even differentiate between thrombosis and embolism

DD

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Intestinal occlusion
  • Ruptured extrauterine pregnancy
  • Posterior MI

Prognosis

  • Mortality 80-93%

Treatment

  • Quick metabolic rebalancing → volemic and acid-base restoration with at least 2 i.v. lines
  • CVP monitoring
  • Blood transfusion
  • Nasogastric aspiration
  • Antibiotics
  • Peridural infiltration - advantages: analgesia, to fight shock, improvement of microcirculation of non-ischemic intestine; contraindication: collapse (aggravates hypotension)

Intraoperative decision making depends on

  • Condition of intestine
  • Assessment of mesenteric vascularization
  • Presence or absence of peritonitis

In incipient infarction with injuries considered potentially reversible and vascular trunk obstacle, vascular procedures are required, such as:

  • a) Embolectomy
  • b) Thrombendarteriectomy followed by venous or synthetic patch
  • c) Re-implantation of mesenteric artery into aorta
  • d) Aorto-mesenteric bypass
  • These procedures must be initiated within first 6-8 h
  • Drug therapy in early stages: anticoagulants, antiplatelet, vasodilators, streptokinase
  • After 12-36 h → 2nd laparotomy to look for possible irreversible lesions → enterectomy of necrotic loops + washing and drainage of peritoneal cavity
  • Diffuse ischemia doesn’t require resection → mesenteric arterial catheter
  • In extended lesions at advanced stages any surgical intervention is useless → Venous thrombosis is solved with difficulty and uncertainty → Portal vein thrombosis contraindicates intestinal resection → BUT if intestinal injury is reversible → direct portal thrombectomy may be performed with anticoagulation therapy Results
  • Embolectomy → 60% mortality
  • Thrombendarteriectomy → 80% mortality
  • Venous thrombectomy → 95% mortality
  • Resection without vascular procedures → 60-95% mortality

5. Tumors of the small intestine

  • Represent 1-5% of GI tract neoplasms
  • Mainly benign
  • Frequency from less to most affected: duodenum → proximal jejunum → terminal ileum
  • > 45 years
  • Asymptomatic (only 10% symptomatic) → symptoms mainly caused by malignant lesions (hemorrhage, occlusion, intussusception)
  • Low incidence explained by → fast movement of nutrients (short time contact with mucosa) → Liquid consistency of intestinal chyme → Alkaline pH → High levels of benzilperoxidase, IgA → Lymphoid tissue (solitary lymphoid nodules/ Peyer’spatches)

Risk factors

  • Familial adenomatous polyposis
  • Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC or Lynch syndrome)
  • Celiac disease
  • Heavily salted food
  • Smoking
  • Alcohol consumption
  • Often synchronous tumors (primary one in colon)

A. Benign neoplasms

Polyps/ adenomas

GIST

Juvenile polyps or retention polyps

Endometriosis

Leiomyomas, schwannomas, lipomas, hemangiomas

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Polypoid hamartomas

Gardener’s syndrome/ FAP

  • Have malignant potential in time
  • Adenomatous or villous
  • Often solitary
  • Manifested by bleeding or occlusion by invagination/ intussusception

= gastrointestinal stromal tumors

  • Originating in interstitial Cajal cells
  • Malignant potential
  • Extraluminal growth, highly vascularized → bleeding
  • Hematogenous metastasis
  • Treatment: Imatinib (Gleevec); surgical resection
  • May complicate with hemorrhage or occlusion by invagination
  • They occur more frequently in colon
  • May be eliminated spontaneously by self-amputation before adolescence
  • May become symptomatic by hemorrhage or occlusion, acute abdomen representing surgical indication
  • Solitary in patients without associated lesions
  • Usually multiple in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome = diffuse polyposis of whole GI tract and hyperpigmentation of mucosa and around orifice
  • Very low malignancy potential
  • Surgery for symptomatic cases and when polyps > 1 cm must be removed

= characterized by familial polyposis located to colon and small intestine, associated with osteomas and fibromas or subcutaneous sebaceous cysts

  • Premalignant lesion after age of 40
  • Increased incidence of duodenal periampullar cancers

B. Malignant neoplasms

Adenocarcinoma

Lymphoma

Leiomyosarcoma

Carcinoid tumors

Secondary tumors (metastasis)

= most frequent primary tumor

  • Usually affects proximal jejunum or distal ileum
  • Asymptomatic → 80% have metastases when diagnosed
  • Produces intestinal occlusion
  • Late lymphatic dissemination and metastases
  • Segmental resection with adjacent mesentery, adenopathies involving upper mesenteric artery may create problems
  • Survival after 2 years is 25%
  • With ileal starting point infiltrates submucosa and transforms affected portion into rigid segment
  • 1/3 of patients present malabsorption syndrome
  • Wide segmental resection + splenectomy, retroperitoneal ganglia biopsy and liver biopsy for staging
  • Frequently in children and young adults
  • Tend to ulcerate and bleed
  • Jejunum
  • 50% due to malignant melanoma metastases
  • Other cancers with metastases in small bowel = cervical, renal, pulmonary
  • Surgery in patients with good general condition
  • Originate in endocrine cells in intestine
  • Secretory or non-secretory (benign)
  • Associate with neoplasms of other enterochromaffin tissues (medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma)
  • Age group: 25-45 years
  • Ranks 2nd place after appendix
  • Usually in ileum
  • Macroscopic: firm, yellowish nodules situated under mucosa
  • Slow evolving tumor, but fast metastasizing
  • Asymptomatic, diagnosed often with l.n. or liver metastasis
  • Can cause pain, bleeding, occlusion or carcinoid syndrome (flushed skin, diarrhea, bronchial constriction assoc. with right heart valve disorders)
  • Serotonin, histamine, catecholamines, bradykinin, kalikrein, prostaglandins, ACTH and calcitonin
  • Elevated serum serotonin and urinary 5-HIA

Treatment

  • Segmentary enterectomy + lymphadenectomy
  • Whipple procedure for duodenal tumors
  • Right hemicolectomy for distal ileum
  • Primary tumor: uterus, ovaries, stomach and malignant melanoma
  • Hematogenous metastasis
  • Poor prognosis

Signs and symptoms

  • Diffuse abdominal tenderness
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Hemorrhage – occult/ melena/ hematochezia
  • Anemia
  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception) – König syndrome (alternating diarrhea and constipation)
  • Palpable mass (late diagnosis)

Complications

  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception)
  • GI hemorrhage - occult (anemia)/ acute (melena/ hematochezia)
  • Perforation → peritonitis

Diagnosis

  • Barium enema, enteroclysis
  • Enteroscopy, endoscopic capsule
  • Abdominal ultrasonography: tumors > 4cm
  • CT scan: >2 cm
  • Selective arteriography, Angio CT
  • Exploratory laparoscopy

title: Colon cancer
html:
Anatomy

  • Located between ileo-cecal valve and colorectal junction
  • Divided into caecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure (or right flexure), transverse colon, splenic flexure (or left flexure), descending and sigmoid colon
  • Sigmoid colon continues with rectum at colorectal junction
  • Arterial: SMA = “ right colon” (caecum, ascending colon, right flexure and right half of transverse colon) → ileo-colic, right colic and middle colic a.

IMA = “ left colon” (left half of transverse, left flexure and descending colon) → left colic artery and sigmoid a.

  • Veins: Right colon → follow arteries and drain into superior mesenteric vein and further in portal vein Left colon → follow arteries and drain into inferior mesenteric vein and splenic vein or portal vein
  • Lymphatics also follow vascular branches
  • Ascending and descending colon attached to posterior abdominal wall by Told’s fascia → non mobile
  • Only transverse colon and sigmoid colon are mobile and can be used for anastomosis and stomas

Avascular areas

Colon/ rectum covered by serosa

= intraperitoneal

  • Cecum, Transverse, Sigmoid
  • Anterior descending
  • Anterior ascending
  • Rectosigmoid
  • Upper third and anterior wall of middle third of rectum → Those subsites must invade the serosa before spreading to adjacent tissues and/or organs

Colon/ rectum without serosa

  • Posterior ascending
  • Posterior descending
  • Lower third of rectum (rectal ampulla) → Invasion into adjacent organs and tissues occurs without peritoneal involvement

Epidemiology and etiology

  • Rising incidence in developed countries
  • Peak incidence 70-80 y

Risk factors

  • Age > 50y
  • Previous polyp → adenomatous ≥ 2cm
  • IBD
  • Family history (FAP, Gardner’s, HNPCC)
  • Personal history of bowel CA
  • Diet (animal fat, meat and low fibers

Colorectal CA

  • Synchronous → 3-12%
  • Metachronous → 3%
  • Other polyps → 30%

Metastasis

  • Up to 70% of pat. with colorectal CA develop liver metastasis
  • 50% are isolated liver metastasis
  • 25% are synchronous
  • 5-10% are resectable

→ promote anaerobic bac. → bile salts transformed into carcinogens)

  • Exercise
  • Obesity
  • Smoking and alcohol

Hereditary

Sporadic

  • FAP
  • Environmental factors
  • HNPCC → Lynch syndrome I and II

* hereditary non polyposic colorectal cancer

  • 5-10% of colon CA
  • Familial clustering
  • If they don’t fit a defined syndromes → micro-satellite instability (mis-match repair)
  • All need surveillance

FAP

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Malignancy occurs at age of 30
  • > 100 adenomatous polyps and microadenomas in the large intestine
  • 100% cancer risk at age of 40
  • Gardner syndrome – associates besides familial polyposis, desmoid tumors located in midgut or abdominal wall and bone tumors

Diagnosis based on

→ Polyps → Family history → Confirmed by identification of mutation

Management

  • Colectomy

+ IRA (ileorectal anastomosis)

+ IAP (ileoanal pouch)

+ Ileostomy → 30% risk by 60 y → Don’t forget desmoids and duodenal tumors → Don´t forget rectal CA

HNPCC

  • Lynch syndrome I and II
  • NO polyps
  • 90% risk of developing CA
  • Lacks clear phenotypic characteristics

Diagnosis based on

→ Family history (Amsterdam criteria (specific, not sensitive) or Bethesda criteria) and earlier age of onset (< 45 y) → Demonstration of defective MMR (MSI) → Confirmed by identification of mutation

  • Genes implicated → MSH2, 6/ MLH1, 3/ PMS2, 1/ TGFBR2

Lynch syndrome I → familial colon cancer

Lynch syndrome II → HNPCC assoc. with other cancers of

GI tract or reproductive system

Management

  • Annual colonoscopy
  • CA125
  • CT

IRA

IAP

Amsterdam I criteria

Amsterdam II criteria

Modified Bethesda criteria

→ 3 relatives (linked) with CRC → 1 is 1st degree relative → 2 generations of CRC → 1 CRC before age 50y → FAP is excluded → > 3 relatives diagnosed with HNPCC related cancers (CRC, endometrial, small bowel, ureter, renal pelvis), one of them is 1st degree relative → 2 generations of CRC → 1 CRC before age 50y → Individuals in families that meet Amsterdam criteria → Individuals with 2 HNPCC-related cancers including synchronous and metachronous CRC or assoc. extracolonic cancers → Individuals with CRC and a 1st degree relative with CRC and/or HNPCC

Cancer development

Normal epithelium → APC loss → hyperproliferation → early adenoma → K-ras mutation → intermediate adenoma → chromosome 18 loss → late adenoma → p53 loss → cancer → Polyp removal leads to CRC prevention = prophylaxis ! → Polyp is surrogate marker Adenomatous polyps → benign, BUT high risk of developing into adenocarcinoma over time

Inflammatory bowel syndrome

  • After 10-15 years evolution → cancer
  • High risk polyps → Flat → Villous → 3 or more → > 1 cm → High grade dysplasia
  • Colonoscopy → Long term surveillance
  • Low risk = 1-2 polyps < 1cm → 5 years until negative/ none
  • Intermediate = 3-4 small or 1 polyp > 1cm → 3 years until 2- ve
  • High risk > 4 or > 2 polyps > 1 cm → 1 year then 3 years
  • 1% per year over 10 years
  • Extensive colitis
  • Colonoscopy surveillance
  • Proctocolectomy for → Cancer → Severe dysplasia

Pathomorphology

  • Vegetating, ulcerative vegetating or infiltrating (scirrhous) tumor
  • Mostly adenocarcinoma
  • Rarely - mucinousor anaplastic carcinomas, sarcomas or lymphomas

Symptoms (exam !!!)

Ascending colon

  • Anemia
  • Palpable tumor
  • Diarrhea
  • Fever

Descending colon

  • Obstruction
  • Altered bowel habit/ transit
  • Tenesmus
  • Pain

General → Malignant syndrome

  • Weight loss
  • Loss of appetite
  • Low grade fever
  • Pallor, Fatigue

Rectosigmoidian syndrome: rectorrhagia; tenesmus; blood, pus or mucus in stool Dissemination pathways

  • Direct invasion through wall into other organs/ carcinomatosis/ Krukenberg tumors/ Blumer's shelf
  • Lymph node metastasis
  • Portal vein/ hematogenous metastasis (to liver and lung)
  • Intraluminal seeding (metastatic tumors further down in colon)

Complications

  • Jaundice, hepatomegaly → liver metastasis (rarely lung metastasis)
  • Ascites, carcinomatosis nodules → peritoneal carcinomatosis
  • Peritonitis → perforations (especially of caecum (diastatic perforation))
  • Intestinal obstruction → obstructing tumor (more common in left/ descending CRC)
  • Hemorrhage → anemia
  • Neighbor organ invasion (colo-vesical and colo-vaginal fistulas)

Investigations and staging

Colonoscopy and biopsy

Blood samples

Chest X ray

Barium enema

US

CT (+ contrast)

MRI

PET

CEA

Visualization, location, + treatment of potential pre-neoplastic pathology Liver and kidney function, diabetes, CBC, tumor markers Lung metastasis Location, specify no. of lesions, stenosis, NO biopsy Colon wall thickening → not specific; peritumoral collections due to perforation; liver metastasis or carcinomatosis Location, stenosis, presence of complications (perforation, obstruction), presence of intraabdominal injuries (liver metastasis, carcinomatosis); Virtual colonoscopy BUT NO biopsy or treatment Same details as CT Detecting metastasis and relapse after radical treatment; NOT routinely Used to monitor postoperative colon cancer → Measured pre- and post-op reevaluated at predetermined time range → if ↓ = treatment was radical; if ↑ = relapse, metastasis

DD

Ascending colon

  • Pseudo tumoral form of appendicitis
  • Appendicular tumors
  • CD
  • Ileo-cecal tuberculosis
  • Other intra-abdominal tumors

Descending colon

  • Diverticular disease
  • Granulomatous colitis
  • Other intra-abdominal tumors

Colon cancer staging → Duke staging

  • Confined to bowel wall Dukes’ A → 85%
  • Through wall Dukes’ B → 65%
  • Spread to lymph nodes Dukes’ C → 35%
  • Spread to liver (metastasis) Dukes’ D → 10% → TNM staging

Primary tumor (T)

TX

Primary tumor cannot be assessed

T0

No evidence of primary tumor

Tis

Carcinoma in situ: intraepithelial or invasion of lamina propria

T1

Tumor invades submucosa

T2

Tumor invades muscularispropria

T3

Tumor invades through the muscularispropria into the pericolorectal tissues

T4a

Tumor penetrates to the surface of the visceral peritoneum

T4b

Tumor directly invades or is adherent to other organs or structures

Regional lymph nodes (N)

NX

Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed

N0

No regional lymph node metastasis

N1

Metastasis in 1-3 regional lymph nodes

N1a Metastasis in 1 regional lymph node

N1b Metastasis in 2-3 regional lymph nodes

N2

Metastasis in 4 or more lymph nodes (N2a – 4-6 LN; N2b →7 LN)

Distant metastasis (M)

M0

No distant metastasis

M1

Distant metastasis

Treatment

  • Surgery is only way to cure (>40%)
  • Chemotherapy
  • Other treatment (immunotherapy)
  • Support

Radical

Palliative → unresectable

  • Resections
  • Stoma
  • Internal bypass

1) Preparation for surgery

  • Informed consent
  • Stoma counselling
  • Bowel preparation → Fortrans, Macrogol
  • Thromboembolism prophylaxis
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis

2) Radical surgical treatment

  • For R0 resection → 10 cm margins in both directions + removal of mesocolon + lymphadenectomy Right hemicolectomy

Extended right hemicolectomy

Left hemicolectomy

Extended left hemicolectomy

Segmental colectomy

Sigmoidectomy

= resection of last loop of ileum, caecum, ascending colon, right colic flexure and first third of transverse colon

  • Restoring digestive transit through ileo-transverso-anastomosis
  • Indicated for tumors in caecum until proximal third of transverse colon
  • Segmental colectomy on transverse colon with colo-colic anastomosis
  • Indicated in tumors located in the second third of transverse colon

= resection includes distal third of transverse colon, left colonic flexure, descending colon with/without sigmoid, completed with transverso-sigmoido-anastomosis or transverso-rectal anastomosis or terminal colostomy and closing distal stump

  • Indicated in tumors located from left colonic flexure to descending colon or sigmoid
  • Spleenic flexture tumors
  • Uncommon
  • Tumors on second third transverse colon
  • Resection of transverse colon with colo-colic anastomosis
  • Tumors located in sigmoid colon
  • Colorectal anastomosis or terminal colostomy with closure of rectal stump (Op. Hartmann)

High anterior resection

Limited left or right resection

Lymph nodes: Epicolic, Paracolic, Intermediate colic, Superior mesenteric nodes, Inferior mesenteric nodes

  • ➔ Since left hemicolectomy goes together with inferior artery resection → complete oncologic resection
  • ➔ Since right hemicolectomy uses only resection of some arteries → incomplete oncologic resection

3) Palliative stomas and bypass

Colostomy

Temporary

Definitive

Lateral colostomy

Lateral/ Loop

Protective colostomy

Palliative treatment

Terminal/ end

OP Hartmann *

Rectal resection

Terminal and loop colostomy

1: Ileostomy

2: Colostomy (transverse colon or sigmoid colon → movable)

  • Transversostomy, Sigmoidostomy

* Only for sigmoid colon, often used in emergencies

Ileo transverso anastomoses for cancers located between caecum and proximal third of transverse colon Transverso sigmoido anastomosis for cancers located between distal third of transverse colon and descending colon

4)

Endoscopic treatment

Oncologic treatment

Radiation therapy

Immunotherapy

  • Useful in patient with obstruction due to tumor
  • Inserting trans-tumoral stent to release obstruction
  • By this method the patient can be operated in a single surgical procedure, not in successive surgeries
  • In addition, patient could be operated as elective surgery, after preparation, not as emergency
  • Chemotherapy that is given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or postoperative (adjuvant) depending on tumor staging
  • Some single-agent chemotherapy: 5-FU, Vincristine, Irinotecan, Oxaliplatin, Capecitabine, Bevacizumab, and Cetuximab
  • But most often multiagent chemotherapy: FOLFIRI: folic acid, 5-FU, Irinotecan; FOLFOX: Oxaliplatin, 5-FU, Leucovorin; 5-FU with Vincristine
  • Not used for colon cancer, only for rectal cancer → Levamisole or Interferon, may be given in conjunction with 5-FU chemotherapy
  • Make sure immunotherapy is first course treatment

5)

Obstructing cancer

  • Presentation at more advanced stage
  • Survival rate worse → More aggressive tumors
  • Bypass, Stoma or Stent

Perforation with/ without diastatic obstruction

  • Operative mortality = 30-40%
  • 5-year survival rate = 7-15%
  • Colonic resections with colostomy

6) Post-op complications → most important one = anastomotic fistula → may lead to peritonitis

  • Was reduced by pre-op colon preparation and use of mechanical staplers

Follow-up

  • At least for 2 years → at 3 months - abdominal US, Chest X-ray and CEA → at 6 months - CT and colonoscopy
  • After initial 2 years an annual follow-up should be done until 5 years

Screening

  • Population = simple, cheap, reliable, safe, acceptable
  • High risk → Positive FH, FAP, IBD, Adenomas

Population screening

  • Endoscopic removal of adenomas >1cm reduces risk
  • Population screening improves survival → Detection of adenomas and early cancers → Carcinomas most prevalent at 65-75 yrs → Adenomas most prevalent at 55-65 yrs
  • Aim screening at 50/ 55-75 y.
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy

title: Benign colonic disorders
html:
1. Ulcerative colitis

  • Causes ulcers in lining of rectum and colon
  • Can happen at any age, but usually between 15-30 y.
  • More frequent in women
  • Family history (20% hereditary)
  • Jewish population
  • Smoking has protective factors ! (DD for CD)

Pathomorphology

  • Macroscopic appearance
  • Initial phases: diffuse erythema and hyperemia with granular mucosa
  • Advanced stage: friable mucosa, nodular erythematous appearance and inflammatory pseudopolyps → ulcerations and bleedings
  • Worst at distal colon/ rectum (sparing of rectum = DD for CD)
  • Lesions are continuous without normal areas in between (DD to CD)
  • Microscopic appearance
  • Wide spectrum of areas with acute and chronic inflammation appearance, distorted and dilated crypts with abscesses, infiltrated and thickened muscularis mucosae
  • Limited to mucosa (DD for CD)

Etiology

  • Still unknown
  • Vascular (ischemia), autoimmune, immunological bacterial interactions, allergic mechanisms, genetic

Symptoms

  • Intensity of clinical signs and symptoms usually reflects extension and severity of colic mucosal lesions !
  • Usually has intermittent evolution with periodic exacerbations and remissions
  • Yet, 10% have continuous progressive evolution which does not respond to medical treatment Common
  • Abdominal pain
  • Diarrhea
  • Weight loss
  • Rectal bleeding and mucus

Less common

  • Poor appetite
  • Fever, night sweats
  • Rectal pain

I) Ulcerative proctitis = inflammation limited to rectum (15 cm above anal verge)

  • Often mild, intermittent rectal bleeding (rectorrhagy) is only symptom
  • If more severe → rectal pain, urgency, tenesmus, diarrhea → DD: infective proctitis (biopsy), CD (anal fistulas are not present in UC), ischemic proctitis, post-radiation proctitis, proctitis secondary to colostomy
  • Rarely extends upstream
  • Usually does not requires surgical treatment

II) Proctosigmoiditis = inflammation of rectum and sigmoid colon (25-30 cm from anal verge) → rectal bleeding, urgency, tenesmus, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain/ cramps, fever, weight loss

  • Harvesting multiple biopsies is paramount as macroscopic lesions can be exceeded by microscopic ones (reflecting real extension of disease !)

III) Left-sided colitis = inflammation from rectum to left colon → bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, weight loss, left-sided abdominal pain IV) Pancolitis or universal colitis = inflammation affecting entire colon → bloody diarrhea very frequent, abdominal pain and cramps, weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, anemia, dehydration V) Fulminant colitis = rare but severe form of pancolitis → Pat. are extremely ill with anemia, dehydration, severe abdominal pain, protracted diarrhea + bleeding, shock → Risk of developing toxic megacolon and colon perforation Extraintestinal manifestations

  • Arthritis and spondylitis → HLA-B27
  • Dermatological lesions = nodular erythema, gangrenous pyodermitis
  • Ocular lesions = uveitis, episcleritis, keratoconjunctivitis
  • Hepatic = primitive sclerotic cholangitis !

Colitis activity assessment → Truelove and Witts Severity Index

MILD

SEVERE

Stools (#/day)

<4

>6

Blood in stool

Intermittent

Frequent

Temp° C

Normal

< 37.5

Pulse

Normal

> 90

Hemoglobin

Normal (> 11)

< 75 % of normal (< 11)

ESR (mm/h)

< 30

> 30

Radiography

Normal

Thumbprinting

Abdominal exam

Normal

Tender, no rebound

FULMINANT

>10

Continuous

> 37.5 (fever)

> 90 (tachycardia)

Transfusion required

> 30

Dilated colon

Distended, +/- rebound

Complications

  • Persistent hemorrhage with consequent anemia
  • Ulcers larger > 5 mm in diameter or of > 10 ulcers of any diameter over a 10 cm colon length → spontaneous hemorrhage = criteria for severe form!
  • Fulminant colitis and Toxic megacolon
  • 10-13% of cases
  • 5-44% mortality!
  • Tachycardia and fever (negative role of corticotherapy → suppress clinical picture and “hide” perforation)
  • Repeated plain abdominal X ray, ultrasound, CT important for evaluation of efficacy of treatment
  • Dilation of transverse colon > 6 cm, loss of haustrations = radiological criteria for toxic megacolon
  • High risk of perforation
  • Perforation
  • Increase in body temp. and appearance of colic pneumatosis on X ray → indicate imminence of perforation
  • Stenosis
  • In time colon becomes rigid, shortened, haustrations disappear, stenoses, local smooth muscle hypertrophy
  • Stenotic areas usually do not exceed 2-3 cm
  • Stenoses longer > 5 cm, more likely malignant !
  • Cancer
  • 3-5 fold increased risk

Risk factors include

  • extensive involvement of colon (pancolitis)
  • evolution > 3 years
  • onset in childhood or adolescence → Even patients with asymptomatic pancolitis/ colo sigmoiditis require periodic endoscopy

Toxic megacolon

  • Dilation > 5.5 cm on X-ray
  • Fever (38.5°C)
  • Tachycardia (120)
  • Leukocytosis (10.5)
  • Anemia
  • Dehydration
  • State of consciousness
  • Electrolytes
  • Hypotension

Etiology

  • CD
  • Colitis due to Clostridium difficile
  • Other infectious diseases → Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, CMV assoc. with HIV, amoebae
  • Ischemic colitis
  • Ineffective peristalsis → paralysis of myenteric plexus
  • Distension leads to perforation
  • Sepsis and death

Imaging

  • Colonoscopy + biopsy (s. pathomorphology)
  • Barium enema: not routinely performed anymore, but number of elements are characteristic - initial rigidity and diminished distendibility of inflamed segment, effacement of haustrations, “tubularization”, shortening/ retraction of colon, mucosa takes granular, nodular appearance, ulcers, continuity from rectum all the way upstream

DD

  • Crohn’s disease !
  • Dysenteries
  • Rectal/colic malignancy

Treatment

Conventional therapies

  • 5-ASAs/ sulfasalazine !
  • Corticosteroids !
  • Azathioprine/ 6-mercaptopurine, Methotrexate, Cyclosporine, Infliximab

Management of fulminant colitis and toxic megacolon

General

  • I.v. fluid and correction of electrolytes
  • Complete bowel rest
  • Discontinue anticholinergics, antidiarrheals, narcotics !
  • Rule out infectious diseases

Decompression

  • Rectal tube
  • Nasogastric or long nasointestinal tube

Medical care

  • I.v. corticosteroids for inflammatory bowel disease
  • Broad spectrum antibiotics

Surgical intervention - Failed medical care after 48-72 h

  • Progressive toxicity or dilation
  • Signs of perforation
  • Pre-pubertal children

Surgery

  • Curative resection ! (unlike in CD)
  • Removes threat of life-threatening complications
  • Obviates need for medical therapy
  • Reasonable quality of life
  • Indications for elective surgery

1. Lack of response to medical treatment

2. Malignization

3. Increased risk of malignization (dysplasia)

4. Extra intestinal manifestations

5. Stature weight retardation in children

  • Indications for emergency surgery

1. Fulminant colitis resistant to medical treatment

2. Toxic megacolon

3. Perforations, abscesses

4. Important hemorrhage

5. Acute bowel obstruction

1) Elective surgery

  • Total proctocolectomy + ileostomy: resection of entire colon and rectum, ileal stump externalized, mesentery is keept (in contrast to cancer)
  • Total colectomy + ileo-recto anastomosis: less frequent, mild or no rectal involvement, disadvantages appearance of ulcerative proctitis, risk of malignization and great number of soft stools
  • Total colectomy + stripping of rectal mucosa and ileo-rectal anastomosis: s. oben + detachment and excision of rectal mucosa over 5-6 cm above dentate line
  • Ileostomy: terminal, continent reservoir (Koch), J or S or W shaped reservoir 2) Emergency surgery
  • Subtotal colectomy + ileostomy

Success rates not perfect

  • 64% clinical remission
  • 23% “rescue” colectomy
  • 30-40% of those hospitalized with acute, severe colitis require colectomy Predictors of colectomy
  • > 8 stools/ day
  • Increased CRP
  • > 3 stools/ day after 3rd day of admission → 85% colectomy

Complications in colon surgery

  • UTI retention
  • Significant hypokalemia
  • Ileus
  • GI tract → abscess, leak, SBO
  • Cardiac
  • Atelectasis (requiring bronchoscopy)
  • Pneumonia

2. Colonic diverticulosis

  • Affects 50% of individuals > 60 years → only 20% develop symptomatic disease
  • Prevalence among females and males similar, males present at younger age
  • Diverticulosis is rare in underdeveloped countries, where diets include more fiber
  • Pseudodiverticulum → involves only protrusion/ herniation of mucosa through muscularis propria of colon
  • Occurs at point where vasa recti penetrate through muscularis propria up to peritoneal serosa
  • Diverticula commonly affect sigmoid, followed by descending colon (high-pressure zone)

Pathogenesis

  • Chronic intracolonic overpressure (chronic constipation (low fiber diet))
  • Collagen defect or other disturbances of colonic parietal structure

Clinically

  • Mainly asymptomatic
  • Abdominal discomfort, borborygmus, change in rhythm and nature of defecation
  • Crampy pain in left iliac fossa; may last for hours or days → Being exacerbated by food and partially relived by defecation or gas emission

Complications

  • Diverticulitis = inflammation of diverticulum due to retention of particulate material within diverticular sac and formation of fecalith Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis
  • Fever
  • Leukocytosis
  • Anorexia
  • LLQ abdominal pain
  • Obstipation
  • Localized or generalized peritonitis
  • Air-fluid level in LLQ on plain abdominal film

Complicated diverticulitis

  • Peridiverticular abscess
  • Perforation → free → peritonitis (rare) → localized → abscess
  • Stricture/ stenosis → partial or even complete obstructions
  • Fistula (perforations usually occur gradually and colonic segments become sticky due to inflammation → erosion into vagina, urinary bladder, small intestine or skin)
  • Vasa recti are eroded by fecalith → bleeding
  • Most common cause of hematochezia in patients > 60 y
  • Increased risk for bleeding → hypertension, atherosclerosis, NSAIDs
  • Most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest

Hinchey classification system → Staging of perforated diverticular disease Stage I Stage II Stage III Stage IV

Pericolic or mesenteric abscess

Walled-off pelvic abscess

Generalized purulent peritonitis

Generalized fecal peritonitis

Paraclinical diagnosis

Irrigoscopy/

  • Effective, but nowadays not common anymore irrigography
  • Barium will opacify diverticula - round, clear-cut, possible fistulas

CT

= best method

  • Thickened colonic wall > 4 mm, strictures
  • Inflammation within pericolic fat +/- collection of contrast material or fluid (abscess)

Abdominal US

  • May also provide useful information (colonic wall, intra-abdominal collections, fistulas) at much lower cost Colonoscopy
  • Accurate information regarding mucosal changes, possibly source and therapy of hemorrhage, but does NOT provide data on pericolic changes
  • Extremely important that endocolic pressure during exploration does not increase excessively (risk of perforation)
  • Essential in detection of other concomitant lesions (benign, malignant tumors)
  • Followed closely with repetitive colonoscopy, looking for evidence of colonic ischemia Angiography
  • Important for source and therapy of massive bleeding → Barium enema or colonoscopy should not be performed in the acute setting because of higher risk of perforation
  • Barium enema or colonoscopy should be performed ~6 weeks after an attack of diverticular disease
  • Sigmoid malignancy can masquerade as diverticular disease

DD

  • Ovarian cyst
  • Endometriosis
  • Acute appendicitis
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease

Treatment

Medical treatment

Surgical treatment

Asymptomatic

  • Fiber-enriched diet
  • Glucagon i.m.
  • Avoid nuts and popcorn

Symptomatic

  • Bowel rest with water diet (diverticulitis) - Antibiotics
  • Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole
  • Addition of ampicillin for non-responders
  • IV piperacillin or oral penicillin/ clavulanic acid
  • Nasogastric suction in severe cases
  • 2 attacks of diverticulitis requiring hospitalization
  • Not rapidly improve on medical therapy

Goals of surgical management

  • Controlling sepsis
  • Eliminating complications
  • Removing distended colonic segment
  • Restoring intestinal continuity

Elective

  • Sigmoidectomy
  • Left hemicolectomy

+ colorectal anastomosis

Emergency

  • Sigmoidectomy
  • Left hemicolectomy

+ closure of distal stump and temporary colostomy

  • with restoration of digestive tract after 6-8 weeks

Indications for elective surgery

  • > 2 diverticulitis episodes
  • Immunosuppressed
  • Long duration of corticosteroid treatment
  • First attack of diverticulitis occurring < 40y
  • Subocclusive snd.
  • Impossibility to exclude cancer
  • Fistulas

Indications for emergency surgery

  • Generalized peritonitis (free perforation/ abscess)
  • Abundant bleeding
  • Intestinal complete occlusion

Options for surgical management

1. Proximal diversion of fecal stream with ileostomy or colostomy and sutured omental patch with drainage 2. Resection with colostomy and mucus fistula or closure of distal bowel with formation of Hartmann's pouch

3. Resection with anastomosis (colo-proctostomy)

4. Resection with anastomosis and diversion (colo-proctostomy with loop ileostomy)

  • Patients with presumed bleeding from diverticular disease requiring emergent surgery without localization should undergo a total colectomy → Surgery should be performed if patient is unstable or has had a 6-unit bleed within 24 h
  • Percutaneous drainage recommended for abscesses > 5 cm with well-defined wall that is accessible
  • Paracolic abscesses < 5 cm in size may resolve with antibiotics alone

Contraindications to percutaneous drainage

  • No percutaneous access routes
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Fecal peritonitis

Hinchey stage

I

II

III

IV

Operative procedure

Resection with primary anastomosis without diverting stoma

Resection with primary anastomosis

+/- diversion

Hartmann’s procedure vs. diverting colostomy and omental pedal graft

Hartmann’s procedure vs. diverting colostomy and omental pedicle graft

Anastomotic leak rate%

3.8

Overall morbidity%

3.8

0 vs. 6 mortality

6 vs. 2 mortality
