title: Benign anal and perianal disorders
html:
1. Hemorrhoids

  • Due to dystrophic changes of venous wall (perianal veins) = varix of ano-rectal veins
  • Ano-rectal veinous stasis plays major role
  • Typical lesion is venous dilation at level of hemorrhoidal plexus (between superior hemorrhoidal vein and middle and inferior hemorrhoidal sinus → meeting point of portal and caval system)
  • Internal hemorrhoids are painless (above pectinate line) → lack of sensory innervation
  • External hemorrhoids are painful (below pectinate line) → sensory innervation from inferior rectal nerve
  • Mixed

Etiology

Primitive/ Essential H.

  • Can be due to hereditary predisposal, local irritation, malnutrition
  • Are more common in families with background of hernia and varix of lower limb
  • Can be associated with IBD (CD, UC)
  • Pregnancy → increased pressure and hormonal changes
  • Low fiber-diet
  • Reading on toilet → impaired venous return

Secondary H.

  • Porto-caval anastomosis → any obstacle in their area (e.g., cirrhosis, rectal tumors or large pelvic tumors) → must be ruled out Clinical manifestation
  • Engorged anal mucosa easily traumatized → rectal bleeding (bright red due to high blood oxygen content)
  • Prolapse leads to soiling and mucus discharge → triggering pruritus and predisposes to incarceration and strangulation

Evolution of internal hemorrhoids

Grade I

  • Can reach anal canal during defecation without prolapse but can bleed

Grade II

  • Hemorrhoids may protrude beyond anal verge with straining or defecating but reduce spontaneously when straining ceases Grade III
  • Hemorrhoids protrude spontaneously or with straining and require manual reduction Grade IV
  • Hemorrhoids chronically prolapse and cannot be reduced
  • Usually contain internal and external components
  • May present with acute thrombosis or strangulation

Complications

Natural evolution begins with anitis → spreading of inflammation into veins = hemorrhoidal phlebitis → dilation of affected veins → vein hypertrophy with reflex contracture of sphincter and irreducibility of hemorrhoidal thrombosis → spontaneous healing of thrombosed H. forms a cutaneous flap

  • Bleeding
  • Suppuration
  • Necrosis
  • Fissure
  • Ulcer
  • Phlebitis of portal branches

Diagnosis

  • Inspection with rectal exam
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy → necessary to rule out inflammation or neoplasia
  • Pancolonoscopy is safer if pat. is > 40 y or unspecific symptoms

Treatment

Grade I

  • Usually symptoms relieved by better local hygiene, avoidance of excessive straining, balanced diet with fiber
  • Suppositories and ointments containing cortisone should be avoided on long term basis Grade II
  • Conservative techniques (rubber-band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared photocoagulation, carbon dioxide freezing, heater probe)
  • Rubber band ligation is easy and cheap BUT can lead to severe perineal sepsis and even death Grade III and IV
  • Failure of non-operative therapy and with significant symptoms → hemorrhoidectomy 1) Simple thrombosed external hemorrhoids - excision in office under local anesthesia immediately after onset
  • Ultrasonic scissors, bipolar electrocoagulation, laser can be used for resection
  • Prior to surgery, subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis in valvular patients must be administered 2) Stapled hemorrhoid surgery (Longo technique) = procedure of choice for prolapsed hemorrhoids
  • Purse-string suture placed with help of a plastic funnel-shaped device in mucosa and submucosa above dentate line beneath anvil; stapler is placed and closed
  • Excess hemorrhoid tissue resected by circular scalpel of stapler
  • Hemostasis with interruption of blood supply is ensured by staple-line

2. Anal fissures

= radial tear affecting epithelium of anus

Causes

  • Usually caused by passage of bulky, dehydrated piece of stool in constipated patients
  • Iatrogenic
  • Self-inflicted (foreign bodies)
  • Trauma
  • Inflamed and fragile epithelium in diarrhea can also be affected by anal fissure Chronic fissure = persistent ulcerous lesion with granulation tissue-covered base and fibrotic margins
  • Typically situated on posterior midline (over 90%) and is usually hidden by skin tag
  • Fibers of internal anal sphincter can be visible

DD

  • CD, TBC, Syphilis, Carcinoma

Symptoms

  • Vicious circle pain-spasm-pain associated with constipation (withhold defacation)
  • Small bleedings smear stool surface

Physical exam

  • DRE difficult because of spasm
  • 1-2 % lidocaine gel and gentle spreading of anus can visualize sentinel tag which hides anal fissure

Treatment

Conservative

  • Acute fissures usually heal without any special help
  • Local hygiene and avoidance of constipation
  • Chronic fissures may not respond and need → Anesthetic gel → Warm local bath 5 min before and after defecation → 0.2 % nitroglycerin ointment in anal canal will also ameliorate blood flow → Local injection of botulinic toxin bears risk of recurrence after 3 months Surgical 1) Anal dilation procedure (Lord procedure) → rare nowadays → gentle, progressive anal dilatation (under spinal anesthesia) for several minutes, must allow insertion of 3 fingers, but without tearing internal sphincter 2) Partial lateral internal sphincterotomy (method of choice) → reduces tension in anus and allows fissure to heal → Closed technique (not preferred): inserting thin scalpel between sphincters and cutting only internal component → Open technique: segmental incision between two sphincters, internal sphincter is then dissected and radially cut 3) In recurrent cases plastic procedures using flaps must be considered

Closed

Open

3. Perirectal (anorectal) abscess

  • Arise from cryptitis caused by obstruction of mucus-secreting anal glands which drain into anal crypts

Different types according to its progress and anatomical spaces

  • Submucosal
  • Ischiorectal
  • Pelvirectal
  • Horseshoe shaped
  • Supralevator or pelvisubperitoneal

Signs and symptoms

  • Perianal discomfort, pruritus (fist signs)
  • Inflammatory → swelling, redness, tenderness, elevated temp. of overlying skin (calor, dolor, rubor, tugor)
  • Deep collections can alter general status, fever, chills, nausea
  • Pelvisubperitoneal abscesses can associate urinary signs, particularly dangerous as they spread to retroperitonum

Diagnosis

  • Endorectal and vaginal US
  • CT
  • DRE → protrusion of rectal wall

Complications

  • Perianal fistula

Treatment

  • Percutaneous punction and drainage → Proper drainage can only be performed under spinal anesthesia
  • Cavity must be thoroughly explored digitally, necrotic tissue removed and everything drained (otherwise it may progress towards deeper structures)
  • Drain left in place for 1-3 days to evacuate and avoid premature spontaneous closure
  • Local lavage with antiseptics is useful but high pressure must be avoided (risk of spreading bacteria to healthy tissue)
  • Antibiotics alone not sufficient BUT treatment must be started before surgical drainage
  • Bacterial infection contains colonic flora → Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria (antibiogram !)
  • Sometimes it is so aggressive that it leads to Fournier gangrene

4. Fistula in anno

= hollow tract lined with granulation tissue, usually with proximal end at level of dentate line and distal one in perianal skin

  • Usually from perianal abscess after spontaneous drainage !
  • In complex fistulas → more than one distal opening

Associated conditions with complex fistula

  • CD
  • Diverticulitis
  • Local radiotherapy
  • Steroid therapy
  • HIV infection

Goodsall rule

= postulates that if the cutaneous opening is …

  • anterior → fistula will have a straight radial course to dentate line
  • posterior → fistula will be curved with internal opening on posterior midline

DD

  • Hydrosadenitis
  • Pilonidal sinus
  • Tuberculosis
  • Rectovaginal fistulae
  • Urethral-cutaneous fistulae

Symptoms

  • History of perianal abscesses followed by drainage of pus (slightly hemorrhagic and usually small volume)
  • Cutaneous orifice can close spontaneously → collecting of discharge, inflammation of surrounding tissue, after a few days spontaneous reopening and evacuation of larger amount of puss

Diagnosis

  • DRE
  • Fistulography with iodine-contrast for recurrent cases and for mapping of complex fistulas
  • Endorectal US
  • CT (finds hidden abscesses)

Treatment

  • Classical surgical treatment = fistulectomy and/or fistulotomy
  • Fistulectomy = removes entire fibrotic tract by dissection of tract from skin to proximal opening, injecting a dye through distal end can help to find the tract
  • Fistulotomy: canulation of fistula with probe, opening tract as wide as possible from one end to the other, part of the sphincter situated between fistula and mucosa is also divided
  • This usually does not lead to incontinence, exception - elderly or recurrences of fistulae
  • Thus, it is prohibited to perform more than one fistulotomy at a time, otherwise incontinence cannot be avoided
  • Special fistulotomy: sequential ligatures or seton placement
  • Monofilament or rubber bands passed through fistula
  • First knot tied in surgery, others at 3-day intervals under local anesthesia
  • Last ligature cuts through tissue
  • Band acts as cutting and draining tool
  • Is applied in recurrences, complex fistulae, anterior fistulae in women, Crohn disease and elderly people with low resting pressure

Seton placement

6. Pilonidal sinus

= cavity containing small amount of hair, pus, with walls lined with granulation tissue

  • Pathogenesis: formation of granulative tissue around hair that migrated tran-cutaneously (NOT hair growing “inside” or in “wrong direction”)
  • Usually situated in midline of sacrococcygeal skin of hirsute young men
  • Definitive operative management consists frequently in simple excision without closure
  • Dye (methylene blue) is injected through sinus and entire capsule of fibrotic and granulation tissue is removed and wound left to heal by secondary intention (healing may take 3-4 weeks)
  • Secondary suture after healthy granulative tissue fills gap/ whole

title: Rectal cancer
html:
Anatomy

  • Rectosigmoid junction between sigmoid colon and rectum → 15-17 cm from anal verge
  • Rectum 12-15 cm long and 4-16 cm from anal verge
  • Rectal tumors are < 16 cm from anal verge
  • Located at midpiece of sacrum (S3 vertebra)
  • Rectum is covered by peritoneum → on anterior surface and sides in upper 1/3 → anterior surface only in middle 1/3 → not covered in lower 1/3
  • It is divided into → Lower 0-6 cm from anal verge → Middle 7-11 cm → Upper 12-16 cm Arteries

Veins

Lymphatics

  • Superior Rectal Artery = main continuation of inferior mesenteric artery
  • Middle Rectal Artery  (internal iliac artery = Hypogastric a.)
  • Inferior Rectal Artery  (internal pudental artery)
  • Superior rectal vein → portal vein
  • Middle rectal vein → inferior vena cava
  • Inferior rectal v. (= inferior hemorrhoidal v.) → pudental v. → internal iliac v. → IVC Inferior
  • Superficial inguinal nodes
  • Internal iliac nodes

Middle

  • The middle collecting lymph vessels drain into the internal Iliac chain (= hypogastric lymph nodes) → Aortic lymph nodes Superior
  • Lymphatic nodes accompanying origin of superior rectal artery (its bifurcation or trifurcation = Mondor’s lymph nodes)
  • Inferior mesenteric lymph nodes

Epidemiology

  • 2nd most frequent cancer of digestive tract (after gastric cancer); 60% of total large bowel tumors
  • More frequent in urban areas and developed countries (diet rich in fat and poor in fibers, higher life expectancy)
  • Most important risk factor: age (mainly after 50)
  • Maximum incidence 7th decade (60-69 years old), incidence begins to increase before 40
  • Men/Women = 9/5
  • Higher in African American populations and Ashkenazi Jewish
  • Most large bowel cancers occur in lower left side of colon near rectum-rectosigmoid junction
  • Synchronous tumor in 5 %
  • Metachronous tumors in 3-5 % (second tumor developing after resection of first)

Etiology

Diet

Benign colonic tumors

Inflammatory bowel disease

Radiation

Genetic factors

Surgical intervention on GI tract

  • Diet rich in saturated fats
  • Low-fiber diet
  • Diet rich in smoked foods
  • High alcohol intake
  • Obesity, insulin resistance
  • Smoking
  • Adenoma → adenocarcinoma sequence in large bowel
  • A period of 10 - 15 years of latency

1. Ulcerative colitis (Colitis ulcerosa, UC)

2. Crohn's disease with rectal location

  • Especially pelvis high dose radiation
  • Tumors occur after a latency period of 10 years
  • History of familial adenomatous polyposis
  • Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome I and II)
  • Acromegaly
  • Personal history of colon, rectum, ovary, endometrium, breast CA
  • Ureterosigmoidostomy (↑ risk of sigmoid neoplasm around stomy)
  • Gastric surgery (Billroth I and vagotomies)
  • Cholecystectomy (through increased biliary acids excretion)
  • Colic resections

Protective factors

  • Vit. D, folate, vitamins and antioxidants in fruit and vegetables, high fiber intake, low meat and animal fat
  • Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage)
  • NSAIDs, aspirin
  • Coffee
  • Hormone replacement therapy
  • Physical activity

Pathomorphology

Macroscopic

Microscopic

  • Proliferative, polypoid, exophytic
  • Ulcerative
  • Infiltrative-stenosing
  • Combination
  • AdenoCA = most common → 95%
  • Colloid (mucinous) CA
  • Signet ring cell CA
  • Undifferentiated CA
  • Squamous cell CA
  • carcinoid, GIST, sarcoma, melanoma, lymphoma

Clinical manifestation

  • Lower GI bleeding (often attributed to hemorrhoids, occult, fresh blood; black and tarry stools
  • Abdominal pain (pelvic and/or perineal)
  • Recent onset of bowel habits alteration (diarrhea and/or constipation)
  • Change in stool caliber = “crayon shaped stools” for inferior/ medium rectal tumors
  • Mucus discharge
  • Tenesmus
  • Sensation of incomplete evacuation
  • Anal incontinence → invasion of nerves or internal sphincter
  • When low back pain, locally advanced tumor should be suspected
  • 10% present with bowel obstruction
  • Weight loss, anorexia, asthenia, weakness, fatique

Complications

  • Bowel obstruction
  • Perforation; only for superior part of rectum; sometimes diastatic perforation
  • Fistula with urinary bladder/vagina/urethra
  • Hemorrhage
  • Rectal prolapse
  • Adjacent tissue invasion
  • Metastatic spread

Diagnosis

  • General physical examination: attention to inguinal lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, and jaundice
  • DRE: carcinomas belonging to inferior rectum → felt as hard mass, often ulcerated, with various degrees of circumferential extent, mobile or fixed to surrounding tissues, bleed easily
  • If superior or middle rectal tumor → cannot be assessed digitally, but strings of blood or even stool sample may be present on examination glove → RECTAL EXAM – COMPULSORY! Lab analysis → CBC
  • Hb decreased → iron deficiency anemia
  • Leukocytosis
  • ALP, GGT increased → hepatic metastasis
  • Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) increased

Imaging

Total colonoscopy

  • Mandatory
  • Biopsy + macroscopic aspect
  • Be aware of synchronous cancer of colon !
  • Determining distance between inferior margin of tumor and anal verge → determine whether anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection is needed Anorectal/ Endorectal - T and N staging: penetration of wall layers and nodal status US → uT1: tumor confined to submucosa (not penetrating muscularis propria), with intact bright middle hyperechoic layer (muscularis mucosa) → uT2: tumor invading muscularis propria with no disruption of third hyperechoic layer → uT3: tumor penetrating muscularis propria to involve perirectal fat and tissues, tumor edge is usually irregular with disruption of 3rd hyperechoic layer (muscularis propria) → uT4: tumor invading an adjacent structure
  • Overstaging occurs due to inflammatory reaction around carcinoma and differentiating T2 lesions from T3 might sometimes become difficult Abdominal US
  • Rectal tumor-superior
  • Regional lymphadenopathy
  • Hepatic metastasis > 1 cm in diameter
  • Carcinomatous ascites

CT thorax, abdomen,

  • M staging pelvis
  • Superior to abdominal US

Pelvic MRI

= Golden standard

  • High accuracy for rectal fascia propria invasion, distance from anal verge, presence of adenopathy, evaluation of mesorectum
  • Best for describing relationship between lesion, levator ani and sphincter X-ray thorax
  • Pulmonary metastasis

PET scan

  • Suspicion of recurrence - or pulmonary metastasis

X-ray abdomen

  • Useful in emergency service (bowel obstruction or intestinal perforation)

Urography/cystoscopy - Fistulas or invasion

Irrigoraphy

Simple or double contrast; not routinely used

Screening

  • 5-year survival rate after resected colorectal cancer is 65%

Mild risk

  • Age, diet, physical inactivity, obesity, smoking, alcohol → Colonoscopy every 10 years after age 50 Intermediate risk - Personal history of colorectal cancer, strong family history → Colonoscopy every 3-5 years after age 40 High risk
  • Familial colorectal cancer syndromes → for familial polyposis after age of 10 → for Crohn/ RCH with 10 years evolutions (annually) → for family history – 10 years before family member had cancer

DD

IBD

Rectal benign tumors

Secondary rectal tumors

Other rectal diseases

  • UC, CD, Radic rectitis
  • Polyp/ adenoma
  • Teratoma
  • Hemangioma
  • Tumoral invasion from adjacent organs (ovaries, cervix, prostate)
  • Gastric cancer pelvic metastasis (Blumer´s shelf)
  • Rectal teleangiectasia
  • Simple ulcer of rectum
  • Ulcerations of venereal etiology
  • Ischemic rectal colitis or stenosis
  • Actinic stenosis
  • Hemorrhoidal disease

Dissemination pathway

Direct pathway

Progressive “step-by-step” dissemination into adjacent tissue

  • In axial direction
  • Circumferential
  • Into rectal wall thickness
  • ”frozen pelvis”

Lymphatic pathway - Superior rectal nodes → sigmoid nodes → inferior mesenteric nodes

  • Internal iliac nodes (hypogastric nodes) → paraortic nodes
  • Inguinal nodes (anal canal carcinoma)

Serous pathway

  • Via peritoneum, only for superior rectal tumors → peritoneal carcinomatosis Venous pathway → Superior rectal artery → portal vein → liver → Middle rectal veins → internal iliac vein → cave vein → lungs → Inferior rectal veins → external iliac vein → cave vein → lungs Perineural spread Sites of metastasis Via blood Via lymphatics Per continuitatem
  • Liver, Lung, Brain, Bones
  • Lymph nodes
  • Abdominal wall
  • Nerves
  • Vessels

Tumoral grading

G1 Well differentiated → Low grade

G2 Moderately differentiated

G3 Poorly differentiated tumors

G4 Undifferentiated → High grade

= most aggressive

Tumor staging

  • ➔ Astler-Coller staging system

Stage A

  • Limited to mucosa
  • No lymph node involvement

Stage B1

  • Extending into muscularis propria
  • No lymph node involvement

Stage B2

  • Penetrating through muscularis propria
  • No lymph node involvement

Stage C1

B1 + lymph node involvement

Stage C2

B2 + lymph node involvement

Stage D

Distant metastatic spread (liver, lungs, bone)

  • ➔ TNM staging

T

Tis

Carcinoma in situ: intraepithelial or invasion of lamina propria

T1

Tumor limited to mucosa (invades submucosa)

T2

Tumor invades muscularis propria

T3

Tumor invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/ pericolic/ perirectal tissues T4 Tumor directly invades other organs/ perforates N N0 No regional lymph nodes N1 Metastasis in 1-3 regional lymph nodes N2 Metastasis in > 4 regional lymph nodes M M0 No distant metastasis M1 Distant metastasis present

  • ➔ Rectal cancer clinical stage grouping

Clinical stage

Stage I

T1-2, N0M0

Stage II

T2-4, N0M0

Stage III

T1-4, N+M0

Stage IV

Any T, any N, M1

Treatment

1) Surgical treatment

  • TNM determines local excision (T1), radical resection (T2) or neoadjuvant therapy (T3); nodal involvement (N+) eliminates chance for curative local excision → radical/ palliative Colon preparation methods Fortrans solution method - Doesn’t get absorbed by intestinal wall
  • Undegradable by intestinal flora
  • 3-4 sachets of Fortrans get dissolved in 1 L of water each
  • To be ingested the noon of the day preceding the surgical intervention

Fast-track method

  • Method currently used
  • Enema preparation, previous evening and morning of surgery
  • Antibiotics (cephalosporines + metronidazole), previous evening and morning of sur.
  • Ingestion of 250 ml 10 % Glucose (morning of surgery)

Surgical treatment

Local excision

  • T1 only, N0, inferior rectum (within 8 cm from anal verge), well/ moderately differentiated, mobile and small tumor (< 3 cm), with no vascular or perineural spread
  • Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery (TEM) - full-thickness excision with R0 margins, defects sutured
  • Complications are rare (urinary retention, hemorrhage, suture dehiscence, perirectal fat infection, rectovaginal fistulae)
  • Local recurrency possible (usually due to understaging or small positive lymph nodes (< 5 mm) usually not visible)

Radical resection

  • T1 (with high risk features), T2 and no nodal involvement → transabdominal resection is first line
  • Gold standard = total mesorectal excision (TME) - full rectal mobilization, preservation of urinary continence and sexual function (sparing hypogastric plexus and nervi erigentes), sharp dissection with free radial margins
  • Dissection of mesorectum 5 cm below inferior margin of tumor
  • Fixation of tumor to neighboring structures might be inflammatory
  • Unresectable if metastasis → colostomy might still be performed to avoid bowl obstruction
  • Middle rectal cancer: anterior resection and abdominoperineal resection possible → safety margin on 1-2 cm have to be achieved
  • In bowl obstruction → Hartmann’s resection (proximal colostomy and closure of rectal stump) offers possibility of tumor removal, time for tissue to heal and reestablishment of intestinal continuity usually after 6 months
  • Anastomosis requires good blood supply for both bowel ends and tension free technique; single or double layer suture or mechanical stapler; air test should be negative (air insufflated in distal rectum when pelvis is filled with saline)
  • Sometimes protective ileostomy, to decrease amount of contents going through anastomosis; reintegrated at a later date (6 weeks - 3 months), but it has not significantly decreased anastomotic leakage
  • In CRC → liver metastasis are always resected

I. Anterior resection (Dixon procedure)

II. Low anterior resection

III. Ultra-low anterior resection

IV. Abdomino-perineal resection (Miles’ technique)

Laparoscopic surgery

  • Part of sigmoid colon and upper rectum removed
  • Colo-rectal anastomosis
  • Used for upper 2/3 of rectum cancer → at least 5 cm from anal verge !!!
  • Adequate resection margin
  • Sphincter sparing
  • Using linear and circular staplers
  • Right above dentate line
  • Sphincter sparing
  • Ultra-low colo-rectal or colo-anal anastomosis
  • Using linear and circular staplers
  • High risk of fistula !!!
  • Lower third of rectum → below 5 cm from anal verge !!!
  • Wide perineal dissection
  • Removal of anus, rectum and part of sigmoid colon
  • End of remaining sigmoid colon is brought out permanently = colostomy
  • Increased anatomical structures
  • Perfect vision while performing deep pelvic dissection
  • Minimal post-Op pain → less pain medication needed
  • Short recovery and hospital stay
  • Reduced risk of wound infections
  • Reduced post-Op ileus
  • Quick social reinsertion
  • Faster administering of adjuvant therapy: ↑ survival rates over time

Significant associated risks

  • Hemorrhage (most significant)
  • Nerve lesions
  • Reoccurence
  • Fistulae
  • Anastomotic stenosis

* Anastomosis is end-end or side-end +/- pouch

A. Anterior resection

B. Abdomino-perineal resection

a. anterior resection with colo-rectal anastomiosis b. abdomino-perineal resection with permanent colostomy

2) Radio-/ Chemotherapy

  • To lower recurrency and improve survival in resectable cancers
  • To allow surgery in primarily irresectable cancers
  • To facilitate a sphincter-preserving procedure
  • To cure patients without surgery: very small cancer or very high surgical risk Radiotherapy
  • Pre-OP (neoadjuvant): IIB - IV
  • Post-OP (adjuvant treatment): I - II A
  • Palliative: inoperable cases
  • External radiation therapy→ linear particle accelerator
  • Internal radiation therapy → local using iridium

Multiple chemotherapy

Neoadjuvant – T3, N0 or any T, N1-2

Adjuvant

  • If pathological finding after surgery equals T1-2, N0 → no adjuvant therapy
  • If pathological findings equals T3, N0 or T1-3, N1-2 → adjuvant therapy → 5FU + levamisol → Irinotecan → Platinum salts → Vascular proliferation inhibitor → Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors (EGFRIs)

3) Immunotherapy

Post-OP complications

  • Abdominal hemorrhage (occurs in first 24 hours)
  • Anastomotic leak (occurs in days 5-7 after surgery; higher rate of occurrence for low and ultra low anastomosis
  • Urinary retention
  • Postoperative ileus
  • Wound infection
  • Evisceration
  • Fecal incontinence
  • Anastomotic stenosis

Fast track protocol

  • Early oral nutrition, early ambulation, postoperative lower dosages of opioid analgesics and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis have shortened postoperative ileus time and reduced length of hospital stay, accelerating patient recovery and contributing to health care budget savings Surveillance
  • every 3-6 months for first 2 years
  • then every 6 months for total of 5 years
  • annual chest/abdomen/pelvis CT for patient at risk for recurrence
  • colonoscopy 1 year after operation, repeated every year if necessary

Colorectal CA prophylaxis

Primary prophylaxis

  • Alimentary education
  • NSAIDs → Aspirin, Sulindac

Secondary prophylaxis

  • Screening tests for precancerous polyps and incipient stages of cancer
  • Hemocult tests – mandatory colonoscopy if positive
  • Polyp diagnostic – endoscopic polypectomy
  • Routine colonoscopy for people at risk → Inflammatory bowel disease → Offspring of individuals known with colorectal CA → Personal history of colon polyps → Molecular screening

Prognosis

  • Good survival rate
  • Stage IV with liver metastasis → 5-year survival rate 28-45%

title: Gallbladder and bile duct disorders
html:
Anatomy

  • Intrahepatic biliary ducts - right and left intrahepatic bile ducts, right and left hepatic duct, join together to form common hepatic duct
  • Extrahepatic biliary tree – common hepatic duct and cystic duct form together common bile duct (CBD)
  • Cystic duct travels along CBD for about 1 cm, junction located right above duodenum, lots of anatomic variations
  • CBD = choledocus duct o Travels down along portal vein and proper hepatic artery, contact to medial wall of D2 duodenum and crossing posterior wall of D1 and posterior head of pancreas o Finally, entering into pancreas parenchyma and joining Wirsung duct = hepato-pancreatic duct o Opening at ampulla of Vater (D2 duodenum) with Oddi sphincter o CBD has 3 sections: supraduodenal, retroduodenal and intrapancreatic
  • Arterial blood supply of hepatocholedochal duct: right hepatic artery, proper hepatic artery, cystic artery, gastroduodenal artery and posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery
  • Venous drainage: paracholedochal venous plexus opening into portal vein
  • Innervation: parasympathetic vagal fibers and sympathetic fibers from celiac plexus
  • Normal sizes of CBD: 7-10 mm in diameter
  • Normal sizes of common hepatic duct: 5 mm
  • Normal sizes of cystic and intrahepatic ducts: 1-3 mm in diameter
  • Gallbladder/ cholecyst = diverticulum of CBD, 7-10 cm, situated inferior of segment V o Its fundus reaching anterior liver margin, body and infundibulum heading posterior towards CBD o Anteriorly – anterior abdominal wall and inferior aspect of liver o Posteriorly – transverse colon and first two portions of duodenum o Arterial blood supply of gallbladder: cystic artery dividing into anterior and posterior branches at level of gallbladder neck o Gallbladder veins draining directly into intrahepatic portal branches, rarely into cystic vein o Lymphatic drainage: directly into liver or into celiac lymph nodes through Mascagni’s lymph node o Innervation: sympathetic fibers originating from celiac plexus, parasympathetic fibers of vagal origin
  • Cholecystectomy safety triangle = Calot triangle → cystic duct, right side of CBD and inferior face of liver; crossed by cystic artery

Physiology

  • Bile = main exocrine liver secretion → 1000-1500 ml day
  • Produced by hepatocytes
  • Normal bile pressure = 9-10 cm H2O in CBD, 8-10 cm H2O in gallbladder
  • Pressure increases to 14-18 cm H2O during cholecystitis or 25 cm H2O in colic
  • Bile is predispose to stasis (especially in disturbance of vagus nerve → e.g., gastrectomy)
  • Composition: water mixed with cholesterol, phospholipids (lecithin), bile salts (mainly chenodeoxicholic and cholic acid) and conjugated bilirubin (breakdown product of haemoglobin)
  • Cholesterol is not water soluble → mixing with phospholipids and bile salts → micelles
  • When proportion of bile constituents is unbalanced → bile becomes lithogenic
  • Between meals, sphincter of Oddi is closed top revent reflux and bile accumulating into gallbladder
  • During meals, under neuro hormonal influences, gallbladder pushes its content
  • Bile is acting as detergent, emulsifying fats to facilitate digestion
  • Bile salts/ pigments resorbed in distal ileum and portal venous system back to liver = enterohepatic circulation
  • Absence of distal small bowel → reducing quantity of bile salts in bile → bile becomes lithogenic
  • Absence of bile in intestine (external bile drainage, obstructive jaundice) → malabsorption of fats, fat soluble vitamins (A,D,E,K), alteration of intestinal microbial flora and impairment of intestinal wall trophicity

Morphine causes contraction of Oddi sphincter → counter indicated in colics and acute pancreatitis !!! Relaxation of sphincter → spasmolitics, nitrates, miophilin, curara, lydocain

Imaging

Non-invasive

1. Transabdominal US

  • Essential
  • Presence of stones, thickness of wall (double wall sign), diameter of ducts
  • Not choice for detecting CBD lithiasis (duodenal gas)

Invasive

1. Endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography

(ERCP)

  • Best technique for image of bile and pancreatic ducts
  • Endoscopic, sphincterotomy, contrast through ampulla, instrumentation of CBD
  • Remove stones or insert stents
  • Severe complication (acute pancreatitis, perforation of ducts/ duodenum, peritonitis, bleeding, allergy to contrast, acute cholangitis, acute cholecystitis) !!!
  • Not used for diagnostic purposes !!!

Indication

  • confirmed CBD stones
  • high risk/probability of CBD stones, persistent jaundice
  • CBD > 8/10 mm diameter
  • acute cholangitis

Contraindication

  • Main organ failures with high risk of sedation
  • Severe coagulation disorders
  • Tight esophageal, gastric or duodenal stenoses (no passage of endoscope)

2. Oral cholecystography

2. Abdominal plain X-ray

  • Only 10% of gallstones (cholesterol not visible)
  • Porcelaine gallbladder (calcified cholecyst)
  • Gas in biliary tree (fistula, after interventions on CBD)

3. MRC and MRCP

3. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC)

  • Gallstones and biliary tree well visualized
  • Gives same diagnostic information as ERCP
  • Information about rest of abdominal viscera
  • Lacks therapeutic possibilities

4. CT scan (not a good option, s. X ray)

4. EUS

  • Only contrast spiral CT could visualize sth.
  • Very useful to visualize CBD stones that can´t be seen
  • Best option would be CT cholangiography with contrast with normal US specific for biliary tree → resolution superior to MRC

5. Isotope scanning – 99mTc-HIDA

5. Choledocoscopy

6. Surgical exploration

  • Operative and T-tube cholangiogram
  • intraoperative cholangiography (first choice)
  • intraoperative ultrasound
  • intraoperative cholangioscopy

Lab test

  • Without complications → normal lab tests
  • Leukocytosis: acute cholecystitis, empyema of cholecyst or severe cholangitis
  • Prothrombintime: checked especially in prolonged jaundice, lack of bile impairs absoption of vitamin K
  • Bilirubin (total and conjugated): raised in obstructive jaundice → severe acute cholecystitis, obstacle in CBD; should drop after surgery, otherwise suggests incomplete procedure
  • Alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamil transpeptidase: cholestasis
  • 5-nucleotidase: more sensitive marker of cholestasis
  • Transaminases (ASAT, ALAT): hepatocytolisis in severe cholecystitis and cholangitis

1) Gallbladder lithiasis

Causes

1. Lithogenic bile secretion (inborn, diet)

2. Biliary stasis (anatomical, functional)

3. Infection in biliary tree

4. Abnormalities of gallbladder epithelium

Lithogenic

Rise of cholesterol or loss of bile salt

  • High protein, fat diet, low residue diet
  • Contraceptive pill, pregnancy
  • Obesity
  • Loss of terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation)
  • Gastric resection, truncal vagotomy
  • Total parenteral nutrition
  • Chronic octreotide treatment
  • Hemolitic anemia

Anti-lithogenic

  • Bile salts → Lecithin → Apolipoprotein A, B → Ursodeoxicolic acid

3 types of stones

  • Cholesterol stones: solitary or multiple, different sizes, high levels of blood cholesterol are risk factor, pregnancy, contraceptive pill, family history, obesity, low dietary fibre
  • Pigment stones: irregular, black and small in size, looking as covered with thorns, composed of calcium bilirubinate and carbonate, in haemolytic anaemia
  • Mixed stones: most common, varying size, shape and colour, formed by mix of cholesterol and bile pigments Clinical aspects
  • Asymptomatic 80%
  • Biliar dispepsia snd = non-specific symptoms: migraine, headache, nausea, vomiting, dull pain in epigastrum or right abdominal quadrant
  • Pain → 2-3 hours after meal in right hypocondrum or epigastrum, severe in intensity, increases progressively, lasting for several hours, radiation to inferior scapula
  • Nausea, vomiting, sweating
  • Hypostenic syndrome → bloating, eructation, fatty-food intolerance, post-prandial somnolence, morning bitter taste
  • Hyperstenic syndrome → post-prandial diarrhea, migraines, iritability
  • Biliary colic (cholecyst contracting against obstacle, outflow of bile blocked → dilating gallbladder)
  • Fever (acute cholecytsitis)
  • Acute pancreatis

Complications

Occure when stones gets stuck (usually narrow parts - infundibulum, cystic duct, sphincter of Oddi)

  • a) Infectious – acute cholecystitis
  • b) Chronic cholecystitis
  • c) Mechanical obstruction by migration of stones
  • d) Mechano-inflammatory - fistulas
  • e) Degenerative – gallbladder carcinoma

DD

I. Acute cholecystitis

II. Acute appendicitis

III. Perforated duodenal ulcer

IV. Acute pancreatitis

V. Hepatic diseases (hepatitis, abscesses)

VI. Renal colic

VII. Myocardial infarction

VIII. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome

  • a) Acute cholecystitis (most common)
  • Caused by obstruction of cystic duct or infundibulum
  • Obstruction → concentrated bile → irritated mucosa → inflammatory process → infection
  • Catarrhal → phlegmonous → gangrenous
  • Thickening of wall (edema, inflammation)
  • Bile becomes purulent ±

Clinical

  • Pain – usually of sudden onset, may first be colicky, then constant and throbbing, right hypochondrium
  • Nausea and vomiting – common, mild in nature
  • Pyrexia/ fever and tachycardia
  • Signs: tenderness → guarding and rigidity
  • Palpable painful mass (distended cholecyst and inflammatory adhesions to great omentum, duodenum, colon = subhepatic block)
  • Murphy’s sign +

Diagnosis/ work-up

  • Lab tests: WBC ↑, ASAT, ALAT ↑ (±), BB, AF, GGT, AMY ↑ (±)
  • US → distended gallbladder, thickening of the wall (double layer wall)

Evolution

  • Resolution (stone falls back into gallbladder, but recurrence is almost rule)
  • Progression to gangrene and perforation
  • Gallbladder accumulates mucus → distended, tension, clear transparent content – hydrocholecyst/ hydrops
  • Large stones, rarely swollen gallbladder can press against CBD -> producing obstructive jaundice = Mirrizzi snd
  • Empyema of gallbladder
  • Subhepatic block and subhepatic abscess

Treatment

1. Intravenous fluids and nil by mouth

2. Pain relief (iv and ice-bag on right hypochondrum)

3. Antibiotics

4. Surgical intervention – cholecystectomy/stomy

→ Cholecystectomy for acute Cholecystitis

  • Moment → early/ late
  • Early cholecystectomy

Pro’s

Contra’s

  • Easier to dissect, no sclerosis
  • Short hospitalization
  • Early recover
  • Modified anatomy due to inflammation
  • Difficulties in elements recognition
  • Prone to iatrogenic injuries
  • b) Chronic cholecystitis
  • After repeated episodes of inflammatory attacks → gallbladder’s wall become rigid, fibrotic, moulded on calculi (scleroatrophic cholecystitis) or thick, hypertrophied wall (sclerohypertrophic cholecystitis)
  • Bile content with/ without infected
  • Recurrent bouts of abdominal pain, without fever
  • Fatty meals cause abdominal discomfort and flatulence
  • Attacks of acute cholecystitis can occur
  • DD: chronic dyspepsia (e.g., peptic ulcer), hiatus hernia, coronary insufficiency
  • c) Mechanical obstruction
  • Stones often causes obstruction of CBD

8) Gallbladder CA

= most frequent malignancy of biliary tract

  • very aggressive
  • 5-year survival is around 5-10%
  • Only 1 in 5 patients is diagnosed at early stage

Risk factors

  • Chronic inflammation 95% – gallstones (particularly large), cholecysto-enteric fistulas, porcelain gallbladder (calcification of wall)
  • Adenomas/ polyps of gallbladder – papillary, villous, > 10 mm
  • Carcinogenic substances: nitrosamines, rubber industry
  • Anomalous junction between Wirsung and choledoc with long common channel – chronic angiocholitis
  • Choledochal cysts
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Obesity
  • Female sex

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperplasia → metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma
  • Hyperplasia = reaction to chronic inflammation
  • Metaplasia = chronic irritation – pseudopiloric metaplasia (66-84%), gastric metaplasia (25-50%), intestinal metaplasia (12-52%)
  • Dysplasia = in situ carcinoma

Histology

  • Adenocarcinomas (90 %)
  • Squamous cell carcinomas (10 %)
  • Undifferentiated carcinomas
  • Infiltrates gallbladder wall quickly, then adjacent organs especially liver Clinical
  • Symptoms are stones related or mimicking biliary colic/ chronic cholecystitis
  • Changing of pain features – RUQ, deep, intense, stubborn 75%
  • Weight loss, asthenia, fatigue 60%
  • Jaundice 50%
  • Mass in right hypochondrium 50%
  • Hepatomegaly 40%
  • Fever 25%

  • Hematogenous
  • Direct extension
  • Perineural
  • Intraductal

  • Tumoral markers: CA 19-9 > 20 units/ml , CEA > 4 ng/ml
  • Gene mutation: p53, K-ras

Distal cholangiocarcinoma

Resection of tumor localized distally on common bile duct + resection of duodenum and pancreatic head = Whipple (block resection of main bile duct, gallbladder, duodenum, antrum of stomach and head of pancreas + anastomosis of cephalic portion of pancreas to stomach or jejunum, gastro jejunal and hepatico jejunal anastomosis)

= Traverso Longmire → variant of this intervention with preservation of pylorus

b. & c. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy

  • Role not well defined
  • Might have benefit in survival time → chemotherapy + surgery + radiotherapy d. Palliative treatment
  • To establish continuity of biliary tree and to maintain bile flow
  • Intrahepatic type - percutaneous external hepatic drainage placed under ultrasound guidance, benefit from tumor ablation procedures and chemoembolization
  • Extrahepatic tumors - placing stents through ERCP or by performing biliary digestive anastomosis upstream
sections: CT scan (not a good option, s. X ray)
Intravenous fluids and nil by mouth
Pain relief (iv and ice-bag on right hypochondrum)
Absence of previous operative trauma to biliary system
Sclerosis and stenosis involving all/ most extrahepatic bile ducts
Bile duct cysts and anomalous pancreato-choledocal junction

title: Liver
html:
Anatomy

  • Surgical anatomy is different from classical anatomy → Cuinauds division of liver in 8 segments
  • Division based on hepatic veins and portal branches
  • Surgical lobes divided by Cantlie’s line, portal fissure or main scizura
  • Vena cava inferior and gallbladder bed → first division in surgical right and left liver lobe
  • Next division is into 4 sectors that are separated by scissurae containing three main hepatic veins
  • Main scissura contains middle hepatic vein
  • Right liver divided into anterior sector (segments V and VIII) and posterior sector (segments VI and VII) by right scissura (right hepatic vein)
  • Left hepatic vein divides into segments IV and II + III
  • Finally subdivision of sectors by portal vein → leads to segments which have single portal triad (pedicle) (portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct)

Portal vein = superior + inferior mesenteric + splenic vein

Provides 75% of blood supply → richer in oxigen

Explains possibility of maintaining hepatic function after arterial ligation or embolization Common hepatic artery comes from celiac axis → gives gastroduodenal artery and continues as proper hepatic artery in pedicle (anterior to vena porta and left of main bile duct)

Cystic artery originates from right or proper hepatic artery

Hepatic veins - right, middle and left

Peritoneal duplications on liver surface are mistakenly named ligaments First step of any major liver surgery is mobilization of liver by transecting these ligaments Diaphragmatic peritoneal duplications - coronary ligament → continue at right and left triangular ligaments Falciform ligament connects liver to diaphragm and abd. wall; limit between left and right anatomic lobe Ligamentum teres/ round ligament (obliterated umbilical vein) in inferior part of falciform ligament Runs from umbilicus to umbilical fissure on inferior surface of liver Umbilical fissure contains left portal triad

1) Benign liver diseases

Simple cyst

= serous, biliary, non-parasitic cyst lined by biliary-type epithelium; result from progressive dilation of biliary microhamartomas

  • Contain fluids identical to plasma secreted by epithelium → aspiration of fluid does not lead to resolution
  • No malignant transformation
  • No communication with biliary tree
  • Usually asymptomatic
  • Symptoms are non-specific and usually compressive in large volume cysts
  • Diagnosis by US
  • If complicated by hemorrhage → DD neoplastic cyst → elevated CA 19.9 level in aspirated fluid
  • Multicystic disease = adult polycystic liver disease (congenital) → rupture, hemorrhage, infection and liver failure
  • Surgical (laparoscopic) treatment only in symptomatic cases !
  • After aspiration and inspection of sclerosing liquid → resection of superficialized cysts wall (unroofing) → cavity inspected with telescope
  • If aspirated liquid contains blood or mucus → cytology mandatory

Bile duct cyst

Classification

Complications

  • Lithiasis
  • Cholangitis
  • Malignant degeneration

Treatment

  • Resection → if necessary with hepatectomy and bilio-jejunostomy on Y loop

Traumatic cyst

  • Posttraumatic intrahepatic liquid collections
  • Lesion of biliary and/or vascular structures after blunt abdominal traumas
  • Lacking epithelium, collection is not a real cyst
  • Some may remain asymptomatic
  • If symptomatic or complicated (infection, hemobilia) → treatment
  • Minimally invasive approach with interventional angiography (embolisation of affected artery) and/ or ERCP (+/- ES)

Portal hypertension

= hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) of ≥ 6mmHg

  • HVPG > 10mmHg is clinically significant
  • HVPG = pressure gradient between WHVP and FHPV; pressure gradient between portal vein + IVC
  • Porto-caval anastomosis is affected → shunting of blood → dilation and even rupture of collateral circulation
  • upper gastric and lower esophageal veins → esophageal varices
  • recanalised umbilical vein and abdominal wall veins → caput medusa around umbilicus
  • superior, medium and inferior rectal veins → secondary hemorrhoids

Causes

Pre-hepatic

Hepatic

Post-hepatic

  • Portal vein thrombosis
  • Cirrhosis = most common cause
  • Mostly due to hepatitis B, C; alcohol
  • Budd Chiari syndrome (occlusion of hepatic veins)

Diagnostics

US

Abdominal CT

Esophago-gastroduodenoscopy

  • Cavernous transformation of portal vein
  • Portal vein dilated to > 13 mm (normal < 13mm)
  • SV and SMV diameter ↑ (normal < 10mm)
  • Lack of respiratory variation of SV and SMV (normal ≥ 40%)
  • ↑ blood flow via portosystemic anastomoses using duplex
  • ↑ spleen size (normal < 12cm; < 45cm²)
  • Presence of porto-systemic collaterals
  • Presence of ascites
  • Portal vein thrombosis
  • Assessment and treatment of esophageal varices

Prevention of recurrent hemorrhage

1. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS)

  • Minimal invasive
  • Establishing intrahepatic communication between hepatic vein and branch of portal vein
  • Under US guidance → catheter inserted in right internal jugular vein → inferior vena cava → right hepatic vein → angulated needle inserted until portal vein branch → titanium wire stent left in place
  • TIPSS applied for emergency treatment of hemorrhage from esophageal varices
  • Good method to gain time till matching liver can be transplanted

Other indications for TIPSS

  • Refractory ascites and/or hydrothorax
  • Patients contraindicated for surgical shunt
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome

Contraindications for TIPSS

  • Liver failure
  • Advanced cardiac disease
  • Active peritoneal, intrahepatic, or systemic infections
  • Hepatic tumors likely to be intercepted during procedure

2. Portosystemic shunts

Nonselective = are abandoned because volume of portal blood unprocessed by liver drained directly in systemic flow is too large Selective

  • Like spleno-renal shunt
  • Disadvantage = losing their efficiency in few years → This happens as peripancreatic veins dilate and bring increased blood flow to submucosal varicose veins with recurrent hemorrhage Partial
  • best partial shunt consists in portocaval anastomosis with interposition of calibrated 8-9 mm teflon graft
  • If larger there is important risk of encephalopathy
  • If smaller thrombosis will inactivate shunt

3. Hepatic transplantation

Liver abscess

Routes of bacterial spread to liver

  • Biliary tree
  • Portal vein
  • Hepatic artery
  • Direct extension of nearby focus of infection
  • Trauma
  • Cryptogenic (microinfarction)

Microorganisms involved

  • E. coli
  • Klebsiella
  • Enterococcus

+ Bacteroides and streptococcal species

  • Due to course of right portal branch (runs almost straight) → seeding of right lobe more frequent Causes of ascending cholangitis
  • CBD lithiasis or other obstructions
  • Intrahepatic stones (more common in Asia)
  • Malignant obstruction (usually after ERCP or stenting)
  • Caroli’s disease
  • Stenotic bilio-enteric anastomosis

Clinical

  • Fever, chills
  • RUQ pain, tenderness
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Malaise
  • Jaundice → preexisting biliary disease or liver failure
  • Secondary peritonitis after rupture is quite rare
  • If situated on upper surface of liver → abscess can cause reactive pleural collection Lab
  • Leukocytosis, CRP and ESR high
  • Altered liver function tests
  • Anemia
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Cultures (+ anaerobic, fungi) from puncture are mandatory

Imaging

  • US can detect > 90% of the cases
  • CT offers better results in areas blocked by inferior lungs and in small abscesses, can identify initial lesion → Both allow guidance of percutaneous punction and drainage

DD

  • Amoebic abscess
  • Echinococcal Garbi IV cyst

Treatment

Medical - Broad-spectrum AB covering gram negative and positive

Surgical - Laparoscopic

  • Must be considered if percutaneous drainage is contraindicated or unsuccessful

Amebic liver abscess

  • Caused by Entamoeba histolytica
  • More frequently in right lobe
  • Mainly males affected
  • Via contaminated water, food or humans → gets into portal flow → liver → produces necrosis
  • Symptoms are same as for liver abscess ++ diarrhea and recent travel !

Treatment

  • Nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, secnidazole, tinidazole)
  • Chloroquine
  • Iodoquinol
  • Dehydroeme
  • Paromomycin
  • Diloxanide furoate

Benign liver tumors

Liver cell adenoma (LCA)

Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)

Hemangioma (H)

= proliferation of hepatocytes

  • Rest of liver unchanged
  • Women with prolonged use of oral contraceptives
  • Oral contraceptives have to be stopped
  • Mostly singular
  • Adenomatosis if over 10
  • Consists of cords of benign hepatocytes, reduced fibrous tissue and small vessels with rich arterial supply (explains risk of bleeding)
  • Rupture with intraperitoneal bleeding (increased risk in pregnancy and subcapsular)
  • Malignant transformation not demonstrated but postulated
  • Resection advisable

= second most common benign solid tumor of liver

  • Central scar and artery, cords of hepatocytes divided by fibrous tracts
  • Percutaneous biopsy possible but not always of help
  • Affects young women
  • Use of oral contraceptives
  • Majority asymptomatic
  • Rarely large
  • Surgery if symptomatic

= most common benign tumor of liver

  • Affects more frequently women
  • Congenital vascular malformation
  • No risk of malignant degeneration
  • Complicated by rupture, superinfection
  • Can lead to Kasbach-Merritt syndrome (thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy secondary to thrombosis)
  • In children large H can act as arteriovenous shunt and lead to heart failure
  • US can raise suspicion
  • MRI - typical peripheral nodular enhancement
  • Biopsy contraindicated !!! (very high risk of bleeding)
  • In symptomatic and complicated cases → surgery with Pringle maneuver
  • CyberKnife system combines robotics and tridimensional liver reconstruction to focus beams of radiation on tumor

Diagnosis

1. Detection usually by ultrasound

2. If suspect mass dynamic CT scan

3. If lesion with uniform contrast enhancement on CT scan without aspect of hemangiomas, viral hepatitis markers and tumor markers (AFP, CEA) to rule out hepatocellular carcinoma and colorectal metastasis

4. If still unclear MRI in selected cases with angiography

5. If HCC possible biopsy

Treatment indication for benign tumors

  • Symptomatic
  • Complicated
  • Suspect of malignant degeneration
  • Very large
  • Fast growing

Treatment types

  • Enucleation (tumorectomy)
  • Atypical resection
  • Segmentectomy
  • Bisegmentectomy or other major resection
  • Transplantation (exceptionally)
  • Embolization (selective)
  • Ablation (several types) → Always remove in a tissue sparing manner

Hydatid cyst

= zoonotic infection caused by tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus causing cystic echinococcosis (CE)

  • Ingestion of food, water or dirty hands contaminated by eggs in feces of definitive host (dog, jackal or carnivore)
  • Cyst is surrounded by inflammatory tissue = pericyst

Organs affected

  • Liver
  • Lung
  • Other organs: spleen, brain, bones, eye

Symptoms caused by

  • Rupture of cyst
  • Infection of cyst or affected organs
  • Compression of any neighbouring organ

Rupture of liver cyst can happen in

  • Biliary tree
  • Free peritoneum
  • Surrounding hollow viscus
  • Erosion into biliary tree = cysto-biliary fistula
  • Causes allergic symptoms: flushing, urticaria, major rupture frequently leads to anaphylactic shock (protein in fluid)
  • Pain, fever, jaundice, asymmetric hepatomegaly in angiocolitis
  • Infection of cavity, with symptoms of hepatic abscess
  • Biliary obstruction by late stenosis of Oddi sphincter due to irritating hydatid liquid
  • Depending on affected organ → content of cyst can be eliminated by vomit, stool or urine
  • Cysts close to inferior surface of liver → open in free peritoneum with long-term risk of hydatidosis (peritoneal seeding of scolex, with multiple cysts developing)
  • Cysts on upper surface of liver → perforate diaphragm but seldomly open in free pleural cavity

DD

Syndromes

  • Jaundice
  • Persistent fever
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Allergic reaction

Diseases

  • Biliary obstruction
  • Acute hepatitis
  • Hepatic abscesses
  • Hepatic nonparasitic cyst
  • Budd-Chiari Syndrome
  • Hepatic tumors, primary and metastatic

Lab

  • ↑ Bilirubin, ALP, leukocytosis → biliary obstruction
  • Eosinophilia → allergic reaction
  • ELISA test = most reliable, 90% sensitivity
  • Casoni test no longer used

Imaging

  • Plain abdominal X-ray is usually normal, seldom calcifications
  • US = best method for diagnosis
  • Intraoperative US
  • CT and MRI (not routinely used)
  • ERCP - more useful in biliary complicated cysts, method of choice for diagnose and minimally invasive treatment (sphincterothomy and membrane extraction)

Gharbi´s Classification

II: hydatic sand

III: daughter cysts

→ If no daughter cysts, hydatid sand or membranes = Gharbi I → DD to non-parasitic cyst is difficult → The parasites are dead when infection or calcification occurs

Treatment

  • ERCP in cysto-biliary fistulae
  • Chemotherapy alone has limited indications (contraindication of surgery, many cysts, more than one organ affected) → useless in complicated and dead cysts
  • Given in combination with another treatment -> Albendazole, mebendazole for 3-6 month
  • PAIR (puncture, aspiration, scolicidal agent injection, re-aspiration after 15 min.) = US guided technique → cavity may be repeatedly washed in same session and is left filled with isotonic saline solution → presence of scolices in aspirated liquid confirmes diagnosis → PAIR can be applied in some contraindications of surgery, but has to be avoided in Gharbi IV and complicated, superficial (spillage and seeding risk) cysts
  • Surgery indicated in most cases -> best option

Total pericystectomy

  • Consists in removing parasite together with whole pericyst
  • Hemorrhage risks higher but postoperative outcome is better (complications associated to residual cavity (biliary fistulae, abscess) are eliminated)

Hepatic resection

  • Avoids risk of seeding but may be too aggressive as it removes also healthy tissue
  • Applied in large cysts when only small part of peripheral liver has to be sacrificed
  • Removes parasite with area of pericyst that is superficial

Cystectomy with partial pericystectomy

  • Suturing edges of pericyst to abdominal wall -> opening cyst and draining it Marsupialisation through skin
  • Obsolete technique

Main objectives of surgical treatment

  • Sterilization of parasite by injecting scolicidal substance
  • Removal of inactivated parasite
  • Reduction of residual cavity

Prophylaxis

  • Proper hands hygiene
  • Correct food processing for humans
  • Proper handling of herbivores feces
  • Dealing with problem of rogue dogs
  • Medical prophilaxy of echinococcosis in dogs
  • Correct food processing for dogs

2. Malignant liver lesions

Anatomical liver resection for liver metastasis

→ Couinaud classification

Most common nomenclature

Right hepatectomy

Extended right hepatectomy

Left hepatectomy

Extended left hepatectomy

Left lateral segmentectomy

Lobectomy

Synonym

Removed segments

Right hepatic lobectomy

Extended right hepatic lobectomy, right trisegmentectomy

V, VI, VII, VIII

IV, V, VI, VII, VIII

Left hepatic lobectomy

Extended left hepatic lobectomy, left trisegmentectomy

II, III, IV

II, III, IV, V, VIII

Left lobectomy, bisegmentectomy

II, III

  • Evaluation of liver tumors starts with ultrasound
  • In metastasis -> local recurrence of primary cancer has to be excluded by colonoscopy and CT
  • Chest x-ray to exclude concomitent pulmonary metastasis
  • CT volumetric analysis necessary for assessment of adequate residual liver volume
  • Must be correlated with function, Child-Pugh classification being widely used for cirrhosis
  • Under normal conditions 20%/ 30% of residual volume sufficient, in cirrhosis at least 40%
  • Principle in resection of liver tumors -> spare parenchyma -> only 1 cm safety margin
  • Number, position and relation to major vessels must be accurately established by CT portography
  • Invasion in major hepatic elements or IVC is not contraindication for surgery
  • Laparoscopic ultrasound allows thorough assessment
  • Intraoperatively bleeding and biliary leaks = major problem and postoperative causes for morbidity
  • Resection in small tumors - wedge resections and non-anatomical resections (tumorectomies)
  • Inflow control to check correct segmental margins -> corresponding portal branch clampt -> change in color of parenchyma delineates resection
  • Pringle maneuver – to prevent hemorrhage -> clamps placed on IVC above and below liver for max. 40 min (better 20 min + 5-10 min. break)
  • Another method to minimize bleeding -> low CVP
  • Adjuvant regional chemotherapy - placing catheter in proper hepatic artery
  • Liver transplantation recommended in primary liver tumors (not in secondary malignancies)

Primary hepatic carcinoma (HCC)

Etiology

  • Cirrhosis (80%)
  • Alcohol (1/3 of HCC)
  • Hepatitis B, C
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Wilson’s
  • Tyrosinemia
  • Glycogen storage disease
  • Aflatoxin

Signs and symptoms

(similar to cirrhosis)

Lab

Imaging

  • Hepatomegaly
  • Jaundice
  • Collateral venous circulation (esophageal varices, hemorrhoids, caput medusae etc.)
  • Variceal bleeding
  • Splenomegaly
  • Spider angiomata
  • Flapping tremor and hepatic encephalopathy
  • Ascites
  • Weight loss - cachexia
  • Usual modified liver values in cirrhosis
  • Alpha-fetoprotein > 20ng/ml (values > 500ng/ml = specific for HCC)
  • US (fist choice & screening)
  • CT
  • MRI = best method → Tumoral invasion in portal branch is characteristic for HCC
  • Angiography may show tumors < 1cm
  • Biopsy caries risk of tumoral seeding and bleeding

Medical care must be recommended considering certain criteria

  • Size, number
  • Location
  • Presence of cirrhosis
  • Patency of portal vein
  • Metastatic disease

Treatment

  • Relatively chemotherapy-resistant tumor -> systemic chemotherapy + immunomodulators (interferon-alpha) to achieve responds
  • Anti-angiogenesis agents (bevacizumab) → inhibiting neovascular formation
  • Chemoembolization
  • In selected cases liver resection is possible → Operative risk must be considered by combining data on class of cirrhosis, comorbidities, overall health status
  • Unfortunately, HCC develops on cirrhotic liver and is usually multicentric
  • Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis for survival after surgical resection
  • Liver transplantation in HCC is advisable if local extent is limited
  • When surgery is contraindicated tumor ablation can be of help

Cholangiocarcinoma

= malignancies of biliary duct system

  • Can be located intrahepatic, perihilar, extrahepatic

S. biliary chapter

Metastatic tumors of liver

  • Usually multiple
  • Metastatic sites is not contraindication for surgical treatment anymore, but not all provide increased survival
  • Colo-rectal metastasis always increases 5-year survival
  • Synchronous liver metastasis resected in single procedure with primary colo-rectal tumor if feasible Most frequent origins
  • Melanoma
  • Pancreas
  • Colon and rectum
  • But any digestive tumor can lead to liver mets !

Treatment

  • Percutaneous ethanol or acetic acid injection (abandoned)
  • Cryotherapy (placed laparoscopically or under US guidance)
  • Radiofrequency ablation (fast vibration of ions) -> rises temp. and coagulates proteins BUT only radius of 3 cm
  • Saline-enhanced radiofrequency ablation (Tissuelink RM) -> increases radius to 5 cm
  • Circulating blood in large vessels has cooling effect -> weaker effect in close proximity
  • Complications: hemorrhage and hematoma, abscess, thrombosis, biliary duct stenosis
  • Microwaves (rotation and vibration of water molecules with heat production)
  • High intensity focused US (HIFU) -> US produces heat -> coagulation with necrosis
  • CyberKnife (combines robotics and tridimensional liver reconstruction to focus beams of radiation on tumor)
  • Surgical resection with safety margins (1cm) !
  • Procedures can be combined depending on accessibility of mets (e.g., resection + ablation)

Outcome in metastatic tumors -> negative predictive factors

  • Lymph node involvement
  • Multiple metastasis
  • Tumor > 5 cm
  • If metachronous metastasis are diagnosed in less than a year
  • CEA > 200 ng/ml preoperatively

Neoplastic cyst

  • Cystadenoma = premalignant lesion → can degenerate into cystadenocarcinoma
  • Very rare
  • More frequently in women > 40 y.
  • Irregular spheroidal surface, septated with polypoid or papillary projections
  • Wall thickened with more solid or even calcified parts
  • Fluid inside must be aspirated and processed (mucus, CA 19-9, cytology)
  • Hemorrhagic or mucinous aspect must arouse suspicion
  • Cystadenoma removed by cystectomy
  • Cystadenocarcinoma resected with safety margin
sections: If suspect mass dynamic CT scan
If still unclear MRI in selected cases with angiography

title: Acute appendicitis
html:
= acute inflammation of vermiform appendix; most common abdominal surgical emergency

Anatomy

  • Located in right iliac fossa
  • Length 6-12cm
  • 2 cm beneath ileocecal valve
  • Mesoappendix = mesentery that connects terminal ileum with appendix
  • Arterial blood supply - appendicular artery - ileocolic artery superior mesenteric artery
  • Venous circulation goes to superior mesenteric vein
  • Appendix has immunological function through immunoglobuline secretion (lymphoid follicles) → number increases during puberty and declines 20-30 years gradually

Etiology

  • Peak incidence 10 - 30/40 years, decreases with age → Coprolites and lymphoid tissue hyperplasia = most frequent causes → Less common: parasites, fruit & vegetable seeds, strictures and tumors
  • Luminal obstruction + continuous secretion of appendiceal mucosa + bacterial multiplication → increased intraluminal pressure → distention of appendix → pain in lower abdomen → interrruption of venous and lymphatic flow → parietal edema, hyperemia and microbial penetration into mucosa Catarrhal appendicitis Phlegmonous appendicitis

Gangrenous appendicitis

  • Initial, limited to mucosa and submucosa
  • Inflammatory process spreads to serosa of appendix and parietal peritoneum → localized pain at right iliac fossa
  • If it progresses further → enlarged, congested, frail appendix; covered with false membranes & purulent fluid
  • Mesoappendix congested and thickened
  • Gradual distension and local circulatory dysfunction → venous and arterial thrombosis → ischemic lesions with necrotic areas
  • Appendix becomes flaccid, dark-red with black necrotic areas, edema of mesentery and intraperitoneal pus
  • Perforation occurs → development of appendicular block, appendicular abscess or diffuse peritonitis

Clinical

  • Abdominal pain (sudden or progressive) → Initially epigastric or periumbilical; later after 4-6 h at right iliac fossa; intensified with effort → Depending on location of appendix Periumbilically Retro-ileal position Right flank Retro-cecal position Right hypochondrium Sub-hepatic position Pelvis Pelvic position
  • Anorexia (constant and early symptom)
  • Nausea, vomiting (rare)
  • Fever (around 38°C)
  • Transit disorders (mainly constipation, rarely diarrhea)

Physical exam

  • Tenderness in right iliac fossa = cardinal sign

McBurney point

Pain, definitive for acute appendicitis (outer 1/3 on a line drawn from umbilicus to right anterior superior iliac spine)

Blumberg sign

Pain during sudden decompression, irritation of parietal peritoneum, always means diffuse peritonitis if present Grassmann Mendel Pain in right iliac fossa on percussion, also only present in diffuse peritonitis sign or Bell sign Guarding Voluntary - due to painful palpation, which can be conscious eliminated Involuntary - abdominal spasm caused by peritoneal inflammation, cannot be suppressed Rovsing sign Palpation of left lower abdominal quadrant increases pain in right lower quadrant Psoas sign Abdominal pain felt by passively extending thigh of patient lying on his side with knees extended or flex thigh at hip Positive in retrocaecal position → irritates iliopsoas muscle Antalgic position Patient in right lateral decubitus, avoids any movement, maintains flexion of right thigh Cutaneous May be first clinical sign hyperesthesia Specific characteristics related to age Infants and children

  • Difficult due to inability to properly communicate and multiple other gastrointestinal childhood disorders
  • Diagnosis is belated till after perforation occurs → evolution to generalized peritonitis is fast, due to inability of underdeveloped omentum to block perforation Elderly
  • Present milder symptoms, fever and leukocytosis only slightly increased, pain is mild or even absent
  • Atypical clinical picture, belated diagnosis and rapid evolution towards perforation → increased morbidity and mortality Pregnant women
  • Difficult → enlarged uterus causes displacement of appendix → alters location of pain, leukocytosis is physiological during pregnancy
  • Many symptoms are non-specific

Diagnostics

  • Leukocytosis (10-18 000), high PMN´s → > 18 000 suggests perforation with/ without abscess; normal values don´t exclude diagnosis
  • Urine analysis → DD with kidney diseases
  • Plain abdominal X-ray → signs of perforation and DD for kidney stones
  • Abdominal US → thickening of appendiceal wall and peri-cecal fluid accumulation; DD genital and urinary tract
  • Abdominal CT → useful in atypical clinical picture, when ultrasound fails to visualize changes, peri-appendiceal abscess, DD genital and urinary tract
  • Laparoscopy → allows intra-abdominal evaluation + can be used as therapeutic method

Complications

Appendicular plastron

= appendicular block

Appendiceal abscess

Generalized/ diffuse peritonitis

DD

Infants and children

Adults

Elderly

  • When surrounding organs adhere to appendix (cecum, ileum, omentum); secured by peritoneal exudate rich in fibrin
  • Usually occurs 3 days after onset of symptoms
  • Regresses after antibiotic therapy and drainage, after 6 weeks it is completely healed and appendectomy can be practiced
  • May develop into an abscess or generalized peritonitis
  • Formed by transforming appendicular block into purulent collection
  • Requires antibiotic treatment
  • When abscess is large → percutaneous/ surgical drainage
  • After 6 weeks, appendectomy can be performed
  • Abscess may form fistula in hollow organ (bladder, small intestine), skin or peritoneum (→ Peritonitis)
  • Direct perforation of appendix (necrosis)
  • Formation of appendicular block → abscess → perforation into peritoneal cavity → generalized peritonitis Treatment: appendectomy, rigorous lavage, drainage and antibiotic therapy
  • Mesenteric lymphadenitis
  • Acute gastroenteritis
  • Intussusception (invagination)
  • Meckel diverticulum
  • Renal or ureteric colic
  • Perforated peptic ulcer
  • Acute gastroenteritis
  • Testicular torsion
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease (adnexitis)
  • Ruptured follicular cyst
  • Torsioned ovarian cyst
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Acute cholecystitis
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Cecum cancer
  • Intestinal occlusion
  • Entero-mesenteric infarction

Treatment

→ Surgical emergency

Classical

  • Performed through oblique incision in right iliac fossa (McBurney incision)

Laparoscopic - Uses at least 3 trocars

  • Nowadays commonly performed

Main operative steps

  • Intraperitoneal examination
  • Identifying cecum and appendix
  • Freeing appendix and deliver it into wound
  • Ligation and transection of mesoappendix containing appendicular vessels
  • Ligation and transection at base of appendix → removing of appendix
  • Closing of abdominal wall wound

Medical treatment targets appendicular block, abscess, generalized peritonitis → Antibiotic therapy, symptomatic treatment (anti-inflammatory, antispasmodic and painkiller)

Post-OP complications

1. Wound infection = most frequent post-operative complication

2. Postoperative bleeding = often caused by slipping of ligature from mesoappendix (contains appendicular artery)

3. Acute generalized or localized peritonitis through slipping of ligature from stump of appendix

4. Intestinal obstruction through formation of post-operative adhesions

5. Cardiac and pulmonary complications → DVT, pulmonary embolism = more frequent in elderly patients
sections: Wound infection = most frequent post-operative complication
Intestinal obstruction through formation of post-operative adhesions

title: GI bleeding
html:
Classification

Amount of blood loss a) Small bleeding: < 10% of total blood volume (500 ml), normal TAS and HR (prognosis)

  • b) Medium bleeding: <20% of blood volume (500-1000 ml), TAS > 100 mmHq, HR <100 beats/min, peripheral vasoconstriction
  • c) Intense bleedings <30% of circulating volume (1500-2000 ml), TAS <100 mmHq, HR> 120 beats/min lipotemia, tachypnea, oliguria
  • d) Severe bleeding: loss >50% (2000-3000 ml), TAS <70 mmHq, peripheral filiform pulse
  • e) Cataclysmic bleeding: rapid and massive blood loss, often fatal

Bleeding site

Upper GI bleeding: between oropharynx and duodenal-jejunal angle (topography)

Lower GI bleeding: between duodenal-jejunal angle and anus

Rate of bleeding

Acute = large amount of blood rapidly lost → significant hemodynamic disturbances Chronic = small, repeated, usually occult losses → severe anemia

1. Upper GI bleeding

  • Blood loss between oropharynx (pharyngo-esophageal junction) & duodenal-jejunal angle (Treitz angle)
  • Externalized by → Hematemesis → Melena → Hematochezia

Etiology

Digestive cause

Annexes of GI tract

Extradigestive causes

Esophagus: esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss snd, esophagitis, benign/ malignant tumors, iatrogenic bleeding, trauma by foreign bodies, Boerhaaven syndrome, esophageal diverticula Gastric or duodenal: gastric or duodenal ulcers, gastritis, malignant/ benign tumors, gastric polyps, trauma, operations, foreign bodies, Menetrier's syndrome, hiatal hernia, aneurisms, syphilis or tuberculosis, ampulloma, Crohn's disease

  • Hepatic and extrahepatic biliary tract trauma, choledochal cancer, iatrogenic causes
  • Liver cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari snd, hemangioma, post-traumatic hemobilia, hepatic a. aneurysm
  • Acute pancreatitis, pancreatic tumors
  • Blood swallowed: epistaxis, hemoptysis
  • Stress ulcer (Cushing ulcers, severe burns (Curling ulcers), toxic-septic shock, surgery)
  • Portal hypertension
  • Hematological (acute leukemias, hemophilia, pernicious anemia, malignant lymphomas)
  • Medically: NSAIDs, steroids, anticoagulants, cytostatic agents, alcohol
  • Most common

Esophageal varices

Gastric and duodenal ulcer

Acute/ chronic gastritis

Stress ulcer

Alcoholism, hepatitis B, C → liver cirrhosis/ HCC, portal vein thrombosis → PTH → esophageal varices

  • Hemorrhagic duodenal ulcers usually located on posterior surface
  • Often multiple erosions at fundus and body of stomach
  • Acute one is frequently hemorrhagic → NSAID’s, alcohol, steroids
  • Chronic one is commonly associated with H. pylori
  • a) Curling ulcer: severe burns
  • b) Cushing ulcer: intracranial interventions or pathologies

Gastric cancer

Clinical manifestation

  • S. unten Tabelle

Classification

Small GI bleeding

Moderate GI bleeding

Large upper GI bleeding

Severe upper GI bleeding

Cataclysmic upper GI bleeding

Blood loss: < 500ml

BP/ HR: normal

Blood loss: 500-1000ml sBP > 100 and HR < 100

+ pallor, cold sweating, tachypnea

Blood loss: 1500-2000ml sBP <100 and HR > 100-200

+ fainting, cold sweating, tachypnea, oliguria

Blood loss: 2000-3000ml sBP < 70

+ weak or no pulse

Massive and rapid bleeding → death in short time before therapeutic intervention could succeed

Ht: > 30%

Hb: 10-12 g/dl

Ht: 25-30%

Hb: 8-10 g/dl

Ht: < 25 %

Hb: 5-8 g/dl

Diagnosis

1. Clinical exam

  • Anamnesis (diseases, alcohol consumption, drugs)
  • Physical exam (pale, cold, moist skin; cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia)
  • Basic life parameters (hypovolemia or shock signs → thirst, dizziness, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, dyspnea, collapse and coma) → BP, HR, O2 sat, ECG
  • Presence of ascites, collateral circulation, palpation of abdominal tumors
  • Digital rectal exam confirms melena or hematochezia

2. Lab

  • Hb, Ht, coagulation
  • Blood group, Rh (cross-matching)
  • Liver function (serum protein, bilirubin, ALP, GGT, GPT)
  • Renal function (urea, crea, electrolytes,)

3. Imaging

  • Upper GI endoscopy
  • Performed after hemodynamic stabilization or in emergency
  • In any patient where bleeding is suspected
  • Can determine bleeding location
  • Therapeutic methods

+ Selective arteriography (can highlight small bleedings)

+ Scintigraphy

+ Angio CT

+ Digestive video capsule (exploration of GI segments which endoscope can’t reach; but no biopsy)

+ Hemoccult test

Positive diagnosis and differential diagnosis

  • Hematemesis – haemoptysis
  • Melena - ingestion of drugs (iron, bismuth, charcoal)
  • Lower gastrointestinal bleeding, swallowed epistaxis, gums bleeding

Prophylaxis

  • Treatment of gastroduodenal ulcers with Helicobacter pylori eradication and systematic administration of PPI
  • Endoscopic treatment of esophageal varices before rupture
  • Early detection of tumors

Treatment

Hemodynamic instable - 2 large i.v. lines or CVC → blood volume restoration

  • Crystalloid solutions i.v. (Ringer's or saline), Blood transfusion
  • O2 administration
  • Nasogastric tube (diagnostic and therapeutic purpose)
  • Diuretic urine catheter
  • Intubation if necessary
  • Monitoring of BP, HR, EKG, temp., laboratory tests

Non-variceal → Pharmacological treatment (prior endoscopy)

  • PPI
  • Somatostatin → inhibition of gastric/ pancreatic acid secretion → Endoscopic treatment (emergency within first 24h)
  • Endoscopic injection of vasoconstrictor (alcohol, adrenalin, collagen)
  • Plasma coagulation
  • Electrocoagulation
  • Application of clips → Surgical treatment

Indications

1. Massive HDS with vital risk that Ø respond to resuscitation therapy

2. Repeat bleeding in first hours/days after endoscopic hemostasis

3. Lack of response to conservative therapy (endoscopic, medication)

4. Prolonged bleeding with loss > 2 liters of blood

Ulcer

I. Chronic gastric ulcer or NSAID induced ulcer

  • Drug therapy → PPI or H2 receptor inhibitors, protectors of gastric mucosa and antibiotic anti-Helicobacter pylori
  • First endoscopic attempt by adrenalin injection
  • If bleeding does not stop, subtotal gastric resection or total gastrectomy II. Chronic duodenal ulcer
  • s. gastric ulcer
  • If hemorrhage does not stop, X-suture in situ hemostasis is preferred or Billroth I or Billroth II gastric resection Hemorrhagic gastritis - Secondary to NSAID´s: stop drugs, administer PPI or H2 blockers, protectors of gastric mucosa (eg. sucralfate)
  • Anti-Helicobacter pylori antibiotics
  • If bleeding does not stop → subtotal gastric resection or total gastrectomy Gastric CA
  • First endoscopic hemostasis
  • If bleeding continues → subtotal gastrectomy or total gastrectomy
  • In unresectable cases → gastric devascularization
  • Selective embolization or selective injection of vasoactive substances by interventional radiologist Hemobilia
  • Embolized by interventional radiology
  • In case of failure → ligation of hepatic artery (branch corresponding to lesion) or resection of affected liver segment Variceal bleeding
  • Endoscopic treatment: intra- or peri-variceal sclerotherapy, ligation with elastic bands, hemo clips
  • Pharmacological treatment: intraarterial injection of vasopressin, somatostatin, propranolol (beta-blockers)
  • If bleeding continues → Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota balloon tamponade
  • If balloon tamponade does not work → transjugular porto-systemic shunt (TIPSS) as emergency intervention until surgery; candidate for liver transplantation
  • If not candidate for liver transplantation → porto-caval shunt, esophageal transsection (Tanner or Sugiura-Futagawa procedures)

Diagnosis and treatment algorithm

2. Lower GI bleeding

= loss of blood in digestive tract between Treitz angle and anus → Melena → Hematochezia → Rectorrhagia

Etiology

Small intestine

Colon

Rectum and perianal region

  • It is rare, of low intensity, it is externalized by melena

1. Meckel’s diverticulum - common in young people and children

2. Intestinal invagination

3. Crohn's disease

4. Entero-mesenteric infarction

5. Intestinal polyps

1. Colon cancer - one of most common causes, associated with weight loss and

transit disorders

2. Colonic diverticulosis - frequent, stool with fresh blood and mucus

3. Angiodysplasias grow in surface with age, more common in right colon

4. Ulcerative recto-colitis

5. Benign polyp tumors

6. Ischemic and radic colitis

  • Relatively frequent, it is externalized through rectorrhagia

1. Hemorrhoids → can cause massive bleedings; hide lower rectal CA

2. Anal fissures

3. Recto-colonic polyposis

4. Rectal trauma

5. Iatrogenic causes

Diagnosis

  • Clinical exam → DRE
  • Lab to detect occult bleeding
  • Imaging → colonoscopy, endorectal US, scintigraphy with marked redness (useful if discontinuous bleeding)
  • Video capsule → radiological exam with contrast/ double contrast for diverticula and tumors

Treatment

→ Endoscopic → Surgical

Hematemesis - vomiting of red blood, indicates upper GI bleeding, coffee-ground emesis is vomiting dark brown, granular material that resembles coffee grounds (upper GI bleeding that has slowed or stopped, hemoglobin digested by gastric acid), DD with hemoptysis (foamy blood, no food, after coughing); requires 800-1000 ml of blood Hematochezia – usually passage of gross, fresh blood from colon (lower GI bleeding) but may result from vigorous upper GI bleeding with rapid transit of blood through intestines, can be mixed with stool, sometimes clots/ sprinkles on stool, can be also without stools; requires 1000 ml of blood Melena - black, tarry stool, badly smelling, typically upper GI bleeding but can be from any source in small bowl or right colon, digested by bacteria; requires 50-100 ml of blood Rectorrhagia – Fresh rectal bleeding, bright red blood on stools, can be without stools Chronic occult bleeding - anywhere in GI tract, detectable by chemical testing of stool specimen, anemia
