title: Spleen
html:
Anatomy

  • Located in left upper quadrant, between fundus of stomach and diaphragm, protected by lower portion of rib cage
  • Covered by peritoneum and splenic capsule → give rise to splenic trabeculae carrying arteries and veins
  • 12 cm long
  • Position maintained by several ligaments a. Spleno-phrenic b. Spleno-renal c. Spleno-colic d. Gastro-splenic – short gastric artery
  • Celiac artery - Splenic artery - 4-5 segmental trabecular arteries - arterial capillaries - red pulp venous sinuses & reticular tissue
  • Venous sinuses - pulp trabecular veins - splenic vein - portal vein
  • Innervation - sympathetic nerve fibers from celiac plexus, left vagus nerve
  • Accessory spleens in 14-30%, usually seen at hilum, greater omentum, ligaments of spleen

Structure

  • 3 zones of pulp a. White pulp – splenic parenchyma consisting of lymphoreticular tissue (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells) b. Red pulp – splenic parenchyma consisting of reticular tissue (cord, sinuses), blood vessels, blood cellular elements c. Marginal zone – poorly defined vascular space between pulps; contains sequestered foreign material, plasma and abnormal cellular elements White pulp = circular structure made mainly of lymphocytes
  • similar to nodules of lymph node

Physiology

A. Filtering

B. Immunologic function

C. Storage function

D. Hematopoietic function

E. Circulatory function

Red pulp

  • surrounds white pulp and contains mainly red blood cells and macrophages
  • phagocytize old red blood cells
  • Splenic blood flow → 350 ml/day
  • Monitors and manages blood cells and immune functions
  • During fetal development, spleen produces red and white blood cells
  • Red cells that pass-through spleen undergo “cleaning” or repair
  • Abnormal and old red cells and platelets are destroyed
  • Cleans also germs, antigens and cellular debris

1. Opsonin production (essential in protection against pathogenic bacteria)

2. Antibody and lymphokines synthesis for complement system (IgM)

3. Protection from infection (promotes phagocytosis and destruction of bacteria)

  • Storage of red blood cells, lymphocytes and other formed elements

1. Platelets → 1/3 are stored in spleen

2. In splenomegaly, up to 80% of platelets may be stored in spleen → thrombocytopenia

  • Lymphoid hematopoiesis (but not primary site)
  • By 5. month of gestation, spleen no longer has hematopoietic function but retains capacity throughout life
  • Provides aortic and portal blood flow dynamics

Clinical diagnosis

1. History

  • Bleeding disorders, anemic syndromes, recurrent infections, abdominal trauma

2. Symptoms

  • Often asymptomatic
  • Discomfort or LUQ pain, with/ without being referred to left shoulder (violent pain attributed to splenic infarction/ abscess)
  • Hemolytic jaundice - acholic stools, coluric urine, lack of itching

3. Physical exam

  • Normally not palpable
  • Felt in 2% of healthy asthenic adults
  • Deep inspiration, pat. in supine or right lateral position, hand under left costal margin
  • Movement during inspiration and expiration
  • Felt in splenomegaly
  • No significant dullness elicited by percussion over spleen
  • In splenomegaly → dullness detected at 9th ICS in left anterior axillary line

4. Imaging

  • US – method of choice, size, collections, hematoma or splenic tumors, splenic ruptures, differential diagnosis to other abdominal tumors
  • Doppler US - traumatic emergencies
  • CT - tumor and traumatic spleen
  • MRI - less useful
  • 99 Tc colloid - scanning of reticuloendothelial system (RES), splenoportal axis

5. Laboratory examination

  • Blood cytology mandatory for peripheral cytopenia: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, anemia
  • Blood cytology in bone marrow in hypersplenism
  • Immunological examinations: direct and indirect Coombs test, autoantibody tests

1. Hypersplenism

= Splenomegaly → exacerbation of normal splenic function → spleen rapidly and prematurely destroy blood cells

  • Reduction in number of RBC, WBC, platelets
  • Compensatory rise in production in bone marrow → reticulocytosis
  • Recurring fever and infection
  • Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia

Primary hypersplenism

  • Diagnosis by exclusion
  • Congenital hemolytic anemia
  • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
  • Splenic neutropenia
  • Immune hemolytic anemia

Secondary hypersplenism

  • Portal hypertension → splenic congestion
  • Lymphoma, Chronic leukemia
  • Chronic bacterial infections: tuberculosis, syphilis
  • RA, SLE, sarcoidosis
  • Thesaurismosis: Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick d.
  • Responds to splenectomy
  • Steroids do not improve condition
  • Does not warrant splenectomy

DD of splenomegaly → tumors in left upper quadrant

  • Abdominal wall tumors
  • Retroperitoneal sarcomas
  • Left adrenal tumors
  • Left kidney tumors
  • Left hydronephrosis
  • Cancer of tail of pancreas
  • Cancer of greater curvature
  • Giant tumors in vicinity
  • Hypertrophy of left hepatic lobe

2. Splenic rupture

  • Very fragile → most affected by abdominal trauma
  • Especially in splenomegaly
  • Disruption of spleen’s parenchyma, capsule, blood supply

Etiology

  • Blunt trauma → spleen contusion, ruptured spleen (immediate rupture, delayed rupture)
  • Penetrating wounds (cold weapons or firearms)
  • Iatrogenic injury (intra-operatory during colon, stomach and pancreatic surgery)
  • Spontaneous rupture → hematologic disorders

Pathology

  • Bleeding → limited (hematoma) or hemoperitoneum
  • Subcapsular splenic hematoma - after blunt trauma, preserved capsule integrity, maybe secondary capsule rupture and delayed hemorrhage, seclusion, abscess or resorption
  • Perisplenic hematoma - capsular effraction, trauma or secondary to subcapsular hematoma, requires careful monitoring under conservative treatment, maybe secondary rupture, c
  • Splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum - mainly on convex side of spleen, can be fatal, splenic pedicle avulsion is very rare
  • Wounds produced by cold weapons - usually avoid hilum, with/ without detachment of parenchymal fragments, firearm can cause "spleen explosion"
  • a) Splenic rupture → Intraperitoneal → 90% of blunt trauma
  • b) Delayed rupture → Interval of days or weeks between injury and bleeding (10-15%) → Quiescent period for < 7 days up to 2 weeks → Related to temporary tamponade of minor lacerations or slowly enlarging subcapsular hematoma
  • c) Occult splenic rupture → Pseudocyst of spleen (1%)

Clinical manifestation

  • Hypovolemia/ hypovolemic shock (anxiety, thirst, faintness, severe skin paleness, cold and wet hands/feet, hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria
  • Localized (LUQ) or generalized abdominal pain
  • Kehr’s sign = pain at tip of left shoulder → phrenic nerve transports diaphragmatic irritation
  • With/ without signs of peritoneal irritation
  • Superficial thrombophlebitis
  • Hemoperitoneum → abdominal distension, shifting dullness to percussion in left flank/ LUQ (Ballance’s sign), paralytic ileus, bulging of Pouch of Douglas

Investigations

Lab

US

Abdominal X-ray

  • CBC → serial Hct determination, anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis
  • Splenic hematoma or hemoperitoneum
  • Fractured ribs
  • Elevated immobile diaphragm
  • Enlarged splenic shadow
  • Medial displacement of gastric shadow
  • Widening shadow between splenic flexure and preperitoneal fat

CT scan

Angiography

Treatment → surgery

1) Regaining vital functions

2) Non-surgical spleen preservation in carefully selected cases (hemodynamically stable, splenic injury without active bleeding, absence of associated lesions), hospitalization for 6-8 days with continuous clinical monitoring and imaging 3) Spleen-preserving surgery (capsular suture, tissue adhesives, argon plasma coagulation)

4) Complete splenectomy in total spleen damage or splenic bleeding that cannot be stopped Spleen laceration

  • Extending from top diagonally across to bottom of specimen, is a large tear in capsule of spleen, exposing pulp
  • Splenic lacerations are common in automobile accidents and are common if spleen has undergone enlargement due to some reason

3. Splenic abscess

Rare purulent collections caused by bacteria or fungi

Infection of trasplenic hematoma or necrotic lesion, hematogenic contamination of splenic infarction Hematogenic spread from primary extrasplenic focus: endocarditis, lung abscess, osteomyelitis, typhoid fever Lymphatic spread from neighboring organs: pancreatic suppuration, left colic tumors Risk factors - systemic infections, multiple trauma or immunosuppressed Sudden occurrence of LUQ pain, tenderness during palpation, superficial thrombophlebitis, fever, malaise Laboratory tests - leukocytosis, positive blood cultures Ultrasound - fist choice, irregular hypoechoic with echoes inside CT scan confirms Treatment - antibiotherapy + surgery → splenectomy or ultrasound-guided percutaneous abscess drainage

4. Splenic hydatid cyst

3rd most frequency after lungs and liver

Single or multiple, varying in diameter, clear or purulent content

May cause compression of neighboring organs

Perisplenitis, adhering to neighboring organs, splenic rupture, splenic calcification (rare)

Splenomegaly

Free rupture produces anaphylactic shock and splenic abscess

Ultrasound-based diagnosis + positive serological tests: Casoni test, indirect hemagglutination test, ELISA Surgical treatment: partial cyst resection, partial splenectomy (after evacuation by aspiration and inactivation with scolicidal agents), total splenectomy

5. Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)

  • Characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytes
  • Most patients are young
  • Clinical symptoms are similar to those of a severe upper respiratory tract infection
  • Spleen is enlarged and palpable in > 50%
  • Splenic rupture may occur

6. Vascular pathologies

Splenic vein thrombosis

Massive splenomegaly

Thrombosis secondary to pancreatitis

Associated with esophageal varices (without hepatic damage)

Cured by splenectomy

Diagnosis → Eco-Doppler, CT and angiography

Main causes: acute or chronic pancreatitis, pseudocysts, trauma, splenic vein abnormalities Other causes: neoplasms (leukemia, lymphoma, metastatic CA), myeloproliferative disorders, increase in RBC destruction (thalassemia major), disorders in immune response (infectious mononucleosis), diseases that infiltrate spleen (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis)

Splenic artery aneurysm

Frequently in women

Atheromatous, destruction of tunica media, trauma, syphilis, pancreatitis or malformative Mostly asymptomatic LUQ pain, referred into left subscapular area, exacerbated by physical effort Rupture and signs of hypovolemic shock Radiologic examinations (doppler, angiography) - calcified splenic artery and dilation Treatment - emergency surgery, aneurysmal sac resection and splenic artery ligation, vascular prosthesis or vascular anastomosis, splenectomy, splenopancreatectomy

Splenic arteriovenous fistulas

Due to aneurysms, trauma, splenectomy, inflammatory pancreatic diseases Symptoms - colicky abdominal pain, splenomegaly, portal hypertension (hyperinflux), heavy breath in spleen area during auscultation

Diagnosis by selective arteriography

Treatment - vein ligation and resection of arterio-venous communication or splenectomy

Splenic infarction

Causes - embolic (valvular heart disease, endocarditis, myocardial infarction, aneurysms) or systemic (sicklecell anemia, chronic myelogenous leukemia, polycythemia vera, lymphomas, osteomyelofibrosis, polyarteritisnodosa, sepsis)

Progression - pseudocysts, abscess, retractile fibrosis

Diagnosis - ultrasound or angiography

Splenectomy

7. Lysosomal storage diseases

Gaucher’s disease

= Inherited disorder of lipid metabolism → result in massive splenomegaly and hypersplenism Accumulation of glucocerebroside in monocytophagocytic system Jewish population Hepatomegaly with hepatic fibrosis → portal hypertension Splenectomy does not cure but remits symptoms and corrects blood cytopenia Bone marrow transplantation

Niemann-Pick disease

Sphingomyelinase deficiency → accumulation of sphingomyelin in macrophages in spleen, liver, lymph nodes, central nervous system and bone marrow Hepatosplenomegaly Splenectomy to reduce symptoms, but it does not influence disease progression

8. Hereditary and Hematological disorders

Hereditary spherocytosis

Autosomal dominant → membrane defects resulting in reduced surface (spherocytes) → not being able to cross inter-endothelial holes → being retained in red pulp cords → destroyed Increased osmotic fragility of erythrocytes → anemia, acholuric jaundice occuring in episodes, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones Hemolytic crises (impaired general condition, tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain)

Lab tests: anemia, reticulocytosis, microspherocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, increased urobilinogen, Coomb's negative

Imaging: US, skull X ray "tower-like" skull

Treatment: splenectomy after age of 6 years, failure when accessory spleens not discovered

Hereditary elliptocytosis

Presence of ovalocytes (erythrocyte cell membrane abnormality)

Clinically – asymptomatic, hemolysis, splenomegaly

Splenectomy in severe hemolysis

Sickle-cell disease

“sickle-shaped” red blood cells containing HgS

Clinically - painful hemolytic crisis, vascular occlusive events

Splenectomy necessary due to high risk of splenic infarction

Thalassemia

Congenital anemia characterized by deficient synthesis of one or more hemoglobin polypeptide chains Homozygous - thalassemia major and heterozygous - thalassemia minor First year of life, progressive anemia, hemolytic jaundice, splenomegaly, delayed bone growth and bone loss Hypochromic microcytic anemia, “target-shaped” red blood cells, indirect hyperbilirubinemia Splenectomy

Splenic neutropenia

Splenomegaly, peripheral neutropenia and normal/hyperplastic bone marrow Histiocytic granulocytes in spleen → excessive intraspleniclysis LUQ pain, splenomegaly and recurrent infections Splenectomy

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

Abnormal production of antibodies

Splenic macrophages and Kupffer cells capture erythrocytes that are attached to autoantibodies Onset after 40 years, chronic hemolytic anemia, fluctuating jaundice, splenomegaly Anemia, presence of spherocytes and microspherocytes, reticulocytosis and erythroid hyperplasia Immunosuppressive medication, blood transfusion, splenectomy

Felty’s syndrome

Syndrome consisting of severe rheumatoid arthritis, granulocytopenia and splenomegaly Severe, persistent and recurrent infections Moderate splenomegaly Splenectomy

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Young women without medical history

Sometimes in systemic lupus erythematosus, Hodgkin's disease, AIDS

Hemorrhagiparous syndrome, peripheral thrombocytopenia, bone marrow megakaryocytes, antiplatelet antibodies Petechiaeon slopeor compression areas (bone prominences), gingival bleeding, epistaxis, bruising, uterine bleeding, hematuria, intracranial haemorrhage Spleen normal sized Corticotherapy, splenectomy

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Severe prognosis

Disseminated obstructions in arterioles and capillaries caused by platelet microthrombi Hemolytic anemia, jaundice, purpura, menometroragy, neurospihic syndrome (aphasia, emiparesis, delirium, seizures)

Corticosteroid therapy, antiplatelet drugs, transfusions of plasma, splenectomy

9. Myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders

Chronic myelogenous leukemia

Clonal bone marrow stem cell disorder characterized by massive splenomegaly associated with proliferation of mature granulocytes, mostly neutrophils presenting Philadelphia chromosome Asthenia, left upper quadrant pain, sweating, fever, weight loss Bone pain, bleeding, extra-splenic myelogenous tumors Splenectomy in hypersplenomegaly, repeated splenic infarction, hypersplenism Chemo, radiotherapy

Myeloid metaplasia

Splenomegaly, bone marrow fibrosis, immature granulocytes

Hepatosplenomegaly, left upper quadrant pain, pallor (anemia), bleeding Splenectomy

Malignant lymphoma

HL or NHL

Painful peripheral lymphadenopathy

Splenic metastasis

Night sweats, fever, itching, intensified by alcohol intake, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting Splenectomy, chemo, radiotherapy

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Accumulation of small lymphocytes in bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes and peripheral blood Asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, fever, infectious complications, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly Alkylating agents, corticotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, splenectomy

Hairy cell leukemia

Splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy and mononuclear cells with villi Asthenia, fatigue, left upper quadrant pain, anemia, bleeding, infectious complications Splenectomy

10. Splenic tumors

Benign tumors o Benign splenic cysts - hydatid cyst, primary cysts (serous cystadenoma, desmoid cyst, cystic hemangioma, cystic lymphangioma), secondary cysts (traumatic pseudocysts, degenerative necrotic cyst, inflammatory abscess) o Benign solid tumors – disembryoplasia (hamartoma), vascular hemangioma, lymphangioma, hemangiopericytoma Cystic lesions comprise parasitic and nonparasitic cysts Parasitic cysts are almost exclusively due to echinococcal disease Non-parasitic cysts classified as primary (true) which have an epithelial lining or pseudocysts (more common)

Symptoms are vague and caused primarily by mass effect (compression of adjacent viscera)

Benign tumors treated surgically only if they become clinically active, with exception → hemangiomas (risk of rupture) o Flattening and filling of cyst, percutaneous puncture, aspiration and sclerotherapy in patients with definite diagnosis and high surgical risk o Aspiration, defenestration and electrocoagulation in case of superficial and uninfected cysts o Partial splenectomy in case of upper polar localization of tumors and small hemangiomas o Total splenectomy in case of large tumors with hilar location and suppurativecysts Primary malignant tumors o Vascular structures: hemangiosarcoma, endothelial angiosarcoma, malignant hemangiopericytoma, lymphangiosarcoma o White pulp elements: brill-symmers disease (gigant follicular lymphoma), lymphosarcoma, plasmacytoma, reticulosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma o Capsule and trabeculae: fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma

Most common angiosarcomas

Symptoms - splenomegaly, malignant impregnation syndrome, pain in case of superinfection, tumor necrosis Treatment - splenectomy +/- adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy

DD - splenomegaly and metastasis

11. Incidental splenectomy

  • Spleen is vulnerable to injury during operative procedures in upper abdomen → When splenic capsule is torn, splenectomy is frequently performed → Morbidity and mortality are higher with iatrogenic injury

Splenectomy

Absolute indications

1. Splenic tumors

2. Metastatic disease

3. Splenic abscess

4. Pseudo-inflammatory tumors of spleen

5. Hereditary spherocytosis

6. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

7. Chronic myeloid leukemia

8. Sarcomas

9. Trauma

10. Benign tumors of the spleen

11. Hydatid cyst of spleen

12. Splenic vein thrombosis with ruptured gastric varices

13. Ruptured aneurysm

Relative indications

1. Congenital or autoimmune hemolytic anemias

2. Sickle cell anemia, thalassemia

3. Hereditary elliptocytosis

4. Thrombocytopenic purpura

5. Felty’s syndrome

6. Chronic rheumatoid arthritis

7. Splenic neutropenia

8. HL and NHL

9. Gaucher’s disease/Niemann-Pick disease

10. Leukemia

11. Myeloid metaplasia

12. Primary splenic pancreatitis

13. Cirrhosis with portal hypertension and

hypersplenism

Contraindications: myeloid leukemia, acute leukosis

→ Prior to removing spleen specific preoperative preparation necessary

  • All patients should receive polyvalent pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugant vaccine
  • Blood products should be available well in advance of surgery

Blood compositional changes in asplenic or hyposplenic patient

  • Absence of functional splenic tissue results in characteristic changes in circulating blood → Some of these are predictable and desirable results → These changes are considered measure of its success when splenectomy is performed for hematologic disease → Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) and thrombocytosis (desired result) → Other findings include target cells, acanthocytes, Heinz bodies and stippled red cells Post-OP outcomes

1. Siderocytes - red blood cells (erythrocyte) which contains iron granules

2. Howell-Jolly bodies and thrombocytosis (desired result)

3. Leukocytosis

4. Increased platelet count

Complications

1. Left lower lobe atelectasis = most common

2. Subphrenic hematoma, bleeding

3. Subphrenic abscess → can occur with placement of drain

4. Pancreatitis → trauma to tail of pancreas

5. Deep vein thrombosis → low dose anticoagulants

6. Fulminant systemic sepsis with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus Pneumoniae, Neisseria Meningitidis, HaemophilusInfluenzae Hematological outcomes Initial a. Thrombocytopenia → rise in platelet count within a few days b. Chronic hemolytic anemias → Hgb level above 10 g/dl Long term a. Increase in platelet count → rise to >150,000 more than 2 months after surgery b. 90-100% success for hereditary spherocytosis Immunological consequences

  • Causes slower and incomplete adaptive immune response against bacteria
  • Low levels of tuftsin, which stimulates phagocytosis by neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes
  • Decreased neutrophil and macrophage activity
  • Increased NK cell activity
  • Limited capacity of circulating B-cells to differentiate into antibody-secreting cells
  • Decreased level of T-cells

Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI)

1. Lifetime risk of severe infection

2. Incidence of 3.2% post-splenectomy

3. Loss of the spleen’s ability to filter and phagocytose bacteria and infected RBC

Most common sources of infections

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae = most common
  • H. influenza
  • Meningococcus
  • Group A streptococci → Presents with pneumonia or meningitis

Prevention

→ Vaccine against

  • Pneumococcus
  • H. influenza
  • Meningococcus → to be given within 7-14 days after splenectomy

+ Booster dose for pneumococcal vaccine every 5-6 years

+ Annual H. influenza vaccine

+ Daily dose of penicillin or amoxicillin for 2 years

title: Pancreas
html:
Anatomy

  • Digestive (exocrine) and hormonal (endocrine) functions
  • Positioned at transpyloric plane (L1) → epigastrium and left hypochondrium regions
  • With exception of tail → retroperitoneal organ
  • Stomach – Separated from pancreas by lesser sac, stomach and pylorus lie anterior
  • Duodenum – D1 lies anteriorly, D2 lies laterally to pancreatic head
  • Transverse mesocolon – Attaches to anterior surface of pancreas
  • Common bile duct – Descends behind head before opening into major pancreatic duct
  • Spleen – located posteriorly and laterally
  • Aorta and IVC pass posteriorly to head
  • Superior mesenteric vessels lie behind neck and anterior to uncinate process → come anterior over D3
  • Posterior to neck → splenic and superior mesenteric veins unite to portal vein
  • Splenic artery traverses superior border of pancreas
  • Composed of head, uncinate process, neck, body, tail
  • Tail lies within close proximity to hilum of spleen
  • Exocrine pancreas: acini → intercalated ducts →
  • intralobular collecting ducts → main pancreatic duct (Wirsung duct) → unites with common bile duct = hepatopancreatic duct → opens into ampulla of Vater and into duodenum via major duodenal papilla
  • Secretions controlled by sphincter of Oddi
  • Arterial supply: splenic artery, head also by superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries)
  • Venous drainage: speenic vein, head drained into superior mesenteric branches of hepatic portal vein
  • Lymphatic vessels: follow arterial supply, empty into pancreaticosplenal nodes and pyloric nodes, then into superior mesenteric and coeliac lymph nodes

1. Benign pancreatic disorders

I. Acute pancreatitis

= inflammatory process of pancreas with variable involvement of other regional tissues or remote organ systems

  • Mild and severe forms
  • In mild acute pancreatitis → only edema of retroperitoneal area, involving especially peripancreatic tissue → organ dysfunction is minimal and recovery without sequelae
  • In severe acute pancreatitis → pancreatic and retroperitoneal fat necrosis with involvement of remote structures (e.g., mesentery) + complications (ascites, haemorrhage, septic shock) and organ failure (first week)
  • Overall mortality - 15%, but rises to 30% in severe AP

Pathophysiology

Trypsinogen = first proenzyme to be activated in duodenum

  • Protective mechanisms against excessive or premature activation → high levels of trypsin inhibit pancreatic secretion → separate packing of proenzymes into zymogen vesicles → combination of zymogen with protease inhibitors
  • Abnormal activation started by lysosomes → activate trypsinogen in zymogen capsules → activated enzymes get in extracellular space → positive chemotactism for neutrophils and macrophages → aggravate inflammation
  • Local edema
  • Elastase damages vascular wall → hemorrhage and necrosis
  • Systemic inflammation mediators → respiratory and renal complications, even death

Etiology

→ I GET SMASHED

  • Gallstones migrating into CBD and irritating sphincter of Oddi (1/3 of cases)
  • Microstones and cholesterolosis easily pass through cystic duct and Oddi
  • Alcohol (1/3)
  • ERCP (1-3%)
  • Injecting iodinated contrast can raise intraductal pressure enough to start enzymatic cascade
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Abdominal blunt trauma (bicycle, hoof, tire explosion) crush pancreas against spine
  • Drug-induced pancreatitis is usually mild → azathioprine, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, valproic acid, estrogens, furosemide, 5-ASA’s, corticosteroids, octreotide
  • Most common infection → mumps
  • Post-OP or iatrogenic AP
  • Hypercalcemia, hyperparathyroidism, toxic doses of vit. D
  • Idiopathic

Signs and symptoms

  • Abdominal pain → severe, upper half of abdomen, increasing intensity, posterior radiation, duration of several days
  • Fever during first days caused by inflammation (not infection) → High fever after 2 weeks due to infection of necrotic area
  • Hypotension and tachycardia
  • Absence of bowel movements, passing stool and gas (paralytic ileus; guarding)
  • Nausea and vomiting

Physical exam

  • Can mimic peptic ulcer or peritonitis (intense pain, tenderness, guarding and rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign)) → DD = negative DRE
  • Early ascites in severe forms
  • Absent bowl sounds and abd. distension due to paralytic ileus
  • Grey Turner sign
  • Cullen’s sign
  • Jaundice (biliary AP)
  • Dyspnea in case of subphrenic collections irritating diaphragm, pleural effusion or ARDS
  • Subcutaneous fat necrosis due to circulating lipase → erythematous nodules + Funduscopic examination of eyes → ischemic injury in severe cases; can lead to blindness + Uncoherence by aggression of phospholypase A on sphingomielines of nervous system

DD → acute abdomen

Need emergency surgery

  • Cholecystitis
  • Cholangitis
  • Duodenal or gastric perforated ulcer
  • Colonic Obstruction
  • Mesenteric infarction
  • Ectopic pregnancy

Acute non-surgical abdomen

  • Myocardial infarction
  • Bacterial pneumonia
  • Reno-uretheral colic

Lab

1. Serum amylase and lipase

2.Trypsin, trypsinogen, trypsinogen activation peptide

3. Cholestasis markers (ALP, total bilirubin)

and cytolysis enzymes (AST, ALT)

4. Cholesterol and TG’s

5. Calcium

6. Glucose

7. WBC

8. Hct

9. CRP !!!

  • 3-10x higher than normal
  • Lipase is more useful due to its longer T ½ (not routinely)
  • Not routinely
  • Can indicate gallstone
  • Hypocalcemia secondary to binding of Ca2+ to fatty acids resulting from saponification of fat
  • Rarely hypercalcemia as cause
  • Usually elevated → initially due to inflammation and after at least one week due to infection of necrotic tissue
  • Usually high at admission because of edema and ascites
  • It may then drop in severe cases due to necrotic-hemorrhagic lesions
  • > 10 mg/dL at 48 hours after onset is prognostic factor for organ failure
  • CRP is not specific for pancreatitis

10. Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen,

creatinine, arterial blood gases must be followed to diagnose any renal or respiratory problems

Imaging

Plain X-ray

Abdominal US

Abdominal CT

ERCP

MRCP

Endoscopic US

  • Not very useful, but can show → Pneumoperitoneum due to hollow organ perforation (DD) → Paralytic ileus → Sentinel loop sign = dilatation of first jejunal loop → Colon cut off sign = associates dilation of transverse colon with empty gas left flexure → Calcification in pancreatic area (stigmata of CP)
  • Limited help because of ileus
  • Technique of choice for detecting gallbladder lithiasis
  • Not reliable for CBD stones

= best imaging method → Balthazar grading scale is based on CT findings A = normal B = enlargement C = peripancreatic inflammation D = single fluid collection E = multiple fluid collections → Risk of infection and mortality - none for A and B; rises from C to E CT (or US) guided needle aspiration → important to asses infection of necrosis

  • Used with caution in biliary AP in first 3 days from onset; later risk of aggravation
  • Offers comparable result to ERCP – without risks !
  • Better data than plain US + biopsy → DD

Prognosis

→ Ranson score → calculated only first 48 hours after onset

  • Each one gives 1 point
  • Mortality rises at 50% for score > 5

WBC

8 mg/dl

Complications

1. Pseudocyst

2. Pancreatic abscess and

infected necrosis

3. Pancreatic duct disruption

4. Hemorrhage

= collection of pancreatic fluid and necrotic debris enclosed by neighboring organs; without walls

  • Pseudocysto-jejunostomy on Y loop = technique of choice → Better than stomach/ duodenum because no food can get into it
  • Transpapillary drainage
  • Percutaneous drainage
  • Transmural drainage
  • Caused by bacteria from intestinal flora
  • Laparoscopic removal (3-4 weeks after onset is best moment)
  • CT guided needle aspiration
  • Associated with extensive pancreatic necrosis
  • If drainage is in place → discharges very high amylase levels
  • Transpapillary stent can be useful
  • Can communicate with pseudocyst
  • Can cause fistulas → have fibrotic tract → fistulo-jejunostomy on Y loop should be performed
  • Rare
  • Due to elastase

Treatment

  • Fluid resuscitation without waiting for lab values (ascites and edema cause severe fluid loss)
  • In order to have exact fluid balance → bladder catheter and gastric aspiration
  • Central venous and arterial line mandatory in pat. with poor status
  • No oral intake allowed → ileus
  • Avoidance of morphine → spastic of Oddi s. → choose other analgesics !
  • AB (meropenem/ imipenem) for 14 days or longer if systemic complications occur
  • Antifungal prophylaxis → fluconazole
  • Octreotide may improve outcome
  • Hemodiafiltration (CHDF) on polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) membranes helps in eliminating cytokines
  • Selective digestive decontamination (SDD) but only in selected patients
  • Total parenteral nutrition not routinely recommended → Endoscopically assisted naso-jejunal feeding tube or surgical jejunostomy preferred → Surgery
  • It has to be avoided first 2 weeks
  • Sterile necrosis has to be treated in conservative manner
  • Sterile necrosis can benefit from surgery if there is tendency to extension or in fulminant AP (organ failure at less than 72 from onset)
  • Infection of necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue has to be operated
  • Technique must evacuate necrosis but has to spare as much tissue as possible
  • Cholecystectomy is mandatory in every gallstone AP or even idiopathic AP to avoid recurrence
  • Minimally invasive approach has to be limited to highly specialized centers → Laparostomy (peritoneal cavity is opened anteriorly and deliberately left open) with necrosectomy + lavage (can be repeated as often as possible)
  • Closed lavage possible but not often used
  • Vac-pac indicated in SAP with abdominal hypertension and compartment syndrome
  • Other method - retroperitoneoscopy

II. Chronic pancreatitis

= continuing inflammatory pathology of pancreas leading to irreversible morphologic changes which causes exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency

Etiology

→ TIGAR-O classification system

Toxic and metabolic factors

Idiopathic

Genetic predisposition

Autoimmune

Recurrence of severe AP

Obstruction

  • Alcohol !! (70%)
  • Tobacco
  • Isolated autoimmune pancreatitis
  • Chronic pancreatitis associated with other autoimmune diseases (Sjorgen syndrome, scleroderma, PSC, primary biliary cirrhosis)
  • After necrosis
  • Vascular disease/ ischemia
  • Post-irradiation
  • Oddi benign/ malignant stenosis
  • Pancreas divisum
  • Diverticula of duodenal window
  • Duodenal polyps
  • Vaterian ampulloma
  • Periampullary duodenal cyst

Morphopathology

= process of fibrosis and sclerosis with pancreatic parenchymal destruction

Symptoms

  • Pain = major clinical symptom (upper abdomen, radiates into lumbar region; intensified by alcohol and fatty meals)
  • If 90% of acinar destroyed → insufficiency signs → steatorrhea
  • Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins
  • Weight loss and muscular dysfunction
  • Diabetes (often requires insulin treatment)

DD

  • Pancreatic CA
  • Gallstones
  • AP
  • Gastric and duodenal ulcer
  • Gastric CA
  • IBS or IBD
  • Malabsorption syndromes

Complications

1. Pain

2. Pancreatic pseudocyst

3. Bile duct stenosis

4. Mesenteric/ splenic vein thrombosis

5. Duodenal stenosis

6. Pseudoaneurysm

7. Pancreatic adenoCA

8. Extrapancreatic malignant tumors

Treatment

  • Drug treatment → reducing pain, treatment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency
  • Special diet → excluding alcohol, tobacco, coffee, reduced fat and raw vegetables
  • Pain therapy → NSAID’s, tramadol
  • Insulin
  • Pancreatic replacement → lipase, trypsin (Kreon)

Surgery

Indications

Surgery for CP

Pseudocysts

Jaundice

Duodenal stenosis

  • Painful syndrome refractory to conservative treatment
  • Suspicion of malignancy
  • CBP obstruction
  • Duodenal stenosis
  • Pancreatic pseudocysts
  • Intracystic bleeding, intraperitoneal or digestive bleeding
  • Extrinsic compression of porto-mesenteric venous axis

1. Drainage surgery

→ When Wirsung duct is dilated (> 7mm diameter) and consists in pancreatico-jejunal anastomosis on Roux-en-Y limb of jejunum

2. Excision surgery → Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure)

3. Denervation surgery → Bilateral thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy

  • US/ CT guided percutaneous drainage
  • Endoscopic treatment → transpapillary drainage
  • Surgery → drainage and excision
  • Stent or biliary-digestive bypass
  • Gastro-entero anastomosis or pseudocyst drainage if this compresses the stomach or duodenum

III. Benign tumors

= rare

Adenoma

Cystadenoma

Cystic papillary tumor

Intraductal papilloma

  • a) Serous (microcyst), no malignant potential
  • b) Mucinous cystadenomas, high malignancy potential, same therapeutic strategy as in pancreatic CA May cause recurring acute pancreatitis and eventually obstructive chronic pancreatitis

Clinical

  • Not characteristic
  • Abdominal pain or compression
  • May be palpable in epigastric region when large

Treatment

  • Surgery for symptomatic and/or voluminous tumors
  • Mucinous cystadenomas require organ and lymphatic resection

2) Malignant tumors

Epidemiology

  • 1% of all cancers, 10% of GI
  • Increasing incidence
  • Too rarely diagnosed on time to allow effective therapy

Risk factors

  • Age (60-80 y)
  • Smoking !!!
  • Alcohol
  • Diet - red meat and fats
  • Coffee
  • Familiy history due to association with other hereditary diseases (familial pancreatitis, Gardner’s snd, polycystic d.)
  • High risk disease (chronic pancreatitis, familial pancreatitis, Peutz-Jeghers, biliary lithiasis)
  • Genetic alterations → Oncogene (KRAS) or Tumor suppressor genes (CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4)

Morphopathology

Macroscopic

  • Mostly located at pancreatic head (70%), then corpus (15%), tail (10%)
  • Solid tumor, hard, irregular, yellowish grey
  • In diffuse, multifocal forms, pancreas forms one single compact, hard tumoral mass Microscopic GX = Grade cannot be assessed G1 = well differentiated tumor G2 = moderately differentiated tumor G3 = poorly differentiated tumor G4 = undifferentiated tumor Most important non-endocrine pancreatic CA types

1. Severe ductal dysplasia/ carcinoma in situ

2. Adenocarcinomas (ductal and acinar) → 81%

  • Squamous adenocarcinoma
  • Giant cell carcinoma
  • Cystadenomas

3. Osteoclastic type tumors

4. Serous cystadenocarcioma

5. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma

6. Intraductal papillary mucinous carcinoma

7. Acinar cell carcinoma

8. Pancreatoblastoma

9. Sarcomas

10. Lymphomas

Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) – non-invasive proliferations of pancreatic ducts epithelium; classified by degree of nuclear atypias: PanIN-1, PanIN-2 → no oncological risk, PanIN-3 lesions → risk Extension

  • Local invasion
  • Lymphatic
  • Hematogenic
  • Perineural (characteristic, loco-regional recurrences)
  • Pancreatic head carcinomas metastasize in liver, lungs and pleura
  • Corpus and tail in peritoneum

TNM classification

Tis carcinoma in situ

T1 tumor diameter ≤ 2cm, with no extension beyond pancreas

T2 tumor limited to pancreatic gland, ≥ 2cm in diameter

T3 extension of tumor beyond gland, but not invading superior mesenteric artery or celiac trunk T4 primary tumor invading celiac axis or superior mesenteric artery (unresectable)

N1 regional lymph nodes with metastasis

M1 remote metastases

Clinical

Status phase = clinical picture becomes suggestive for the locations → usually in advanced stage Pancreatic head Pancreatic body Pancreatic tail Triad: Jaundice, weight loss, pain

  • Rapid and very severe weight loss
  • No specific clinical picture
  • Jaundice is usually first sign, but
  • Later pain: very severe, more intense - Continuous dull pain in LUQ, shows advanced stage ! during night, not influenced by eating, constipation, DM, unspecific (80% unresectable) radiating into back (Chauffard’s dyspeptic syndrome, segmental
  • Earliest sign: dull, intermient pain in pancratico-solar syndr.) portal hypertension epigastrium and left hypochondrium - Mental disturbances
  • Hard palpable tumor, fixed,
  • Advanced signs: Loss of appetite,
  • Anorexia, adynamia, vomiting transversal in epigastrium

Nausea, Constipation or Diarrhea, (duodenal stenosis due to invasion)

Fatigue, Fever

  • Back pain - advanced, unresectable
  • Back pain → celiac plexus invasion case (final stage)
  • Migrant thrombophlebitis (Trousseau
  • DM → typically non-obese, no sign) might occur months before family history, smoker, usually starts - Sectorial portal hypertension few months before onset of jaundice syndrome with upper GI hemorrhage → DM + progressive weight loss = due to ruptured esogastric varices 90% diagnostic specificity ! (splenic v. invasion)
  • Urine color = black beer (choluric urine)
  • Stool yellow, grey, white (acholic)
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Distended, tensed, hard, painless gallbladder → Courvoisier Terrier’s sign
  • Repetitive attacks of acute pancreatitis

General: left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow Troisier sign → distant metastasis), jaundiced, cachectic, ascites

Imaging

1. US

  • Cheap, non-invasive, largely accessible
  • Tumors usually hypoechogenic with irregular contour

+ Enlarged spleno-portal axis, dilated CBD and intrahepatic bile ducts

+ Liver metastasis; lymph node involvement

+ Double duct sign (dilation of main bile and pancreatic ducts)

1.1 CEUS

  • Good for detecting liver metastasis (M)

1.2 Percutaneous US guided biopsy - Histological diagnosis

1.3 EUS

  • Almost 100% accuracy
  • Only technique that detect tumors < 1cm (early cancers) → EUS-FNA – enough tissue samples ! (T)
  • Negative biopsy does not exclude malignancy !

2. MDCECT

= Multidetector contrast enhanced CT scan

  • Using thin slices assessing local extension (T), detecting liver metastasis (M)
  • Lymph nodes (N) > 1cm usually considered malignant

3. ERCP

4. TPC

5. MRI

6. Angio-MRI

7. Cholangio-MRI

8. Staging laparoscopy (SL)

  • Not currently used for diagnosis due to potential complications

= Transparietohepatic cholangiography

  • Transparietal puncture under US/ CT guidance of dilated bile duct, contrast into biliary tree
  • Not currently used due to its complications (hemorrhage, bile leaks (choleperitoneum), bile collection)
  • Higher specificity than CT scan
  • Detect tumoral invasion of adjacent vasculature → portal vein, SMA/V
  • Most accurate technique in detecting bile intraductal obstacles (especially small tumors)
  • DD among periampullary tumors
  • Very useful in detecting “occult metastasis” (small, millimetric peritoneal or hepatic deposits (undetectable even by most CTs)
  • It is systematically indicated in ALL pancreatic body and tail CA’s
  • Video-laparoscopy can be completed with laparoscopic ultrasonography, for more accurate assessment of vascular peritumoral structures or small intrahepatic mets

Treatment

Periampullary tumors !!! = tumors with different origin but same surgical treatment → ampullary tumors, distal cholangiocarcinoma, duodenal carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of pancreas head I. Radical treatment

  • Only chance for cure R0
  • Pre-OP selection: T1, T2, T3, N0-M0, N1-M0 → only 15-25% are candidates
  • 5-year survival after is 10-25%
  • Pre-OP preparation → Jaundice → Malnutrition and malabsorbtion due to obstruction of bile ducts, pancreatic duct and/or duodenum → Hypoalbuinemia Head

► Whipple (Cephalic Pancreatic-duodenoectomy)

  • Resection of
  • Gallbladder
  • Main bile duct
  • Gastric antrum + pylorum
  • Entire duodenum + 10-20cm from initial jejunum (first loop)
  • Pancreatic head
  • Digestive tract reconstruction

1) pancreato-gastro or pancreato-jejunal

2) hepatico-jejunal

3) gastro-jejunal anastomoses

  • Weak pint: pancreatic stump and digestive tract → risk of fistula
  • Sometimes with subtotal/ total pancreatectomy to achieve R0

► Regional pancreatectomy

  • Including irresectable cases with posterior vascular invasion
  • After segmental resection of invaded vessels → restoration
  • portal vein - mesentero-portal end-to-end anastomosis (type I operation)
  • superior mesenteric artery - reimplantation into aorta (type II)
  • hepatic artery - interposing graft between it and aorta
  • Portal vein resection is justified (no morbidity/mortality), arterial resection not → contraindication ! (morbidity/mortality with no survival benefit)

► Pylorus preserving pancreatic duodenectomy/ Traverso-Longmire = gold standard

  • Main advantage: significant earlier post-op weight gain and superior alimentary comfort due to anatomical and functional integrity of stomach

Body/ tail

  • In severe jaundice → biliary decompression by stent/ external biliary drainage necessary before radical OP to prevent fatal post-op acute liver failure
  • Distal spleno-pancreatectomy
  • Resectability and prognosis are even worse

Whipple

Distal spleno-pancreatectomy

Central pancreatectomy

II. Palliative treatment

  • 3 main therapeutical targets → jaundice, duodenal obstruction, pain

Jaundice

  • Biliary decompression via gall baldder, ductus choledocus or ductus hepaticus with stomach, duodenum or jejunum

1. Choleocysto-duodenal or choleocysto-jejunal anastomosis

→ Nowadays exceptionally indicated in cases with very short life expectancy, otherwise high chance of failure due to tumor invasion

2. Choledoco-duodenostomy

→ re-invasion likely

3. Roux-en Y hepatico-jejunostomy

  • Main bile duct is transsected just below hilar bifurcation and anastomosed terminolaterally to Roux en Y jejunal loop; eficient and has longest patency, invasion rarelly occurs, bigger operation with bigger morbidity → only fit patients with longer (> 12-18 months) life expectancy (local extended, nonmetastatic)

Duodenal/ gastric outflow 1. Gastroenterostomy obstruction

  • Latero-lateral bypass, avoids duodenal stenosis

2. Double biliary and digestive diversion

  • Only well selected cases → fit patients, locally advanced tumors, absence of any detectable metastases (T3-4, N0-2, M0)

Pain

  • Chemical splanchnicectomy with alcohol = preferred nowadays
  • Injection in celiac plexus
  • Open, laparoscopic surgery, endosonography guiding, transgastric approach
  • Also thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy possible

Radio- and chemotherapy

  • Radiotherapy - external or intraoperative radiation has no well documented results
  • Chemotherapy - at least 3 agents concomitantly, poor results
  • Chemotherapy + radiation therapy improves survival with advanced pancreatic cancer

I) Tumors of the endocrine pancreas

Insulinoma

Tumor of beta-islet cells → secretes insulin

Mostly benign insular adenoma, 10% malignant

Hypersecreting metastases may be cause of recurrence

Pathomorphology: small nodule, firm, located at head or tail of pancreas, can be ectopic Neuropsychiatric manifestations o Central nervous: diplopia, convulsions, coma o Sympathetic nervous system: flushing, sweating, vomiting, persistent hunger o Psychiatric: restlessness, mental instability, disorientation Signs and symptoms recurr at regular intervals → periodical bouts of hypoglycemia (after physical exercise or prolonged fasting) and subside postprandially (especially sweeets)

Clinical diagnosis based on Whipple triad o Insulin shock (hypoglycemia) induced by exercise or fasting o Low glycemia – under 50 mg% during bouts o Symptoms subside after glucose administration Laboratory: glycemia, insulin, proinsulin, glucose/insulin ratio Imaging: US (percutaneous, endoscopic, intraoperative), CT, MRI, angiography Treatment: Radical surgical excision (local excision, central pancreatectomy, corporeo-caudal pancreatectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy)

Radical resection evaluated intraoperativelly by measuring plasma insulin levels before and after excision !

Glucagonoma

Rare, mainly women

Pathomorphology: pancreatic body or tail (60%), extended to whole organ, head of gland (10%)

Often becomes malignant

Originates in glucagon secreting alpha cells

Clinical features: cutaneous lesions (migratory necrotising erythema), glossitis, vulvovaginitis, diabetes mellitus, anemia due to anorexia and hypoaminoacidemia, weight loss, antianabolic action, deep vein thrombosis Treatment: surgical resection, tumor ablation even in presence of metastases, polychemotherapy Repeated multiple re-excisions for local or metastatic recurrences prolong survival

Gastrinoma

Secreting gastrin → hypersecretion of HCl in stomach → gastric and duodenal ulcers (Zollinger-Ellison snd)

Eutopic (G cells in antrum, duodenal bulb, jejunum) or ectopic (pancreas, mesenteric ganglia, ovary, spleen)

Gastrinomas are often multiple (80%) and malignant (2/3 of cases)

Ulcers refractory to treatment, acid hypersecretion not influenced by treatment, diarrhea and steatorrhea due to large volume of gastric acid Frequently with metastases at time of diagnosis Treatment: suppression of acid secretion by high doses of H2 receptors blockers or omeprazol Somatostatin analogs efficiently inhibit hormonal and gastric secretion (ocreotide)

Surgery - total gastrectomy (less common), vagotomy, tumor enucleation or corpo-caudal pancreatectomy

VIPoma

Originating in insular non-beta cells that secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)

Responsible for Verner-Morrison syndrome (watery diarrhea, hypokaliemia, hypochlorhydria, severe dehydration involving high fatal risk)

Pathomorphology - adenoma (43%), carcinoma (37%) or microadenomatosis

Clinical: diarrhea leading to severe dehydration with hypokaliemia, metabolic acidosis, hypomagnesemia (tetany), hypokalemic nephropathy with uremia, extreme physical fatigue, itchy rashes, heart disturbances (rhythm, failure)

Hypo-achlorhydria (strong inhibitor of acid gastric secretion)

Glucose intolerance

Treatment - surgical (corpo-caudal pancreatectomy), hydroelectrolithic rebalancing, administration of somatostatin analogs (Ocretotid, Sandostatin)

Somatostatinoma

Rare

High malignancy potential, with early metastases

Somatostatin triggers biliary lithiasis, diabetes mellitus, diarrhea and statorrhea Inhibits somatotropic hormone, TSH, insulin, glucagons, gastrin, and cholecystokininpancreazimine scretions Nausea, vomiting, bloating, weight loss Treatment - surgical (cephalic duodeno-pancreatectomy or corpo-caudal pancreatectomy)

Pancreatic polypeptide secreting tumor

Clinical picture not specific, diarrhea, steatorrhea, basal hypochlorhydria, weight loss (inhibitory effect on gallbladder and pancreatic enzyme secretion)

Treatment - surgical (pancreaticoduodenectomy), streptozocin, somatostatin analogs

Carcinoid tumor

Rare, from chromaffin cells

Symptomatology not specific

Flushing, arterial hypertension, oedema around eyes, hypersecretion of saliva and tears, diarrhea, abdominal pain, all occurring in paroxistic bouts High malignancy potential

Treatment - surgical (pancreaticoduodenectomy)
sections: Severe ductal dysplasia/ carcinoma in situ

title: Acute bowel obstructions
html:
= Abnormal persistent suppression of effective bowel movements with local, regional and general consequences

  • pluri-etiologic/ pluri-pathogenic

Classifications

  • a) Topographic
  • Upper/ High
  • Lower/ Low
  • b) Pathogenic
  • Vascular involvement
  • Prognosis decided by presence/ absence of ischemia

Etiology

1. Adhesions (40%) -> post-OP

2. Malignant (cancer) obstructions (20%)

3. External strangulations (15%)

4. Early post-OP (6.8%)

5. Mesenteric vascular occlusion (6.5%)

6. Volvulus (5%)

7. Benign obstructive tumors (3%)

8. Obturator obstructions (2%)

9. Internal hernias (0.5%)

10. Invaginations

Obstructive (mechanical obstruction)

  • Complete or incomplete (subacute) obstruction
  • Without affecting, at least initially, blood supply of intestinal wall

A. Extrinsic compressions

I. Tumors (benign/ malignant)

  • Mesenterial, uterus, ovary, liver
  • Retroperitoneal (primary, kidney, adrenal, pancreas)
  • Lymph nodes

II. Adhesions (visceral, parietal)

III. Foreign bodies (left after surgery)

B. Intramural lesions

I. Congenital stenoses

II. Tumors (benign, malignant, primary, metastases)

III. Inflammatory stenoses (specific: TBC, CD; non-specific: postradiation, scars)

IV. Intramural hematomas

Strangulations

C. Endoluminal obstacles

  • Gallstones (biliary ileus)
  • Food bolus (Phytobezoars)
  • Hair bolus (Trichobezoars)
  • Worms (Ascariasis, Ascarid ball)
  • Accidental (tooth fragments, bones, wood, plastic) -> pylorus, duodenal curvatures, ileo-cecal valve, rectosigmoid flexure, anal canal
  • Obstruction of bowel (“double closed loop”, “one end” closed loop) with interruption of venous/arterial supply -> ischemia, necrosis and perforation A. External
  • Hernias
  • Incisional hernias
  • Eviscerations

Vascular (bowel infarctions)

B. Internal

  • Internal hernias
  • Invaginations (intussusceptions)
  • Volvulus
  • Obstructing/ strangulating – ischemic adhesion
  • By far most severe variant, with highest mortality !

Functional (non-mechanical/

Paralytic ileus)

A. Acute arterial obstruction

  • Embolus, thromb-embolus

B. Acute venous obstruction

C. Acute microcirculation obstruction

  • Occur at segmental level or entire length of intestinal tract
  • Produced by exaggerated, prolonged spasms -> bowel paresis (adynamic ileus)
  • Absence of any mechanical obstruction with intact intestinal vascularization A. Metabolic causes
  • Severe acidosis (diabetes mellitus, “status asthmaticus”), uremia, severe electrolyte imbalances (hypopotassemia, hyponatremia), hypothyroidism, hypoproteinemia
  • Severe anemias
  • Abdominal (pelvic) irradiation
  • Neurologic lesions: epilepsy, brain tumors, MS, colon pseudo-obstruction B. Reflex causes
  • Post-operative bowel paresis
  • Mesenterial torsion / cavitary organs distension
  • fallopian tube torsion
  • reno-ureteral colic
  • biliary colic
  • acute urinary bladder distension
  • Thoracic disorders (pneumonia, thoracic traumas, myocardial infarction – bowel paresis associated with epigastric pain and shock ! )
  • Retroperitoneal disorders (hematomas, acute pancreatitis, abscesses)
  • Sterile intraperitoneal fluid collections
  • acute onset of ascites in liver cirrhosis
  • hemoperitoneum
  • chemical peritonitis

C. Septic causes

  • Localized/ diffuse peritonitis
  • Septic conditions adjacent to peritoneal serosa (pelvic, retroperitoneal abscess) double closed loops (volvulus, strangulations)

Pathophysiology

→ 3 major initial events a. Motility ceases b. Obstruction of bowel c. Obstruction of vascular → 4 main types

1. Functional (a)

2. Obstructive (b)

3. Strangulated (b+c)

4. Vascular (c)

  • Alterations of homeostasis initially start at affected loop and of intestinal tract upstream
  • At onset -> noxious stimulus due to increased intralumenal tension -> increase in peristaltism and excessive enteral gland secretion
  • Peristaltic fight followed by energy exhaustion of muscle fibers -> onset of distension and inability to reabsorb fluids -> endolumenal accumulation of fluids and gas => huge atonic upstream bowl reservoir containing enormous fluid and gas accumulations
  • Fluids come from: saliva, gastric juice, biliary fluid, pancreatic juice, enteral juice
  • Results in severely dehydrated (3rd space fluid loss) and electrolyte imbalance
  • Gas accumulations from swallowed air, biochemical reactions and activity of microbial flora
  • Increased intestinal distension -> pressure increases -> bowel wall squashed -> venous circulation closed
  • > eventually capillary collapse -> wall edema -> ischemia and necrosis (irreversible)
  • Ascites common (another third compartment)
  • Mixed (metabolic and respiratory) acidosis
  • Obstruction by strangulation -> necrosis is specific -> closely followed by infection and toxaemia
  • > rapidly septico-toxic and/ or hypovolemic shock

Clinical manifestation

  • Pain: colicy, intermitent pain, rapid increase in intensity (max. of 30-60s) followed by rapid and total decrease
  • Initially located at level of obstruction and subsequently becomes generalized
  • Pain free time interval between colics has clinical relevance
  • Obstruction in proximal jejunal - 5 min, ileum - 5-20 min, colon more - > 20 min.
  • Strangulations and enteromesenteric infarctions - permanent, high intensity pain, cannot be controlled by pain killers
  • Volvulus – rapid, complete, brutal, syncopal onset, with same continuous high intensity pain
  • Paralytic ileus - pain diffuse, continuous, low-moderate intensity
  • Vomiting: initially reflex (pain, distension), later becomes effortless, abundant and productive with regurgitation, due to antiperistaltic waves and “overfullness
  • Brings no relieve to patient !
  • High, proximal obstructions - vomiting is early, repeated, persistent, clear biliary fluid
  • Low ileal obstructions - initial containes food remains, then becomes bilious, later porraceous (turbid bile) and finally fecaloid (false fecal vomiting)
  • Low, distal (recto-sigmoid) - occurs late and is less common
  • Faeculent vomit = sign of severity, due to abnormal overgrow of faecal bacteria at 24-48 hours after onset
  • Absence of fecal and gas transit (obstipation)
  • In high obstructions, initial passage from distal intestine possible (dangerous delay of diagnosis)
  • Subocclusive (König) syndrome = characteristic for incomplete obstructions of small intestine and ileocecal segment -> colicy pain at fixed point (level of obstruction), increased meteorism, hydro-aeric noises, borborgym, finally diarrhea and gas passage (relief); similar episodes reoccur
  • Bloody-glaireous stools in some invaginations and enteromesenteric infarction (late clinical sign – severe

prognosis !)

Physical examination

Abdominal signs

Inspection

  • Meteorism is characteristic, occur during first 24 hours, abdominal distension
  • Functional ileus - distension is intense and diffuse, yet painless

Mechanical obstructions of distal ileum - distension in center of abdomen Distal rectosigmoid obstructions - meteorism is extensive, but localized in flanks and epigastric Sigmoid volvulus - most extensive abdominal distension, asymmetrical, ovoid, oriented from left iliac fossa towards right upper quadrant Small bowel volvulus - central and asymmetrical balloon Abdominal distension absent in extremely high occlusions, Richter type hernias, early phases of all bowel obstructions Visible peristaltism at abdominal wall in lean patients with mechanical obstruction If constant location and fixed point -> König syndrome Also detect postoperative scars, external hernias

Palpation

  • Migrating tumor masses – invaginations and faecalomas, fixed tumor masses (stenosing tumors)
  • Inflamatory tumors
  • Localized areas of tenderness and/or rigidity in ischaemic obstructions (strangulations, torsions, intussusceptions, infarctions)

Percussion

  • Tympanism that covers hepatic dullness
  • Meteorism
  • Localized dullness in case of loops filled with liquid
  • Shifting dullness in ascites

Auscultation

  • Hydro-aeric bowel sounds and borborygmi
  • In functional bowel pareses - “abdominal quiet”
  • “death silence” in bowel infarctions

Rectal exam

  • Compulsory
  • Empty rectal ampulla (Hochwag sign)

Extra-abdominal signs

  • Initially, normal pulse, no fever, only anxiety, tachycardia during colicky episodes
  • Eventually, general condition progressively alters, finally occlusive septic-toxic shock
  • “tormented” facies by ischemic colic or strangulation
  • Signs of severe dehydration (thirst, dry tongue, hypotonic eye globes, persistent flaccid cutaneous fold)

+ decreased diuresis (empty urinary bladder at initial catheterisation)

  • Fever - infected necrosis or diffuse peritonitis
  • Marmoreal skin, hemodynamic collapse and hypothermia - late, terminal phases of septico-toxic shock

Paraclinical examination

  • Plain abdominal radiography - most valuable, gas-fluid levels 4-6 hours of onset o Functional bowel paresis - hydro-aeric images uniformly distributed, from stomach to whole intestine (“chessboard” images) o Small bowel obstructions - hydro-aeric images numerous, in central abdominal area, large transverse diameter o Distal colic - gas-fluid levels less numerous, outline colic frame, large vertical diameter
  • Irrigography – nowadays not used routinely

Abdominal ultrasound - routine techniques, degree of loop distension, wall thickness, presence of peristaltism, fluid in peritoneal cavity, etiology of occlusive syndrome Abdominal CT - most valuable technique, establish underlying cause Mesenteric angiography/Angio MRI - extremely useful although rarely used, determine site of vascular obstructions in ischemia Endoscopy - less frequently in emergency, detect duodenal obstructions Laparoscopy - extremely useful for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, care must be taken to prevent iatrogenic bowel’s lesions due to meteorism

Differential diagnosis

  • Chest trauma, pneumonia, basal pleurisy, right ventricle myocardial infarction
  • Acute adynamic bowel distension in severe, prolonged bronchial asthma episodes (“status astmaticus”) characterized by continuous anal gas emission (not by failure to pass flatus !)
  • Acute gastric distension (usually postoperative) subsides on application of nasogastric suction tube
  • Acute ascites after hepatic portal decompensation
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Painful subumbilical “tumor” - important urinary bladder distention
  • Neglected diffuse peritonitis
  • Psychogenic distension in “ghost pregnancy”

Clinical variant

  • Proximal small bowel obstructions o Sudden onset, rapid evolution o Early, frequent, profuse vomiting o Rapidly and highly unbalancing fluid-ion losses -> hypovolemic shock o Abdominal distension initially absent (“flat abdomen”) o Gas and stools emissions spontaneously or by enema

Distal ileal obstructions o Slower evolution o Third compartment extremely extensive o Vomiting occurs later, abundant, turbid, later faeculent o Colicky episodes less frequent, every 15-20 minutes o Abdominal distension symmetrical, central o Dehydration occurs later but is severe

Low (recto-sigmoid) obstructions o Long progressive, well tolerated evolution ove several days (4-7 days) o Less intense colicky episodes, intervals > 20 minutes o Vomiting absent or late o Important abdominal distension (flanks and epigastric, later generalized) o Rectal digital examination frequently detect cause o Majority caused by malignant tumors (aged patients, multiple comorbidities) o Diastatic perforations -> severe faecaliod diffuse peritonitis with very high mortality rates

  • Repeated abdominal X-ray examinations for early detection of cecal distension close to 1213c m (“critical cecal diameter”) o Colic perforations just above obstructive tumor (extended necrosis of obstructed colon)

Volvulus o Rotation (torsion) of bowel loop by > 180° with “double closed loop” ->interruption of circulation o Sudden onset, continuous (not intermittent-colicky !), very intense pain; vomiting o Abdominal distension - central, symmetrical in jejunal volvulus; lower, asymmetrical, left iliac fossa to right upper quadrant in sigmoid volvulus o Due to full, heavy, long, mobile and hyperperistaltic loops, posterior parietal insertion points are fixed and close to one another o Mortality high

Intestinal intussusceptions (invaginations) o Frequent in children o Sudden onset with typical intermittent colic, with longer periods of calmness o Rectal bleeding in 25% o “migrating tumor” can be detected by palpation only in 20% of cases o Metorism at late stage o Can be chronic recurring o Venous circulation (later arterial too !) blocked o After 48 hours adhesions between invaginated cylinders already tight -> irreversible -> ischemia and necrosis o Usually triggered by inestinal tumor (adenomatous polyps, diverticula, foreign bodies) (triggering enteral tumors are mostly benign, colic tumors are malignant !) o Can be entero-enteral, ileo-colic, ileo-cecal, colo-colic

Internal hernias o Entrapment of mobile loops in orifices, recesses, pouches within peritoneal cavity with or without strangulation o Aquired (abdominal-or thoracic trauma, surgery) or congenital o Internal hernias in preexisting orifices and fossettes

  • paraduodenal hernias
  • paracecal (Rieux) hernias
  • hernias through foramen of Winslow (Treitz)
  • congenital diaphragmatic hernias o Internal hernias through traumatically or iatrogenically generated orifices
  • diaphragmatic
  • transmesocolic (after gastrojejnostomies, Roux en Y loop, etc.)
  • transmesenteric (retro-anastomotic after gastro-jejunal tube placement) o Mortality rates high

Strangulated external hernias o Strangulated intestinal content (double closed loop) initiating ischemic necrosis o Violent (abrupt onset of intense, continuous pain at strangulation, vomiting, pallor, sweating) o Examination promptly detects strangulation -> diagnosis established early o Femoral hernias have highest risk of strangulation, but inguinal hernias more frequent o Femoral hernias with lateral (incomplete) strangulation do not cause intestinal occlusion, but manifest by diarrhea (resulting in dangerous delay in diagnosis and treatment !)

Incisional hernias o With or without strangulation o Intrasaccular adhesions or at level of fibrotic hernial rings

Treatment

  • Main therapeutic targets o Restoration of water-ion and acid-base balance o Relieve gastrointestinal distension o Treat cause of enterocolic obstruction o Prevent future episodes

Preoperative preparation o Placement of naso-gastric suction tube (evacuation of gastrointestinal content, suppression of vomiting, relieving of distension, breaking vicious circle between distension and wall ischemia; no aspiration, allows general anaesthesia, no fluid and ion loss) o 2 large iv lines or CVC -> fluids and rebalance (the longer the obstrusction, the more time it takes for re-equilibrium and until surgery can be performed) + monitoring of CVP o Placing urinary catheter (evaluation of rehydration) o Large spectrum antibiotics o Alpha/ beta blocker or preferably, continuous epidural catheter -> opening of intestinal microcirculation o Pain killers

Surgical treatment

o 2 major objectives: removal of obstruction and removal of toxic intestinal content and peritoneal effusions o Timing of operation chosen depending on type of obstruction (ischemic or non-ischemic); duration of evolution; coexistence of associated diseases o

Immediate emergency surgery in

  • All types of bowel strangulations
  • Acute colic obstructions with “critical cecal diameter”
  • All small bowel obstructions hospitalized before severe water-ion imbalances
  • Any occlusive variant with ischemia

o

Delayed surgery to do re-equilibration

  • Mechanical non-ischaemic obstruction with water-ion imbalances
  • Severe concomitant life-threatening visceral failures

o o

Approach route - median sub- and supra-umbilical laparotomy

Criteria for assessment of viability of loop: color of loop, peristaltism, arterial pulsations

o o

o

o o

If loop not viable -> resection compulsory with/ without restoration of digestive tract continuity If loops viable -> decompression of digestive tract with evacuation of toxic-septic content

  • “retrograde milking” up to level of naso-gastric or large suction tube
  • decompression of colon by thick transanal Faucher tubes
  • decompression by opening digestive tract

In small bowel obstruction - dividing adhesions; devolvulation; disinvagination,; release from internal/ external hernias; enterotomy with extraction of calculus/ foreign body with enterorrhaphy; excision of tumors (uterine, mesenteric tumors); segmental resection in inflammatory/ malignant stenoses In resectable colorectal tumors -> “all-in-one” strategy = resection of lesion + anastomosis In irresectable colorectal tumors -> internal by-pass

  • ileo-transversostomy - in cecal, ascending colon or right flexure obstructive neoplasms
  • transverso-transversostomy - in mid transverse colon obstructions
  • transverso-sigmoidostomy - in splenic flexure malignant stenoses
  • external diversions (permanent or temporary enterostomies, colostomies -> radical resection accomplished 2-3 weeks later if possible with concomitant reconstruction

Postoperative treatment o Maintenance of nasogastric suction until resumption of digestive transit o Volemic, ion and acid-base re-equilibration continued o Antibiotherapy o Symptomatic treatment (pain killers, ...)

Functional occlusions (paralytic ileus) o First intent is to find cause and treat it o Post-OP transit should re-occur after 72 h o Conservative treatment usually enough o Surgery only for underlying cause (e.g, appendicitis, peritonitis) or complications (e.g., perforation) o Initial bowl rest o IV fluids, analgesics o Nasogastric suction tube (not always neccessary) o Stimulation of intestinal transit

  • Continuous peridural infiltration
  • Laxatives or prokinetics
  • Early initiation of enteral feeding if tolerated
  • Mobilisation as soon as possible

Complications

  • Untreated development
  • Necroses
  • Diastatic caecal perforations
  • Diffuse/ localized peritonitis
  • Septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures

Pre- and intraoperative complications

Gastric/ intestinal content aspiration -> severe bronchopneumonia

Bowel perforations -> peritonitis

Postoperative complications

Eviscerations

ARDS

Acute cardiac, respiratory, renal, hepatic failures

Acute stress digestive lesions (UDH)

Pulmonary thrombembolism

Acute gastric dilation

Anastomotic fistulae, abdominal abcesses, peritonitis, sepsis

Multiple recurrent obstructive episodes

Blind loop syndrome (consequence of internal diversions that exclude large, extended bowel segments)

Short bowel syndrome (after extended bowel resections)

1. Obstructions

→ SHOCK!!!

  • Critical fluid loss (9%)
  • Hypersecretion + absorption ceased
  • 3rd parasytic hydric compartment

1. Fluid/ electrolyte redistribution

2. Septicity (bact. translocation)

Metabolic acidosis

1. Predominant alkaline loss

2. Cellular catabolism

3. Respiratory acidosis

Intraenteric pressure (normal 1.4-2.8 mmHg) → Arterioles 30-35 mmHg → Capillaries 15 mmHg → Venules 10mmHg! → Double closed loop → 45 mmHg

2. Strangulations

→ Necrosis and sepsis

  • Viability of bowel early compromised
  • Requires immediate emergency surgery
  • Clinical features are alarming

Signs and symptoms

  • Pain: acute, continuous, sudden
  • Vomiting
  • Abdominal distension: early
  • Constipation
  • Anxious, pale, tachycardic, sweating, tendency to shock
  • Abdomen is painful on palpation, localized muscle defense

Radiology

  • Plain X-ray
  • CT

DD

1. Acute gastric distension

2. Acute obstruction of urinary bladder

3. Acute ascites

4. Pregnancy/ dyspepsia

5. Asthma

6. Chronic constipation (fecaloma)

7. ABOS + SHOCK (acute pancreatitis, mesenteric infarction, acute MI)

Treatment

Pre-OP

Intra-OP

= 1-3 → 12h

1. CVC (ZVK)

2. 2 PVC’s

3. Nasogastric tube (NGST)

4. +/- epidural catheter

5. Urinary catheter

MAIN GOALS

  • Pulmonary function improvement
  • C.V.P. → 5-12 cm H2O
  • AP → optimal
  • CF → <100-120/ min
  • Urine → 30-60ml/h
  • Pain
  • Antibiotics
  • OP timing
  • Emergency → but not too late and not too late

Strangulations → As early as possible!

Germs → endotoxins → catecholamine-like (MCRØ), DIC, mitochondrial block → DEATH Intra-OP evaluation of intestinal viability → Very important (resect/ not resect?)

  • Color
  • Pulsations
  • Bowel movements
  • Intra-operatory bowel recovery

Short bowel syndrome

  • Small bowel
  • Limits (survival: 30-60cm; acceptable: 100-120cm)

Aggravating factors

  • Ileum resection
  • Right hemicolectomy associated
  • Pervious gastric resection → Consequences

Jejuno-ileal insufficiency syndrome (Bennet-Hardwick)

  • Intestinal alterations
  • Malabsorption syndrome → Hypoproteinemia/ hypoalbuminemia → Anemia → Cachexia, vit. insufficiency Post-OP
