title: Abdominal trauma
html:
Definitions

Traumatic lesion - Exchange of energies between victim and environment that goes beyond resistance body Polytrauma

  • At least 2 different anatomical regions
  • At least 1 has life risk
  • Example: traumatized abdomen and limbs with spleen rupture

Poly-contusion

  • Lesions in several topographic regions without vital risk

Poly-fractures

  • Several fractures without involving vital prognosis

Etiology

  • External compressions - extreme intraabdominal pressure resulting in hollow organ ruptures
  • Abrupt decelerations - tear solid or hollow organs, especially mesenteries along vascular pedicles
  • Crushing - solid organs against posterior rigid abdominal wall (spine, ribs), intra- and retroperitoneal hemorrhages
  • Car accidents 50%
  • Work-related accidents 18%
  • Aggression 14%
  • Household accident 7%
  • Sports accidents 6%
  • Other causes (falls from heights) 5%

!!! The wound by the firearm has a complex pathogenesis

Classification of abdominal trauma

1. Closed abdominal trauma (contusions) - 60-79% from abdominal trauma

= blunt trauma

  • Mainly road accidents

2. Open abdominal trauma (wounds)

A. Penetrating when vulnerable agent has entered peritoneal cavity

  • Simple
  • With visceral lesions
  • With complex lesions: neighboring anatomical areas (thoracoabdominal, abdominal-pelvis, thoracic-abdominal-pelvic wounds)

B. Non-penetrating, when they do not enter peritoneal cavity

Incidence of visceral lesions in abdominal wounds

  • Small intestine 26%
  • Large intestine 14%
  • Spleen 7%
  • Pancreas 3-5%
  • Diaphragm muscles 3-5%

Incidence of visceral lesions in abdominal contusions

  • Small intestine 16%
  • Liver 15%
  • Diaphragm muscles 1-3%
  • Pancreas 1-3%

Location can indicate affected organs

  • Midline sterno-abdominal contusions - aorta, heart, spleen, left hepatic lobe and small bowel
  • Left lateral impacts - left lung, spleen, left kidney
  • Right lateral impacts - right lung, right hepatic lobe, right kidney

Wound’s classification

Depending on traumatic agent

Depending on age, wounds may be

Depending on microbial contamination, they can be

  • a) By cutting
  • b) By shooting
  • c) Contusion
  • a) Recent (less than 6 hours)
  • b) Old (more than 6 hours)
  • a) Clean
  • b) With minimal contamination
  • c) Contaminated
  • d) Infected

Topographic classification

  • Solitary abdominal trauma
  • Lower abdominal trauma, usually associated with pelvic fracture
  • Abdominal parietal
  • Abdominal parieto-visceral
  • Abdominal wall trauma
  • Thoraco-abdominal trauma (trauma affecting the space between the 5th rib → costal rim)
  • Extra-abdominal lesion associations

Clinical manifestation

Peritoneal irritation syndrome

Internal bleeding syndrome

  • Distended abdomen
  • Muscular defense or not (tenderness, guarding)
  • Abdomen motionless with breath
  • Sensitive Douglas pouch
  • Disappearance of liver dullness
  • Agitation
  • Anxiety
  • Thirst
  • Pallor
  • Tachycardia
  • Decreasing BP
  • Shock

Mixed syndrome

Physical exam

Local exam

Percussion

Palpation

Auscultation

  • Overall appearance, immobility with breathing, retraction or distension
  • Skin changes: abrasion, bruises – “traumatic mark”
  • It is painful; Mandel sign → peritoneal irritations
  • Disappearance of liver dullness → cavity organ immunity
  • Dullness is movable on flanks (shifting dullness) → peritoneal effusion
  • Temperature, elasticity and humidity of skin
  • Cold skin, corroborated with pallor found at shock
  • Fixed, firm, painful kneading → intraperitoneal hematoma
  • Subcutaneous fluctuating collections

Signs

  • Muscular defense (tenderness)
  • Muscle contractions → permanent generalized beyond self-control (guarding)

! false acute abdominal trauma!

  • Muscle ruptures
  • Retroperitoneal hematoma
  • Irritation of roots on nerves D2-D12
  • Basal pneumonia
  • Blumberg sign
  • Absence of intestinal noise → 65-93% sign of visceral lesions

Paraclinical exam

  • Laboratory exam
  • Chest and abdominal radiography (spleen rupture or liver rupture)
  • Abdominal US (FAST)
  • CT (best method)
  • Selective arteriography
  • Urography
  • Peritoneal lavage with 200-300 ml saline (in pat. with negative FAST US) to see bile, food of blood

General treatment approach

  • Primary evaluation
  • RAPID – SYSTEMATIC - THOROUGH in order to detect immediately life-threatening lesions !
  • Primary survey (ABC), anamnesis, brief physical examination, signs of hypovolemia/ hemorrhage/ hemodynamic instability
  • Situations that hide acute abdominal lesion: altered mental status (brain lesions, shock, intoxication), chest bowl injury, severe external lesions (open limb fractures)
  • Signs of instability: tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, acidosis
  • FAST US for presents of free fluid (hemoperitoneum, pericardial, pleural fluid, pneumothorax)
  • In negativ US → thorough search for other possible bleeding sources !

Patient’s stabilization

Venous access, massive transfusions, transfusion ratio 1:1:1 Plasma: red cells: platelets

Secondary evaluation

Other imaging

KEHR – abdominal pain irradiated to left shoulder, left thoraco-abdominal trauma → signifies splenic rupture CULLEN – periumbilical ecchymosis – retro/properitoneal hematoma TURNER – uni-or bilateral flanks ecchymosis – retroperitoneal hematoma SEATBELT SIGN – skin abrasions, erytema, erosions; pancreatic, duodenal, small bowel, mesentery lesions, T12-L2 fracture; neck or cervical vessel lesions Solid organs - hemoperitoneum; spleen and liver generate intra-peritoneal bleedings Kidneys and pancreas - retroperitoneal hematomas Hollow viscera - localized or diffuse peritonitis Vascular - hemorrhagic shock due to intaperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding

Definitive care

Initial truncated surgical procedure focused exclusively on immediate life-threatening lesions → no longer than 1 hour After 24-48 hours of postoperative resuscitation → programmed final reoperation follows with removal of initially placed intra-abdominal hemostatic packs, reparations of visceral damages, abdominal wall reconstruction Liver ruptures will be packed, lacerated spleen will be resected, important vascular structures will be ligated Massive Transfusion Protocol Simple sutures of ruptured bowels or urinary bladder, rapid resection of largely compromised bowel loops followed by temporary stappled-closing of bowels’ ends, never reconstructive anastomosis! Brief peritoneal lavage with warm normal saline, bowels exteriorized and all 4 abdominal quadrants temporarily packed → prevents intraabdominal postoperative diffuse bleedings due to coagulopathy Suturing abdominal wall not indicated; temporary closure by vacuum device Often develop very severe combination of metabolic deregulations = “lethal triad” (hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy)

Monitored, ventilated, corrected, aggressive large-spectrum antibiotherapy and total par-enteral nutrition

1. Closed abdominal traumatism

1. Patient

hemodynamically unstable and peritoneal

signs which goes directly

into operating room

2. Stable hemodynamic

pat.

  • Intubated or unconscious patient
  • Patients with “belt mark”
  • US
  • Peritoneal lavage. (1000 erythrocytes is criteria for performing exploratory laparoscopy. This can reduce rate of negative laparotomies by up to 10%)
  • In absence of ultrasound in receiving area it is sent directly to operating room
  • Abdominal US
  • CT

Indications for surgery

  • Hypotension
  • Peritonitis
  • Hypotension despite rebalancing
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Diaphragm injury
  • Intraperitoneal rupture of urinary bladder
  • CT or US diagnosis of severe traumatic lesions of pancreas, spleen, liver, kidney or gastrointestinal tract

2. Open abdominal traumatism

1. Hepatic trauma

  • Large organ, parenchymal → easily injured
  • Liver is only partially protected by the right hypochondrium

Clinical signs

  • Pain in right hypochondrium
  • Peritoneal irritation
  • Hypotension – collapse
  • Psychic signs
  • Signs of hemobility

Grade I

Grade II

Grade III

Grade IV

Grade V

Grade I

Grade II

Grade III

Grade IV

Grade V

Grade VI

  • Subcapsular hematoma < 10% of surface
  • Plague < 1cm deep
  • Subcapsular hematoma 10-50% of surface or intra parenchyma <10cm diameter
  • Wound 1-3cm deep and < 10cm long
  • Subcapsular, > 50% of liver surface or growing; subcapsular or intra parenchyma ruptured hematoma; intraparenchymal hematoma > 10cm
  • Wound > 3cm deep
  • Wound: rupture of parenchyma involving 25-75% of hepatic lobe or 1-3 Couinaud segments in single lobe
  • Wound: rupture of parenchyma involving> 75% of lobe or > 3 Couinaud segments of single lobe
  • Vascular: suprahepatic lesions, vein retrohepatic vein. Major hepatic hepatitis → Small laceration with minimal bleeding Treatment: Usually bleeding has ceased at laparotomy; drainage is sufficient → Moderate laceration with active and significant bleeding Treatment: Compression, argon beam coagulation, bipolar coagulation, radiofrequency, fibrin glue → Large intraparenchymal hematomas Treatment: Intraoperative drainage and hemostasis is mandatory → Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches of hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic vein or bile ducts, but amenable to suture repair Treatment: Pringle maneuver necessary during surgery and visible affected elements must be separately ligated. Ligation of proper or common hepatic artery has been largely abandoned as is may lead to abscess formation → Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches of hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic vein or bile ducts Treatment: Requiring resection of portion of hepatic parenchyma Large lacerations associated with injury of retrohepatic veins and vena cava resulting in massive hemorrhage Treatment: Sometimes total vascular exclusion may be necessary to visualize and suture injuries to hepatic veins and VCI. To gain access to suprahepatic VCI it is necessary to extend midline incision into mediastinum by splitting sternum

Treatment

Conservative

Surgical

  • Only hemodynamically stable ones (gr. I-III)
  • CT monitoring
  • Hepatorafia
  • Plumbing fill
  • Typical or atypical hepatectomies
  • Vascular sutures
  • Sutures of biliary tract
  • Additional surgical procedures may be required due to intra- and extra-abdominal injuries
  • Stab wounds cause mainly minor injuries (Types I-III)
  • Gunshots and blunt trauma cause serious injuries (Types IV-VI) in half of these situations
  • Preoperative assessment includes ultrasound, CT scan, puncture lavage
  • Complications of liver trauma include abscesses, biliary fistulae, hemobilia, liver failure, secondary bleeding, parenchymal necrosis
  • Hemobilia is defined a bleeding draining in the biliary tree with subsequent biliary colic, raised cholestasis enzymes and melena
  • Arteriography may be of help by detecting the source and obtaining hemostasis by selective embolization

2. Splenic trauma

  • Most affected viscera in abdominal trauma

Signs and symptoms

  • Left hypochondrial pain
  • Signs of acute anemia
  • Kehr sign (irradiated pain in the left shoulder)
  • Abdominal distension
  • Contracting
  • Left or displaceable hypochondriac

Severity of splenic trauma

I

  • Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma <10% of the surface
  • Wound without bleeding <1 cm depth

II

  • Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma, <10-50% of the surface
  • Non-expanding intra-parenchymatous hematoma with diameter <2 cm
  • Capsular lesion with active bleeding
  • Parenchymal lesion with a depth of 1-3 cm that does not involve the trabecular vessels III
  • Subcapsular hematoma> 50% of the surface or expansively
  • Subcapsular hematoma ruptured, with active bleeding
  • Hematoma intra-parenchymatos with diameter> 2 cm or expansive
  • Parenchymal lesion> 3 cm or with trabecular vessel damage

IV

  • Broken intraparenchymal hematoma, with active bleeding
  • Injury involving the segmental or spleen vessels, with the production of major devascularization (> 25% of the spleen)

V

  • Crushing of the spleen
  • Avulsion

Treatment

Non-surgical

Surgical

  • Conservative
  • Embolization of vessels

= classic/ laparoscopic

  • Partial splenectomy
  • Splenectomy

3. Stomach

  • Most common affected in abdominal wounds of left hypochondrium
  • In contusions by crushing steering wheel
  • Clinical signs of peritoneal irritation
  • Pneumoperitoneum (cavity organ)

Injury grade

I

Single wall injury

II

Penetrating lesion

III

Minor parietal destruction

IV

Injury requiring minimal resection

V

Injury requiring resection of more than 35% of the stomach

Treatment (depending on lesion)

1. Wound suture

2. Gastric resection

3. Gastrectomy

4. Pancreas

  • More common in wounds
  • Difficult to diagnose → late clinical signs
  • Delayed diagnosis → late interventions lead to increased morbidity and mortality

Treatment

I

  • Conservative treatment
  • Drainage

II

III

  • Distal pancreatectomy
  • Drainage

IV

  • Subtotal pancreatectomy
  • Drainage

V

  • Cephalic Duodeno-pancreatectomy
  • Cephalic pancreatectomy

5. Duodenum

  • Rare lesions
  • Usually coexists with other visceral lesions (90% of cases)
  • Pain
  • Muscular defense

Injury grade

I

  • Hematoma of a single portion of the duodenum
  • Incomplete wound

II

  • Hematoma involving more than one portion
  • Wound: 50% of the circumference

III

  • Wound: 50-75% the circumference of D II
  • Or 50-100% of the circumference D I, D III, D IV

IV

  • Break> 75% of circumference D II, involving the ampule or distal common duct V
  • Massive rupture of the duodeno-pancreatic complex
  • Devascularization of the duodenum

Treatment

  • Decompressive duodenal drainage
  • Anastomosis and resection
  • Pedicle graft
  • Duodenal resections
  • Cephalic duodeno-pancreatectomy

6. Colon and rectum

  • More affected in abdominal wounds

Signs

  • Perforation of the visceral cavity
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Hemoperitoneum

Injury grade

I

Serosa injury

II

Single parietal lesion

III

Less than 25% of the wall

IV

More than 25% of the wall

V

Major involvement of colonic wall and blood supply

Treatment

  • Wound suture
  • Segmental resections
  • Hemicolectomy
  • Colostomy
  • Suture of rectal lesion + colostomy

7. Aorta and vena cava

  • They are rare, usually by stabbing or firearms
  • Signs of severe acute anemia
  • Needs urgent intervention
  • Vascular wound repair

8. Gun wound

Unipolar/ blind wound

Bipolar wound

  • Only in form of penetration hole
  • Projectile remained in tissues
  • Projectile inlet and outlet port
  • If you are only interested in superficial plans, it is called wound in seton

Areas of trauma

  • Channel itself
  • Primary necrosis area
  • Molecular contusion

= Illustration of gunshot wounds

title: Peritonitis
html:
Anatomy

  • Boundaries: diaphragm, posterior abdominal wall (spine and Quadratus lumborum), antero-lateral abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, oblique, transversus with their fascia and aponeurosis), diaphragm of the pelvis (Levator ani, coccigeus muscles)
  • Peritoneum = closed sack wrapped in thin membrane, which covers the internal surfaces of the abdomen (parietal peritoneum); the posterior parietal peritoneum reflects anterior and wraps most of abdominal organs (intraperitoneal organs, transverse mesocolon and mesentery) and becomes “ visceral peritoneum”)
  • Intraperitoneal organs: stomach, liver, gallbladder, first part of duodenum, pancreas (only tail), spleen, small bowel, appendix, transvers colon, sigmoid colon
  • Retroperitoneal space situated behind peritoneal cavity, between posterior parietal peritoneum and posterior muscular wall
  • Retroperitoneal organs: esophagus, aorta, vena cava, duodenum, pancreas (head and body), bladder, ureters, kidneys, adrenal glands, ascending and descending colon
  • Peritoneal organs have a serosa
  • Retroperitoneal organs have an adventitia

Definition

= inflammation (vascular congestion, edema) of visceral and parietal peritoneum, triggered by local, regional or general pathology

Classification 1

  • a) Diffuse peritonitis (generalized)
  • b) Abdominal abscess (localized)

Classification 2

Primary/ secondary/ tertiary

Macroscopic

  • Peritoneal serosa, greater omentum and loops are hyperemic + exudate in peritoneal cavity
  • Sequestration of fluid in a true “third sector” → hypovolemia or hypovolemic shock
  • Accumulation of intraluminal fluid → hydroelectrolytic imbalance
  • Loops are distended and immobile = dynamic occlusion explained by Stoke’s law (inflammation of visceral peritoneum causes paralysis of subjacent loop musculature)
  • Pneumococci pus is creamy, yellow and without smell
  • Pyocyanic bacillus (Pseudomonas) = nosocomial flora; greenish pus with specific aromatic odor
  • Serous fluid at opening of peritoneal cavity becomes opalescent and totally purulent at site of perforation

Presentation → extremely variable and depending on

  • Location
  • Time since its onset
  • Initial state of perforated organ
  • Biological state of patient
  • Possible treatments administered prior or during course of disease

Pain

Vomiting

Transit disorders

General

signs

Position

Physical exam

Inspection

Palpation

Percussion

Auscultation

  • Insidious onset, initially reduced and progressively increases → corresponds to visceral inflammation towards perforation
  • Sudden appearance of violent, stabbing epigastric pain → perforated ulcer
  • Location of pain usually corresponds to site of perforation
  • Is inconsistent
  • Appears in advanced stages
  • It increases hypovolemia
  • Most frequently due to dynamic ileus
  • Primitive peritonitis may have diarrheic onset

= not constant

  • Fever (38-39°C) may be absent
  • Gonococcal peritonitis starts with 40°C fever
  • Tachycardia (increases with fever; absence of this correlation is a sign for severity)
  • Shock or persistent hypotension → renal failure
  • Polypnea as a result of fever
  • Tachypnea and superficial respiration due to meteorism and diaphragmatic irritation
  • Pat. with peritonitis walk with their trunk flexed and hand on abdomen
  • Immobile
  • Superficial respiration
  • Tenderness to palpation
  • Increased abdominal wall rigidity = earliest, most reliable sign of peritonitis
  • Voluntary and involuntary guarding
  • Blumberg sign (not very specific)
  • Cutaneous abdominal reflexes disappear and cutaneous hyperesthesia occurs = Dieulafoy’s sign
  • Rectal or vaginal exam is painful and may evidence a fluctuant Douglas pouch
  • Disappearance of prehepatic dullness → pneumoperitoneum due to perforations
  • Bell or Grassmann-Mandel sign defines pain produced on percussion of peritonitis
  • Usually reveals abdominal silence, in accordance with Stoke’s law

Lab/ imaging

  • Leukocytosis with left shift (neutrophilia) → Leukopenia is a sign of severity
  • Upright plain abdominal X-ray → pneumoperitoneum; fluid collection causes loss of psoas shadow; distension of loops with air-fluid levels secondary to dynamic ileus → Post-OP pneumoperitoneum persists for 3 days
  • Chest X-ray for exclusion of thoracic causes
  • US → intraperitoneal fluid collections; limited for gaseous loop distension
  • CT and MRI → diagnosis of collections (rarely used in emergency)
  • Lavage puncture (paracentesis) and diagnostic laparoscopy should be carefully used → injury risk
  • Laparoscopy has advantage of changing in favorable cases from diagnostic procedure into therapeutic gesture

I. Primary peritonitis (PP)

= spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)

  • 2 main characteristics
  • Mostly monomicrobial (>90%) !!!
  • Low level of proteins and leucocytes count in ascitic fluid → Adults

Gonococcal

Tuberculous

Pneumococcal → Children

Pneumococcal (Streptococcus pneumoniae)

Hemolytic streptococcal

  • By gram negative ! (E. coli, Klebsiella) or gram positive (S. hemolyticus)
  • Mostly in preexisting ascites due to cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari snd, lupus, carcinomatosis
  • Germ migration from
  • a) Intact bowels (transmural intestinal)
  • b) Blood stream in bacteriemia (hematogenous)
  • c) Infected fallopian tubes (direct ascending peritoneal contamination)
  • Vulvo-vaginitis always precedes peritonitis
  • Ascending trans-fallopian migration of vaginal and fallopian purulent secretion with direct peritoneal contamination
  • Clinical manifestations: violent, significant alteration of general condition
  • Abdominal pus: abundant, green
  • Bilateral purulent gonococcal salpingitis always associated
  • Concomitant with an active focus of tuberculosis
  • Contamination: hematogenous, lymphatic, trans-fallopian
  • Sometimes even late after its apparent sterilization
  • Aggravates evolution of pat. with cirrhosis, alcoholics, HIV, Hep. C, during severe pneumonia complicated with septicemia
  • Severe complication in nephrotic syndrome, pneumococcal respiratory infections (septicemia) or juvenile liver cirrhosis (bacterial trans-mural intestinal migration)
  • During scarlet fever or streptococcal tonsilitis

Clinical features

Children

  • Violent
  • Acute, intense, diffuse abdominal pain
  • Guarding, tenderness and rebound tenderness
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Ileus
  • High fever
  • Irritative diarrhea → same for adult females with gonococcal primary peritonitis Adults
  • Tuberculous PP → onset is progressive, not acute; abdominal distension, nausea, moderate pain, usually without guarding or tenderness; fever and typically night sweats
  • Liver cirrhosis → signs for peritoneal irritation might be absent; onset is gradual; mild fever 37.8-38 °C, metabolic acidosis; ileus; sometimes hypothermia; most relevant - acute, apparently unexplained liver decompensation; altered mental status
  • Some cases are totally asymptomatic !

Paracentesis and ascitic fluid examination

  • Leucocyte count: PMN > 250 cells/mm³
  • Bacterial culture (usually similar results with blood culture)
  • Protein concentration < 1g/dL
  • Glucose < 50 mg/dL
  • Lactate > 25mg/dL
  • pH < 7.35

Treatment

→ Non-surgical broad-spectrum AB

  • Has to be proven without any doubt → patients with secondary bacterial peritonitis eventually die under conservative treatment, while patients with primary bacterial peritonitis + cirrhosis die after surgical treatment
  • Starting with empiric AB therapy (never wait for bacterial culture results !)
  • Usually with Claforan or Rocephine i.v. for 10-14 days
  • Clinic improvement should occur after 48 hours
  • Concomitant leukocyte decrease in ascitic fluid
  • AB therapy should be modified according to results of culture

DD to secondary peritonitis

  • Culture (primary = monobacterial; secondary = multibacterial with aerobic and anaerobic bac.)
  • X ray/ CT scan shows air = pneumoperitoneum in secondary PP

II. Secondary peritonitis (SP)

  • Can be bacterial peritonitis or chemical peritonitis
  • Multi-microbial → aerobic and anaerobic
  • Local vasodilatation → peritoneal (parietal and visceral) edema + constant plasma intra-peritoneal diffusion → fluid sequestration (third fluid compartment) → hypovolemic shock and kidney injury
  • Germs produce endo- and exotoxins → penetrate peritoneal membrane → systemic inflammatory response
  • Dynamic ileus additionally increases fluid sequestrations and aggravates cardio-pulmonary effects due to important abdominal distension
  • Untreated → sepsis, septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures and death 1) Bacterial
  • Commonly from perforation of an intra-abdominal hollow viscera (aggressiveness of contaminating bacteria is exponentially increasing from upper to lower segments of digestive tract → colon perforation is the worst → gram negative and anaerobic, exo- and endotoxins producing germs !)
  • Sometimes from abscesses located in intra-peritoneal, retro-peritoneal or pelvic parenchymatous organs (liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, urinary bladder, uterus, ovaries) a. Severe inflammation or ischemia → necroses, gangrenes → perforations
  • Perforated appendicitis - most common cause, usually causes only peri-appendicular abscess
  • Perforated duodenal ulcer - most typical picture with “wooden abdomen” and pneumoperitoneum in 70%
  • Perforated pyosalpinx – pelvic-peritonitis, well defined local signs, general good state
  • Perforated colic diverticulitis - rarely results in diffuse peritonitis; more frequently pericolic abscesses
  • Acute cholecystitis - rarely perforates into greater peritoneal cavity
  • Peritonitis with hepatic starting point caused by superinfected hepatic abscesses or cysts (very uncommon)
  • Bowel infarctions
  • Torsions
  • Internal strangulated hernias
  • Meckel’s diverticula
  • Malignant bowel perforations
  • Toxic mega-colon perforation
  • Fistulas b. Abdominal traumatisms
  • Traumatic visceral ruptures/ perforations by blunt abdominal trauma
  • Stab wounds or gunshots (perforation of an organ might not be present)
  • Foreign-body-triggered digested tract perforations c. Iatrogenic
  • After abdomino-pelvic surgeries or accidental perforations (e.g., ERCP)
  • Peritoneal catheter (adult patients with feeding jejunal tubes, juvenile patients with peritoneal dialysis)

2) Chemical

  • Contaminant initially sterile
  • Classically biliary peritonitis due to gangrenous (ischemic) necrosis of gallbladder or due to biliragia (duodenal perforation, CBD perforation, liver injury)
  • Acute pancreatitis with parenchymal necrosis (pancreatic enzymes)
  • First hours after gastric perforation (hydrochloric acid)

DD

  • Acute abdomen BUT becauses surgery is indicated in any secondary PP, less important → False medical acute abdomen
  • MI (→ EKG)
  • Basal pneumonia, pericarditis, pleuritis (auscultation, X-ray)
  • Lower chest neuromyalgias (history of erythematous lesions, X-rays)
  • Type 1 and 5 hyperlipidemia (epigastric pain)
  • Advanced RF and decompensated DM (intense abdominal pain)
  • Typhoid fever
  • Acute arsenic poisoning
  • Food poisoning

Medical acute abdomen includes

  • Biliary colic
  • Renal colic
  • Tabetic gastric crisis
  • Chronic lead exposure (specific gingival line)
  • Acute intermittent porphyria → DD Watson-Schwartz test and on change in color of urine exposed to light

Diagnosis

  • General appearance → deeply suffering person, anxious look, sunken eyes immobile
  • Even slightest movement (deep breathing, sneezing, coughing) generates pain
  • Nausea common; hiccough and vomiting are very painful
  • Abdominal pain has an abrupt onset, severe and continuous; initially localized but soon becomes diffuse Inspection Palpation (most important)

Percussion

Auscultation

DRE

  • Initially flat abdomen, completely immobile, shallow respiratory movements
  • Later (after 6-8 hours) abdominal progressive distension develops
  • Causes very intense pain
  • Diffuse abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, guarding, rigidity (classically described in peptic perforated ulcers as “wooden abdomen”)
  • Positive Blumberg sign
  • These clinical findings fade after 6-8 hours, due to abdominal muscle exhaustion, rigidity diminishes and finally disappears → replaced by abdominal distension
  • Abdominal cutaneous hyperestesia, abolishment of abdominal cutaneous reflexes
  • Particularly painful (Bell sign and Grassmann-Mandel)
  • Intense tympanism (liver dullness obliterated) especially in cases with hollow organ perforation
  • Concomitant presence of fluid (pus, bile, infected ascitis) revealed as dullness
  • No bowel sounds → “silentium abdominis”
  • Mandatory and reveals swollen and very painful Douglas pouch

Imaging

Abdominal X-ray

  • Useful when perforated peptic ulcer is suspected
  • Shows classic “pneumoperitoneum”

Abdominal US

  • Reveals fluid in abdomen, distended bowels without peristaltic movements and other specific elements concerning underlying cause (perforated lithiasic gallbladder, perforated appendix, free air in hollow organ perforation)

CT

  • By far the best imaging technique, able not only to confirm diagnosis but also underlying cause Laparoscopy
  • Very useful procedure, diagnostic and therapeutic

* NEVER do endoscopy (pumps even more air into the peritoneum

Treatment

= surgical emergency → even with correct treatment, high mortality

1. Preoperative preparation

  • Concomitant with blood-tests and EKG
  • Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Pain control after positive diagnosis has been established (opioids)
  • Prompt and efficient re-hydration (large venous catheters)
  • Naso-gastric suction tube to obtain gastric vacuity !!!
  • Oxygen per mask
  • Urinary catheter

2. Surgery

→ Has three main goals (treatment principles by Kirschner)

I. Control contaminating source

  • Removal of affected organ (appendix, gallbladder)
  • Resection of organ or perforated segment (stomach, enterectomy, colon)
  • Limited resection of affected area and suture (duodenal ulcer)
  • Plain suture or suture and omentoplasty of perforation
  • Externalization of perforated segment with restoration of digestive continuity in 2nd stage (e.g. Hartman’s surgery)
  • Lavage of peritoneal cavity

II. Eliminate septic abdominal content

  • Pus, feces, bile, urine, digestive tract content removed by thorough and abundant peritoneal lavage
  • Washing with many litters of warm saline fluid → Attention in several narrow spaces (left and right sub-phrenic spaces, Douglas pouch, spaces between bowel loops)
  • Good, efficient peritoneal lavage prevents early and late postoperative adhesions and developing of residual intra-abdominal abscesses III. Drain peritoneal cavity
  • Multiple abdominal drainages placed in narrow spaces to prevent abscesses
  • All tubes are exteriorized through abdominal wall and removed after 48-72 hours
  • Procedures done laparoscopically
  • In long-standing, neglected peritonitis with intraabdominal adhesions → large xypho-pubic median laparotomy
  • First maneuver after entering into abdominal cavity, is to obtain a sample of pus (or whatever contaminating agent) for bacterial culture

Prognosis

→ Gold time period (first 6 h) are very important, later mortality rapidly increases !

Acute localized peritonitis

= inflammatory process, purulent collections, localized in part of peritoneal cavity

  • Occurs due to blocking of appendix, gallbladder or duodenal ulcer perforation by greater omentum
  • Intraperitoneal abscesses occur secondarily to generalized peritonitis
  • Depending on location, abscesses can be

Subphrenic

Suprahepatic

Submesocolic

  • Also termed supramesocolic are supra- and subhepatic
  • Right and left inter-hepato-diaphragmatic and intersplenophrenic
  • Interileal, perisigmoid, right and left parieto-colic, left mesenterico-colic, subcecal and periappendicular

Clinically

  • Guarding with general infection signs
  • Fever, tachycardia
  • Suppressed transit, irritation diarrhea being quite frequently found
  • Hyperleukocytosis with neutrophilia (proportional to infection)
  • Interhepato-diaphragmatic abscesses occur after biliary and liver surgery (hydatid cyst, hepatectomy)
  • Clinical exam: lower respiratory amplitude, lower inferior liver margin, possibly basal pleural collection
  • Radiological exam: high hemidiaphragm, pneumoperitoneum → Replaced by US (additionally allows assess the content, walls and volume of abscess)

III. Tertiary peritonitis (TP)

  • Usually develops in patients with severe comorbidities or immunocompromised (e.g. AIDS/HIV, diabetic, advanced neoplasias, aged, malnourished, hypoalbuminemic, anemic, cirrhotic)
  • Represent intra-peritoneal infections that persist or recur 48 hours after initially efficient surgical and antibiotic

treatment

Aggravating factors

  • Multi-resistant nosocomial bacteria → Enterococci, Enterobacter and fungi
  • Diagnosis is not simple → re-laparatomy
  • Earlier diagnosis by repeatedly followed values of C-reactive protein
  • If strong suspicions raised, early re-laparatomy with peritoneal lavage and abdominal fluid culture mandatory

title: Acute abdomen
html:
= group of syndromes with rapid, severe (lethal if untreated) acute evolution, triggered by virtually any organ into abdomen

  • Term emphasizes how prompt surgeons’ diagnostic and therapeutic response must be to prevent patient’s death
  • Not every acute abdomen requires surgery (sometimes even contraindicated)

Main types

Peritonitic

Obstructive

Hemorrhagic

Ischemic

  • Peritonitis (localized or diffuse)
  • Acute appendicitis
  • Diverticulitis etc.
  • All variants of acute nonvascular bowel obstructions
  • Ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemorrhagic ovarian cyst
  • Mesenterial infarctions
  • Fallopian tubes’ torsion

Diagnosis (anamnesis) → Pain is dominant!

Onset

  • Abrupt → perforated peptic ulcer, fallopian tube torsion, acute mesenteric artery obstruction
  • Progressive → acute appendicitis, cholecystitis

Location, migration,

  • Location of pain corresponds to abdominal wall projection of underlying organ radiation (somatic pain)
  • Initial pain may differ from one during examination (migration)
  • Epigastric pain: liver (left lobe), biliary, acute pancreatic disease
  • Hypogastric pain: uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, urinary bladder, distal ureters Typical radiations
  • Renal colic (nonsurgical abdominal emergency) - pain radiates from lumbar location along abdominal topographic projection to hypogastric region and genitals
  • Ovarian/ fallopian tube - pain radiates cranially
  • Acute cholecystitis or subphrenic abscess - pain radiates up to right shoulder (diaphragmatic irritation)
  • Ectopic ruptured pregnancy or ruptured spleen - pain radiates to left shoulder Continuous/
  • Septic intra- or retroperitoneal conditions generate intense and continuous pain intermittent (typically perforated peptic ulcer)
  • Same continuous pain but more intense by ischemic emergencies (bowel infarction, fallopian torsion, bowel torsion, strangulated hernias, acute pancreatitis)
  • Intermittent, colicky pain → initial phases of nonvascular acute bowel obstructions
  • After 6-12 hours abdominal distension becomes dominant, while colicky pain’s intensity and frequency diminishes due to bowels’ muscular layers exhaustion Intensity of pain,
  • Intense pain - organ perforations or ruptures → peritonitis aggravating and
  • Even more intense - acute ischemia (abrupt, brutal onset, shocking intensity, cold relieving factors sweating, no respond to painkillers, decreases after 10-12 h due to total destruction of bowl including nerves (delusive lull = delayed diagnosis and treatment !)
  • Pat. are agitated, restless (necrotic pancreatitis, ischemic conditions, renal colic)
  • Pat. with diffuse peritonitis are still, motionsless, scarcely breathing
  • Anorexia, nausea, vomiting - always associated → Typical for acute appendicitis (first anorexia, then pain, nausea and vomiting follow after) → In acute pancreatitis repeated vomiting does not relief nausea → Proximal small bowel obstruction → vomiting frequent, with clear bile → Lower obstructions → vomiting rarer, voluminous and turbid → Distal small bowel obstructions especially 12-24h after onset → vomitus is voluminous and fecaloid
  • Bowel movements - reflex reaction to any peritoneal injury (localized or diffuse, chemical or purulent peritonitis, bowel or other abdominal organ ischemia or perforations, hemoperitoneum, acute pancreatitis, etc.)
  • Conditions that cause bowel paresis but are to a surgical acute abdomen → surgery is prohibited in such cases !!! → Abrupt, brutal liver failure → Severe ascites in cirrhotic pat. → Acute diabetic ketoacidosis → Severe uremia → Severe electrolyte imbalance (especially hypoK) → Severe asthma attacks → Acute and prolonged urinary retention → Hip fractures → Acute basal pneumonia; pleural effusions
  • ATTENTION: sometimes paradoxical acceleration of bowel peristalsis → irritation diarrhea → partial, lateral bowel strangulations, small femoral or obturator hernias, long- lasting unrecognized diffuse or localized peritonitis
  • Fever
  • a) Non-perforated acute appendicitis: starts sub-febrility (37.3-37.8ºC), but when appendicular gangrene, perforation or abscess develops → fever will climb up to 38.5-39.5ºC → same happens in all similar abdominal conditions
  • b) Paradoxically normal body temperature in immuno-suppressed patients (AIDS, advanced disseminated cancers, DM, aged, patients under chemotherapy or chronic corticoids treatment)
  • Past medical history, age, gender, previous surgeries
  • Appendectomy in young female → suspicion of right fallopian or ovary condition
  • Cholecystectomy in female patient → acute cholangitis, acute pancreatitis due to remnants
  • Surgery for acute obstructions → suspicion for bowel adhesions
  • Female pat. with dark colored genital bleedings, delayed menstruation → ectopic pregnancy
  • Most frequent causes in young males - acute appendicitis and hernias
  • Most frequent cause in young females - rupture of graafian follicle or hematic ovarian cyst
  • In male adults - perforated peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis due to alcohol
  • In adult females - pelvic inflammatory disease, acute lithiasic cholecystitis and ectopic pregnancy

Physical exam

Inspection

Auscultation

Palpation

Percussion

DRE

+ Vaginal exam in females

  • Altered respiration due to pain
  • Abdominal distension may be impressive
  • Post-OP surgical scars
  • Hernias
  • Ask pat. to show you where pain is
  • “noisy abdomen” with colicky pain → initial phase of acute obstruction
  • In late phases over 12-24h bowel paresis can occur “silent abdomen”
  • Most severe condition (bowel infarction) has very early paresis
  • Start away from pain, gentle, observe reaction
  • Localized or diffused tenderness
  • Muscle rigidity
  • Rebound tenderness
  • “jarring test” - outstanding accuracy in detecting localized peritoneal inflammation (patient is asked to jump abruptly on his/her heels after rising on his/her toes; provoked pain is localized accurately on abdominal wall projection of underlying inflamed viscus)
  • May be very painful
  • May confirm bowel distension, ascitic fluid, inflammation, tumoral mass → Mandatory!

title: Laparoscopic surgery
html:
Insufflating system

  • Incision at umbilicus
  • Create pneumoperitoneum with 3-6 l CO2 = “work room” → max. 12-14 mmHg (otherwise barotrauma)
  • Insertion of first trocar (keep gas inside)

Video system

  • Inserted next to see and do new incisions for more trocars
  • Composed of laparoscope connected to camera that transforms image into electrical signal → converted into image on monitor
  • Another module is light source
  • It has photo and video recording devices; some are even 3D

Wash-out suction

  • Pumps saline at body temp. into peritoneal cavity system
  • Another module for suction (washing liquid in external collecting vessels)

Electrosurgical

A. Monopolar mode closes electrical circuit between active electrode pole (usually hook system electrode) and passive electrode (grounding plate) through patient tissues, thermal effect being achieved at tip of active electrode pole B. Bipolar module closes electrical circuit between bipolar electrodes without passing electrical energy through other areas of patient's body New instruments: ultrasound dissection systems, blood vessel sealing systems, circular or linear staplers, argon beam, intraoperative US, extraction basket or Fogarty probes, lithotripsy

Advantages

  • Aesthetic aspect
  • Socio-professional reinsertion
  • Increased intraoperative visibility
  • Reduced immunology and metabolic reaction
  • Reduction of need of analgesics
  • Early mobilization
  • Reduction of postoperative ileus
  • Reduction or absence of parietal complications (immediate, early and late)
  • Reduction of intraperitoneal adhesions
  • Reduction of hospitalization period

Basic techniques in laparoscopic surgery

1. Operative setting

  • Elective NOT emergency!
  • Skin shaved and disinfection (betadine or alcohol)
  • Thrombosis prophylaxis with elastic bandages and LMWH
  • Depending on type of surgery nasogastric, urinary catheter are inserted
  • AB prophylaxis
  • General anesthesia is mandatory to ensure proper relaxation of abdominal wall

2. Induction of pneumoperitoneum

  • Usually made in umbilical point and Veress needle inserted
  • By blowing 3-6 l of CO2 through inflator

3. Isobar chamber

  • In some situations, it is necessary to create isobaric pneumoperitoneum (ventricular-peritoneal drainage)
  • Achieved by suspending abdominal wall using special laparo-lifts

4. Introduction of trocars

  • 1st 10 mm trocar inserted at umbilical site
  • Then laparoscope inserted and peritoneal cavity viewed
  • Under endoscopic control rest of trocars are inserted

5. Diagnostic laparoscopy

= mandatory procedure at beginning of each intervention → detection of iatrogenic injury, surgical diseases or evaluate operability of case

6. Laparoscopic dissection

  • Follows same basic principles as in open surgery
  • Can perform blunt or sharp dissections

7. Hemostasis, laparoscopic suture ligatures

  • Mostly by electrocoagulation or clips
  • There are situations where it is necessary to perform hemostatic suture or ligature
  • New laparoscopic devices (LigaSure) perform coagulation and section
  • Vascular staplers can accomplish same thing

8. Complications

  • Blowing into pro-peritoneal space
  • Injuring abdominal viscera
  • Pneumo-omentum
  • Gas embolism
  • Respiratory and cardiovascular complications
  • + specific complications of each type of surgery

9. Conversion to open surgery

  • Indicated when occurrence of complications that cannot be solved through laparoscopic way, presence of conditions that require open surgery or if surgery laparoscopic lasts well beyond standard duration and progression procedure is very slow Modern improvements
  • NOTES surgery (Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery) - no scar surgery → natural body orifice
  • Robotic surgery - perform fine movements in confined spaces, increased precision, speed during surgery
  • Telesurgery - remotely perform entire surgery using robot coordinated from one console
  • Augmented reality - superimpose real image of operative field (classic or laparoscopic) with threedimensional images reconstructed by computer tomography

title: Bariatric surgery
html:
Obesity → BMI

Underweight

Normal weight

Overweight

Obesity

< 18.5

18.5-24.9

25-29.9 (Grade I)

≥ 30

Grade II: 30-39.9

Grade III: ≥ 40

Interactions of obesity

Respiratory

Malignant

Psychological

Cardiovascular

CNS

Surgical

Pelvic

Obstetric and perinatal

GI

Orthopedic

Metabolic

Reproductive

Cutaneous

Extremities

Miscellaneous

Sleep apnea, higher risk for respiratory infections, bronchial asthma, Pickwickian syndrome (obesity hypoventilation syndrome)

Associated with endometrial, prostate, colon, breast, gallbladder and lung cancer Social stigmatization and depression CAD, essential hypertension, LVH, cor pulmonale, atherosclerosis Stroke, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meralgia paresthetica Increased surgical risk and post-OP complications including wound infections, post-OP pneumonia, DVT, pulmonary embolism Stress incontinence Pregnancy related hypertension, fetal macrosomia, pelvic dystocia Gallbladder disease (cholecystitis, cholelithiasis), NASH, fatty liver, reflux esophagitis Osteoarthritis, coxa vera, chronic lumbago, Blount and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease DM 2, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome, dylipidemia FEMALE → anovulation, early puberty, infertility, hyperandrogenism, PCOS MALE → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Intertrigo, acanthosis nigricans, hirsutism, increased risk for cellulitis and carbuncles Venous varicosities, lowe extremity venous and/or lymphatic edema Reduced mobility and difficulty maintaining personal hygiene

Secondary causes of obesity

  • Hypothyroidism
  • Cushing’s syndrome
  • Insulinoma
  • PCOS
  • Genetic syndromes (Prader Willi etc.)
  • GH deficiency
  • Oral contraceptives
  • Pregnancy
  • Hypogonadism
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism
  • Tube feeding related obesity

What to do?

1. Diet

2. Physical activity

3. Behavior modification

→ Food addiction! → Psychotherapy → Medication → Surgery

Bariatric surgery

  • Aimes at decreasing weight of obese patients by performing operations on stomach or small intestine
  • Should be considered as treatment of last resort after dieting, exercise, psychotherapy, drugs have failed Indication for surgery
  • BMI > 40 kg/m2

Or

  • BMI > 35 kg/m2 in combination with high-risk comorbid conditions (sleep apnea, Pickwickian syndrome, DM1, degenerative joint disease, dyslipidemia, NASH)

Or

  • BMI 30-35 with at least one of the following: uncontrolled DM2, metabolic syndrome

Contraindications for bariatric surgery

  • Bulimia nervosa
  • Age > 65
  • Pediatric pat. before end of growth
  • Untreated depression
  • Major psychosis
  • Drug and alcohol addiction
  • CV disease with high anesthetic risk, coagulopathies difficult to correct
  • Pregnancy
  • Cirrhosis

Pre-OP preparation

  • Psychological evaluation !
  • Previous weight loss
  • Type of eating mistakes
  • Encourage pat. to begin physical exertion
  • Identify health-related risk behaviors
  • Quit smoking
  • Gastroscopy and H Pylori test
  • Ventilatory test should be performed
  • Cardiac, liver function
  • Doppler if previous DVT or hypercoagulability → Prophylaxis by heparin (LMWH)
  • PPI/ anti H2
  • Single dose AB prophylaxis
  • Calf compression and DVT prophylaxis by administration of low molecular weight heparin Post-OP
  • Pre-/ peri- and post-OP nutrition program
  • Assessment and improvement of comorbidities (hypertension, DM2, OSA, COPD, malnutrition)
  • Avoidance of pregnancy in first 18-24 months after surgery

Principles of bariatric surgery

1. Capacity reduction of digestive canal which will physically make patient incapable of eating same quantity of food – Restrictive operations

2. Capacity reduction of digestive canal of absorption of food - Malabsorptive operations

3. Restrictive + malabsorptive operations

1. Restrictive operations

→ Adjustable gastric banding

Silicone plastic ring placed around eso-gastric junction

Internal circumference which is inflated with saline (injection port placed subcutaneously in left upper quadrant)

Reducing esophageal lumen

Pre-OP

  • Must lose 5-10 kg to reduce glycogen and fat content of liver → lowers volume and liver friability
  • Intake of sufficient amount of quality protein
  • Avoid refined sugars and saturated fats

Contraindications - Pat. unable to comply with dietary restrictions imposed by ring

  • Allergy to ring components
  • Pat. with infection that may contaminate ring
  • Coexistence of diseases with high risk of hemodynamic instability (esophageal varices, intestinal telangiectasia)
  • Pat. with psycho-emotional problems severe enough to affect post-OP follow-up
  • Autoimmune diseases affecting esophagus (scleroderma, lupus erythema)

Advantages

  • Short interval for recovery
  • No segment of digestive tract opens or resects
  • Anatomy does not change but area of fibrosis appears under ring
  • Few long-term complications are not as low as supporters claim
  • Good long-term results in terms of weight loss

Complications

  • Small pouch/ esophageal dilatation
  • Digestive hemorrhage
  • Esophagitis due to stasis in dilated oesophagus
  • Ring slipage
  • Gastric stenosis at level of ring
  • Infection at port site
  • Foul belching
  • Fistula between pouch and fundus of stomach
  • Intraoperative rupture of ring
  • Loss of saline from system

Post-OP care

  • Liquid diet first week
  • Disinfection of skin by applying a swab with antiseptic for 10 minutes before calibration is mandatory
  • Maximum volume that can be injected in ring is 9 ml
  • Each calibration of 0.5-1ml should be spaced by 1-2 months

2. Malabsorptive operations

→ Sleeve gastrectomy (SG) or gastric plication

Sleeve = partial gastrectomy

  • First choice of all options
  • removes most of vertical part of stomach
  • detaching blood supply to larger curvature
  • calibration tube of 32-38 French is slipped in stomach close to lesser curvature
  • using linear cutter 70% of stomach is removed beginning from antrum and progressing upwards to Hiss angle Plication = 2 layers which folds greater curvature into lumen of stomach
  • first week vomiting is quite frequent
  • stomach dilates after 2-3 years and most of patients regain weight close
  • operation is reversible for 1-2 weeks then adhesions become dense and almost irreversible
  • patient profile: young female, moderate obesity, single, with intensive support from entourage, able to play sports and willing to change their eating habits
  • Both cause limits food intake due to → Reduced gastric reservoir (remaining tube 100 ml) and early satiety → Reducing hunger (↓ ghrelin production from gastric wall)
  • Advantage: does not require foreign materials

Indication

  • Primary operation for obesity, especially in patients with type 2 diabetes
  • Bridging to gastric bypass
  • Replacement of adjustable ring (2 steps necessary)
  • Suitable for ages under 14 or over 70

Pre-OP care

  • Weight loss in order to reduce volume of frail fatty liver
  • High protein intake
  • Avoid sugar and saturated fat
  • Vitamins and protein shakes 10 days pre-operatively

Post-OP care

  • First 10 days only liquid diet
  • 2nd post-OP day methylene blue given to detect fistulas (can appear after 2 weeks and become symptomatic even at 1 month)
  • On day 6. advisable to administer water-soluble iodinated contrast agent to highlight any fistulas
  • Resumption of diet: soups - mashed items - cream soup - diluted yogurts - mashed meat
  • Feeding is resumed progressively in a manner similar for infants
  • Food discipline - no carbonated drinks, avoiding high calorie food
  • Adequate fluid intake very important to avoid dehydration and hemoconcentration (risk of portal thrombosis)

Outpatient care

  • Prolonged mastication
  • Stop eating when satiety or regurgitation occurs
  • Adequate fractionated fluid intake
  • Avoid drinking during meals, 15 min before and 30 after
  • iv infusion if on 2 consecutive days an intake of 1500 ml is not possible
  • Progressive testing for tolerance
  • Progressive increase volume of physical activity

Complications (rare but can lead to death)

  • Bleeding
  • Stapling line fistulas, appear especially immediately subcardially and can be difficult to treat
  • Marginal ulcers of gastric tube, due to ischemic disorders
  • SG has higher incidence of postoperative gastroesophageal reflux disease due to gastric tube in which endoluminal pressure is increased
  • Megaloblastic anemia due to lack of intrinsic factor (produced by stomach, requires vitamin B12) → necessary to supplement Vit. B12

3. Restrictive and malabsorption surgeries

→ Gastric bypass (short Roux-en-Y or long Roux-en-Y → Duodenal switch

  • BMI > 40 or
  • BMI of 35 with obesity related illness (DM2, CHD, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis)

! Followed by major disorders and were abandoned

Which procedure?

  • Sweet eater → gastric bypass
  • Volume eater → sleeve gastrectomy, duodenal switch
  • Addiction to food → duodenal switch

Procedure

  • combines gastric restriction with malabsorption
  • 50 ml gastric pouch obtained by transecting in transverse fashion stomach at 3 cm under esogastric junction, without removing distal part
  • malabsorbtion ensured by Y jejunal loop with biliary limb much longer than usually (200 cm)
  • patients require lifelong dietary and vitamin supplements and need to be followed by multidisciplinary team Post-OP care → Eating 1. First days: clear liquid diet → clear broth, diluted fruit juices or sugar-free gelatin desserts

2. Blended or puréed sugar-free diet for at least two weeks

3. Diet that is relatively high in protein and low in fats and alcohol

4. Daily multivitamin pill for life to compensate for reduced absorption of essential nutrients Weight loss in first 10 months

  • Biliopancreatic diversion → 53kg
  • Roux-en-Y gastric bypass → 41kg
  • Open → 43kg
  • Laparoscopic → 38kg
  • Vertical banded gastroplasty → 32kg

title: Organ transplant
html:
Liver transplantation

Factors that have led to widening indications for transplantation are

1. Increasing number of donors

  • a) Use of expanded donors has shown that age is not factor in liver transplantation
  • b) Living donor transplantation
  • c) Split-liver transplantation - liver is divided, usually into two unequal parts, of which the highest returns to adult and lowest to a child
  • d) "domino" transplantation
  • e) Xenotransplantation - using as donor an animal, especially primates

2. Advances in immunology

  • Should be followed ABO system compatibility rule
  • Preferable that donor and recipient have same blood type
  • HLA compatibility in renal transplantation is very important, it plays no role in liver transplants

3. Improvement in surgical

  • a) Extend of "piggyback" techniques without use of extracorporeal techniques circulation
  • Used for whole liver transplantation in which implantation of IVC of donors is made termino-lateral to IVC of receiver
  • b) Techniques with reduced liver transplant ("reduced size") used if pediatric donors (by Bismuth)
  • Advantage to resolve pediatric cases that need urgent liver transplantation

4. Deep studying of immune

tolerance

Brain death diagnosis → Brain death is equivalent to death of patient

Diagnosis has 3 steps

1. Determining causes of brain damage

2. Eliminating causes that can simulate brain death (hypothermia, neuro-depressant drugs)

3. Clinical testing (includes 12 reflex absence) and paraclinical (EEG, transcranialcerebral Doppler US, cerebral arteriography for the four main vessels)

Indications for liver transplant

  • Chronic liver disease in terminal stage
  • Acute liver failure
  • Acute hepatitis with liver failure
  • Primary unresectable tumors limited to the liver
  • Other metabolic liver diseases without therapeutic alternatives
  • Transplant rejection

Contraindications for liver transplant

Absolute

  • HIV, uncontrolled sepsis, severe pulmonary hypertension, liver CA, extrahepatic CA, advanced active alcoholism or drug addiction, severe brain damage (in acute liver failure)

Relative

  • Portal vein thrombosis, hep. B antigen positive and HBe positive, extreme ages, liver cancer, previous interventions of biliary tree
  • Compensated cirrhosis
  • Extrahepatic malignancy
  • Severe and uncontrolled extrahepatic infection
  • Advanced cardiopulmonary disease
  • Multisystem organ failure
  • Active substance abuse
  • Anatomic abnormalities that preclude performing surgical procedure of liver transplantation

Hepatic transplant involves

1. Heterotopic transplant

  • With total liver
  • With partial liver

2. Orthotopic

  • With total liver transplantation
  • With liver part → Orthotopic liver transplantation has become only method of transplanting with long-term survival Technical liver transplantation with cadaver graft
  • Starts with total hepatectomy of receiver
  • Hepatic pedicle dissection
  • Liver mobilization by dissecting round ligament, falciform ligament, coronary and triangular ligaments
  • ICV isolation – suprahepatic and subhepatic segments
  • Vascular exclusion of liver
  • Ablation of liver
  • Hemostasis after hepatectomy

Total orthotopic liver graft implantation involves 2 techniques

1. Standard technique by

  • Suprahepatic ICV anastomosis performed by two running- sutures
  • Subhepatic ICV anastomosis - anastomosis is much easier

2. Technical cavo-caval

  • Classic piggyback technique anastomosis with caval
  • Piggyback modifications vein preservation involves - Triangulating cavocavostomy

Next step

  • Involves making portal vein anastomosis and revascularization of graft
  • Then arterial and biliary reconstruction
  • On "reduced size" and “split-liver” transplant technique, liver divided into two parts that are used for two adult recipients
  • Another alternative is living donation transplantation (mainly in children when segments II & III taken from parent)
  • Domino liver transplantation - patient 1 undergoes liver transplantation and in turn donates his liver to another patient 2
  • Xenotransplantation - transplantation of liver from animal to human

Complications of liver transplantation

General

  • Respiratory complications (pulmonary edema, ARDS, pleural effusion)
  • Hematologic (lymphoproliferative diseases in transplanted patients)
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Diabetes
  • Osteodystrophy

Liver graft rejection

Hyperacute rejection

Acute rejection

Chronic rejection

Specific

1. Vascular complications: arterial thrombosis, vascular

stenosis, portal vein thrombosis, arterial aneurysms

2. Biliary complications: biliary fistula, stenosis

3. Postoperative: hemorrhage

  • Occurs rapidly (minutes to hours) triggered by preformed AB
  • Biliary epithelial lesions and intrahepatic biliary tract, manifested by inflammatory infiltrates
  • 10-15% develops a chronic rejection with irreversible reaction of arterioles from portal space + vascular ischemia and hepatocellular necrosis
  • Vanishing bile duct syndrome can be sometimes observed relatively quickly after transplant = important criteria for the diagnosis of chronic rejection
